Key properties:\n    52\t- Simple graph: no multi-edges, no self-loops\n    53\t- Complete graph K_n: every pair of vertices connected\n    54\t- Bipartite graph K_{m,n}: vertices split into two groups, edges only between groups\n    55\t- Tree: connected graph with no cycles; has exactly n-1 edges for n vertices\n    56\t\n    57\t**Pigeonhole principle:** If n objects are placed in k bins and n > k, at least one bin has at least ⌈n/k⌉ objects.\n    58\t\n    59\t**Handshaking lemma:** Σ_{v∈V} deg(v) = 2|E|.\n    60\t\n    61\t### 2.2 Matchings and Hall's Theorem\n    62\t\n    63\tA **matching** in a bipartite graph is a set of edges with no shared vertices.\n    64\t\n    65\t**Hall's marriage theorem:** A bipartite graph G = (A∪B, E) has a matching saturating all of A if and only if for every subset S ⊆ A, |N(S)| ≥ |S| (where N(S) is the neighborhood of S in B).\n    66\t\n    67\t**Perfect matching:** Matches every vertex. In K_{n,n}, there are n! perfect matchings.\n    68\t\n    69\t**Evaluation criterion:** When a proof claims a matching or bijection exists, it must either exhibit one explicitly or invoke Hall's theorem with verification of the Hall condition.\n    70\t\n    71\t---\n    72\t\n    73\t## Part III: Boolean Lattice and Subset Systems\n    74\t\n    75\t### 3.1 The Boolean Lattice\n    76\t\n    77\tThe power set 2^S of a set S = {1,...,n} with the partial order of inclusion forms the Boolean lattice B_n. Key properties:\n    78\t- |B_n| = 2^n\n    79\t- Ranked by cardinality: rank k level has C(n,k) elements\n    80\t- Graded poset with n+1 ranks\n    81\t\n    82\t**Intervals in the Boolean lattice:** For A ⊆ B ⊆ S, the interval [A,B] = {C : A⊆C⊆B} is isomorphic to B_{|B|-|A|} and has 2^{|B|-|A|} elements.\n    83\t\n    84\t### 3.2 Chains and Antichains\n    85\t\n    86\tA **chain** is a totally ordered subset (any two elements comparable). A **antichain** is a set of mutually incomparable elements (no containments).\n    87\t\n    88\t**Dilworth's theorem:** The minimum number of chains needed to cover the poset equals the maximum antichain size.\n    89\t\n    90\t**Sperner's theorem:** The maximum antichain in B_n has size C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) (take all subsets of size ⌊n/2⌋).\n    91\t\n    92\t### 3.3 Multiplicative Functions on the Boolean Lattice\n    93\t\n    94\tA function f: 2^S → ℝ is **multiplicative** over (∪, ∩) if f(T₁)·f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·f(T₁∩T₂) for all T₁,T₂ ⊆ S.\n    95\t\n    96\tThis is a strong structural condition. Not every function satisfying this for \"many pairs\" satisfies it for all pairs.\n    97\t\n    98\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof that f satisfies the multiplicative condition must verify it for ALL pairs (T₁, T₂), not just specific families. The verification \"one checks by routine computation\" is a placeholder that must be backed by an actual argument. If the proof leaves this verification implicit and it is genuinely non-trivial, this constitutes a critical skipped step.\n    99\t\n   100\t**Characterization theorem:** The non-negative functions f: 2^S → ℝ satisfying f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) are exactly those of the form f(T) = 2^{|T∩A|} for some A⊆S (when f(∅)=1), or f(T) = χ_{[U,U∪A']}(T) extended multiplicatively (when f(∅)=0).\n   101\t\n   102\t### 3.4 Möbius Inversion on the Boolean Lattice\n   103\t\n   104\tThe Möbius function for the Boolean lattice B_n is μ(A,B) = (-1)^{|B|-|A|} for A ⊆ B.\n   105\t\n   106\t**Inversion formula:** If g(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} f(U) for all T, then f(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} g(U).\n   107\t\n   108\t**Application to blue-set counting:** If f(T) = #{blue subsets of T}, then the indicator of whether T itself is blue is:\n   109\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} f(U)\n   110\t\n   111\tThis is the Möbius inversion of f (where f(T) = Σ_{U∈B, U⊆T} 1 = Σ_{U⊆T} 1_B(U) is the cumulative count).\n   112\t\n   113\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof using Möbius inversion must correctly state and apply the inversion formula. An error in the formula (wrong signs, wrong indexing) is a material issue. However, the inversion step itself is \"routine\" and may be cited as a known fact without re-proof in a competition context.\n   114\t\n   115\t---\n   116\t\n   117\t## Part IV: Extremal Combinatorics\n   118\t\n   119\t### 4.1 Optimization with Distinct Elements\n   120\t\n   121\t**Basic setup:** Given n distinct positive integers a₁ < a₂ < ... < aₙ, find the minimum value of max(Σ_{i∈I} aᵢ) or other extremal quantities subject to conditions on subset sums.\n   122\t\n   123\t**Key principle:** For k-element subsets, the one with the largest sum consists of the k largest elements {a_{n-k+1}, ..., aₙ}. The one with the smallest sum consists of the k smallest elements {a₁, ..., aₖ}.\n   124\t\n   125\t**Common technique:** Set a_{m} = c (the \"median\" element), then use inequalities:\n   126\t- a_{m-1} ≤ c-1, a_{m-2} ≤ c-2, ..., a_{m-k} ≤ c-k\n   127\t- a_{m+1} ≥ c+1, a_{m+2} ≥ c+2, ..., a_{m+k} ≥ c+k\n   128\t\n   129\tThese give lower and upper bounds on partial sums, which then constrain the possible values of c.\n   130\t\n   131\t### 4.2 Minimality Arguments\n   132\t\n   133\t**Technique:** To show that a minimum value of some parameter is N:\n   134\t1. **Existence:** Construct a configuration achieving the value N\n   135\t2. **Lower bound:** Show no configuration achieves a value less than N\n   136\t\n   137\tFor (1), the construction must be verified to satisfy ALL the problem's conditions. For (2), the argument must work for GENERAL configurations satisfying the problem's conditions, not just special cases.\n   138\t\n   139\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof that omits the existence direction (just shows the lower bound) proves an upper bound on the minimum, not the minimum itself. A proof that omits the lower bound just gives an example. Both directions are REQUIRED for a complete proof.\n   140\t\n   141\t### 4.3 The Role of Strict vs Non-Strict Inequalities\n   142\t\n   143\tWhen bounding a sum sum_{i=1}^k a_i ≤ kc - k(k+1)/2 (where c is the (k+1)-th element and the elements are distinct integers), the bound comes from:\n   144\ta₁ ≤ c-k, a₂ ≤ c-k+1, ..., aₖ ≤ c-1, so sum ≤ Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ (c-k+i-1) = kc - k(k+1)/2.\n   145\t\n   146\tThis is a UPPER BOUND. The lower bound for a_{k+1},...,a_{2k} uses: a_{k+1+j} ≥ c+j for j=1,...,k.\n   147\t\n   148\t**Evaluation criterion:** Strict vs non-strict inequalities can change the answer by 1. In a minimality problem, if the minimum involves \"≥\" vs \">\" or \"=\" vs \"≤\", check that the proof's inequalities are of the right type.\n   149\t\n   150\t---\n   151\t\n   152\t## Part V: Combinatorial Designs and Constructions\n   153\t\n   154\t### 5.1 Existence Proofs via Explicit Construction\n   155\t\n   156\tWhen a problem asks to show a configuration exists with given properties, the proof must:\n   157\t1. Exhibit an explicit configuration\n   158\t2. Verify EVERY required property for that configuration\n   159\t3. (If asking for minimum) show no smaller/fewer configuration satisfies all properties\n   160\t\n   161\t**Common error:** Exhibiting a configuration and checking only a subset of the required properties, assuming the rest hold.\n   162\t\n   163\t### 5.2 General vs Special Case\n   164\t\n   165\tIf a problem asks to show that for all n (or all k), some property holds, the proof must work for GENERAL n (or k). A proof that only handles specific cases (e.g., n = 1, 2, 3) and extrapolates without justification has a critical gap.\n   166\t\n   167\t**Evaluation criterion:** If the proof shows existence/construction for specific values and claims \"similarly for other values\" or \"by analogous argument,\" check whether the argument is genuinely analogous. If the analogous argument requires non-trivial new ideas, citing it without providing it is a gap.\n   168\t\n   169\t### 5.3 Counting Configurations\n   170\t\n   171\tWhen counting configurations with multiple constraints:\n   172\t\n   173\t**Strategy 1 (Sequential):** Count the number of ways to make each choice in sequence, multiplying at each step (only if choices are independent or conditional counts are computed).\n   174\t\n   175\t**Strategy 2 (Characterize then count):** First show all valid configurations have a specific structural form, then count that form.\n   176\t\n   177\t**Evaluation criterion for Strategy 2:** The \"characterize\" step must be bidirectional:\n   178\t- (⇒) Every valid configuration has the claimed form\n   179\t- (⇐) Every configuration of the claimed form is valid\n   180\t\n   181\tMissing either direction means the count is wrong (either over-counting or under-counting).\n   182\t\n   183\t---\n   184\t\n   185\t## Part VI: Set Systems and Monotone Functions\n   186\t\n   187\t### 6.1 Intersecting Families\n   188\t\n   189\tA family F of sets is **intersecting** if any two members of F have a non-empty intersection. Equivalently, no two members are disjoint.\n   190\t\n   191\t**Key result:** Any intersecting antichain in 2^S has size ≤ C(n-1, ⌊(n-1)/2⌋) (Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem for uniform families).\n   192\t\n   193\tIn the context of proof evaluation, an intersecting family arises naturally from functional conditions like f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) with f(∅) = 0: this forces any two sets in the support of f to intersect.\n   194\t\n   195\t### 6.2 Upward-Closed and Downward-Closed Families\n   196\t\n   197\tA family F is **upward-closed (upset)** if whenever A ∈ F and A ⊆ B ⊆ S, then B ∈ F.\n   198\tA family F is **downward-closed (downset)** if whenever A ∈ F and B ⊆ A, then B ∈ F.\n   199\t\n   200\t**Evaluation criterion:** When a proof concludes that the support of a function is upward-closed from F = {T : T ⊇ U} for some minimal element U, this conclusion requires verifying:\n   201\t- U is indeed in F (f(U) > 0)\n   202\t- U is minimal in F (f(V) = 0 for all proper subsets V ⊊ U)\n   203\t- Any superset of U is in F (f(T) > 0 for all T ⊇ U)\n   204\t\n   205\tThe third point requires explicit verification from the functional condition.\n   206\t\n   207\t### 6.3 Chains in the Boolean Lattice and Order Ideals\n   208\t\n   209\tA **chain** A₀ ⊂ A₁ ⊂ ... ⊂ Aₙ with |Aᵢ| = i is called a **maximal chain** in B_n (since it has length n+1, the maximum possible). The number of maximal chains in B_n is n! (corresponding to the n! orderings of the elements of S).\n   210\t\n   211\t**Application:** When counting pairs of disjoint chains (A₀ ⊂ A₁ ⊂ ... ⊂ Aₙ) and (B₀ ⊂ B₁ ⊂ ... ⊂ Bₙ) with A_n ∩ B_n = ∅ in B_{2n}:\n   212\t1. Choose A_n: C(2n, n) ways (any n-element subset)\n   213\t2. B_n is forced (= complement of A_n since |B_n| = n and A_n ∩ B_n = ∅ and A_n ∪ B_n = {1,...,2n} when n+n = 2n)\n   214\t3. Build the chain inside A_n: n! ways\n   215\t4. Build the chain inside B_n: n! ways\n   216\tTotal: C(2n,n)·n!·n! = (2n)!\n   217\t\n   218\t---\n   219\t\n   220\t## Part VII: Common Proof Structures in Combinatorics Problems\n   221\t\n   222\t### 7.1 Greedy Arguments\n   223\t\n   224\tA greedy algorithm makes locally optimal choices. A greedy proof must:\n   225\t1. Define the greedy choice precisely\n   226\t2. Show the greedy choice doesn't preclude future valid choices (exchange argument or augmenting path argument)\n   227\t3. Show the result of the greedy algorithm has the required properties\n   228\t\n   229\t**Common error:** Assuming greedy is optimal without proving the exchange argument.\n   230\t\n   231\t### 7.2 Induction on Problem Parameters\n   232\t\n   233\t**Base case:** Verify the claim for the smallest valid parameter (n=1, k=0, etc.).\n   234\t\n   235\t**Inductive step:** Assume the claim for all values ≤ n-1, prove for n. The reduction from n to n-1 (or n-k) must be carefully justified.\n   236\t\n   237\t**Evaluation criterion:** If the inductive step says \"apply the induction hypothesis,\" verify that:\n   238\t- The hypothesis applies (the smaller problem satisfies the induction's hypotheses)\n   239\t- The conclusion for the smaller problem correctly implies the conclusion for the larger\n   240\t\n   241\t### 7.3 Extremal Arguments\n   242\t\n   243\t**Setup:** Take an element/configuration with a specific extremal property (minimal, maximal, etc.).\n   244\t\n   245\t**Technique:** Use the extremality to derive structural properties.\n   246\t\n   247\t**Evaluation criterion:** If a proof takes a \"minimal element U in the support of f\" (for example), it must verify that such a minimal element exists (the support is non-empty) and that minimality gives the claimed structure.\n   248\t\n   249\t### 7.4 Bijective Proofs\n   250\t\n   251\tA bijection between two sets proves they have the same cardinality. A bijective proof must:\n   252\t1. Define the map explicitly\n   253\t2. Show it is well-defined (maps valid objects to valid objects)\n   254\t3. Show it is injective (different inputs give different outputs)\n   255\t4. Show it is surjective (every valid output is achieved)\n   256\t\n   257\t**Alternative:** Show the map is a bijection by finding a two-sided inverse.\n   258\t\n   259\t---\n   260\t\n   261\t## Part VIII: Specific Problem Type Guidance\n   262\t\n   263\t### 8.1 Coloring Problems with Multiplicative Condition (proof_13 type)\n   264\t\n   265\t**Problem type:** Color subsets of S blue or red, count colorings where f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) for all T₁,T₂ ⊆ S.\n   266\t\n   267\t**Standard case split:** f(∅) = 1 (empty set is blue) vs f(∅) = 0 (empty set is red).\n   268\t\n   269\t**Case 1 (f(∅)=1):**\n   270\t- For i ∉ T: apply functional condition with T₁ = {i}, T₂ = T to get f({i})·f(T) = f(T∪{i})·f(∅) = f(T∪{i})\n   271\t- This gives f(T∪{i}) = λᵢ·f(T) where λᵢ = f({i})\n   272\t- By induction: f(T) = Π_{i∈T} λᵢ = Π_{i∈T} f({i})\n   273\t- Möbius inversion then recovers the blue sets exactly as subsets of A = {i : λᵢ = 2}\n   274\t- Converse: verify that coloring B = P(A) satisfies the multiplicativity for all T₁, T₂\n   275\t\n   276\t**Critical verification in Case 1 (often skipped):** The Möbius inversion step gives the blue set indicator, but one must verify that this formula gives 0 or 1 (not other values), and that the resulting B satisfies the original multiplicativity. This computation is:\n   277\t\n   278\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} f(U) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} · 2^{|U∩A|}\n   279\t\n   280\tLet T∩A = T_A and T\\A = T_B. For U ⊆ T: U = U_A ∪ U_B with U_A ⊆ T_A and U_B ⊆ T_B. Then:\n   281\t\n   282\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U_A⊆T_A, U_B⊆T_B} (-1)^{|T_A|+|T_B|-|U_A|-|U_B|} · 2^{|U_A|}\n   283\t        = [Σ_{U_A⊆T_A} (-1)^{|T_A|-|U_A|} 2^{|U_A|}] · [Σ_{U_B⊆T_B} (-1)^{|T_B|-|U_B|}]\n   284\t\n   285\tThe second factor = Σ_{k=0}^{|T_B|} C(|T_B|,k)(-1)^{|T_B|-k} = (1-1)^{|T_B|} = 0^{|T_B|}.\n   286\t\n   287\tSo 1_B(T) = 0 if |T_B| > 0, i.e., if T ⊄ A.\n   288\tIf T ⊆ A, then T_B = ∅, so 1_B(T) = Σ_{U_A⊆T_A} (-1)^{|T_A|-|U_A|} 2^{|U_A|} = (2-1)^{|T_A|} = 1.\n   289\t\n   290\tSo 1_B(T) = 1 if T ⊆ A and 0 otherwise, i.e., B = P(A). ✓\n   291\t\n   292\t**This computation verifies Case 1.** A proof that only claims \"one checks\" without this computation has a minor omission (the computation is straightforward).\n   293\t\n   294\t**Case 2 (f(∅)=0):** \n   295\t- Functional condition with T₂ disjoint from T₁: f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·f(∅) = 0\n   296\t- So for any T₁, T₂ in the support of f, T₁∩T₂ ≠ ∅ (support is intersecting)\n   297\t- Take minimal element U in support; show f(U) = 1, B∩P(U) = {U}, support = {T : T⊇U}\n   298\t- Reduce to Case 1 on S' = S\\U via g(W) = f(U∪W)\n   299\t- Converse: verify that any interval [U, U∪A'] satisfies multiplicativity for ALL pairs T₁, T₂ ⊆ S\n   300\t\n   301\t**Critical gap in Case 2 converse:** If the proof claims \"one checks that [U, U∪A'] satisfies the condition\" without doing the check, and the check is non-trivial, this is a critical skipped step.\n   302\t\n   303\t**The check:** For B = [U, U∪A'], we have f(T) = g(T\\U)·χ_{T⊇U}(T) where g(W) = 2^{|W∩A'|}. For arbitrary T₁, T₂ ⊆ S:\n   304\t- If T₁ ⊅ U or T₂ ⊅ U: then at least one of f(T₁), f(T₂) equals 0. Also T₁∪T₂ may or may not ⊇ U, and T₁∩T₂ ⊇ U only if both T₁,T₂ ⊇ U (which fails). So at least one of f(T₁∪T₂), f(T₁∩T₂) = 0. The condition 0·f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·0 becomes 0 = 0 or 0 = 0. ✓\n   305\t- If T₁ ⊇ U and T₂ ⊇ U: then T₁∪T₂ ⊇ U and T₁∩T₂ ⊇ U. Let W₁ = T₁\\U, W₂ = T₂\\U. Then f(Tᵢ) = g(Wᵢ) = 2^{|Wᵢ∩A'|} and similarly. The condition becomes g(W₁)g(W₂) = g(W₁∪W₂)g(W₁∩W₂), i.e., 2^{|W₁∩A'|}·2^{|W₂∩A'|} = 2^{|(W₁∪W₂)∩A'|}·2^{|(W₁∩W₂)∩A'|}. This holds because |W₁∩A'|+|W₂∩A'| = |(W₁∩A')∪(W₂∩A')|+|(W₁∩A')∩(W₂∩A')| = |(W₁∪W₂)∩A'|+|(W₁∩W₂)∩A'| (using |A|+|B| = |A∪B|+|A∩B| for any finite sets). ✓\n   306\t\n   307\tSo the converse IS valid and checkable — but it requires this computation. The proof's \"one checks by routine verification\" is in fact routine (as shown above). However, an auditor must distinguish between (a) \"the proof says one checks and the check is indeed routine/trivial\" (= minor omission, proof essentially correct) and (b) \"the proof says one checks and the check is non-trivial and was actually skipped\" (= critical gap).\n   308\t\n   309\t**Verdict guidance for this problem type:** If the converse verification is ONLY cited as \"one checks\" and similar phrases appear at multiple critical steps, the cumulative effect of all the skipped steps determines the verdict.\n   310\t\n   311\t### 8.2 Grid/Matrix Set Systems with Monotonicity (proof_15 type)\n   312\t\n   313\t**Problem type:** Count collections {S_{ij}} with |S_{ij}| = i+j and S_{ij} ⊆ S_{kl} when i≤k, j≤l.\n   314\t\n   315\t**Standard reduction:** Write A_i = S_{i,0} and B_j = S_{0,j}. By monotonicity:\n   316\t- A_i = S_{i,0} ⊆ S_{i,j}\n   317\t- B_j = S_{0,j} ⊆ S_{i,j}\n   318\t- Hence A_i ∪ B_j ⊆ S_{i,j}\n   319\t- |A_i∪B_j| ≤ |A_i|+|B_j| = i+j = |S_{ij}|\n   320\t\n   321\tThe conclusion S_{ij} = A_i ∪ B_j requires |A_i∪B_j| = i+j, which requires A_i ∩ B_j = ∅.\n   322\t\n   323\t**Critical point:** The argument \"|A_i∪B_j| ≤ i+j = |S_{ij}| implies S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j\" is INVALID without additionally knowing |A_i∪B_j| = i+j. The bound |A_i∪B_j| ≤ i+j combined with A_i∪B_j ⊆ S_{ij} and |S_{ij}| = i+j shows A_i∪B_j ⊆ S_{ij} with |A_i∪B_j| ≤ |S_{ij}|. But this does NOT imply equality — it only shows A_i∪B_j could be a proper subset of S_{ij}.\n   324\t\n   325\tTo CORRECTLY conclude S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j, one needs |A_i∪B_j| = i+j, which requires A_i∩B_j = ∅. Uniqueness follows from Euclid's lemma: if p is prime and p | ab, then p | a or p | b. This prevents cancellation of distinct prime factors.\n    14\t\n    15\t**Common errors:** Proofs that use unique factorization without explicitly invoking Euclid's lemma, treating the uniqueness as \"obvious,\" will have a logical gap if the problem's context does not make unique factorization automatic.\n    16\t\n    17\t### 1.2 Greatest Common Divisor and Bézout's Identity\n    18\t\n    19\tFor integers a and b not both zero, gcd(a, b) is the largest positive integer dividing both. Bézout's identity states: there exist integers x, y such that ax + by = gcd(a, b). The extended Euclidean algorithm computes these coefficients explicitly.\n    20\t\n    21\t**Key consequence:** gcd(a, b) = 1 if and only if there exist x, y with ax + by = 1, i.e., a has a multiplicative inverse mod b.\n    22\t\n    23\t**Evaluation note:** When a proof claims \"since gcd(a,b)=1, we may invert a modulo b,\" this is valid only if the proof has already established or been given that gcd(a,b)=1. Addition and multiplication are compatible with this equivalence: if a ≡ a' (mod m) and b ≡ b' (mod m) then a+b ≡ a'+b' and ab ≡ a'b' (mod m).\n    28\t\n    29\t**Modular inverse:** The inverse of a modulo m exists if and only if gcd(a, m) = 1. When m = p is prime, every nonzero element has a unique inverse in {1, ..., p-1}.\n    30\t\n    31\t**Fermat's Little Theorem.** If p is prime and p ∤ a, then a^{p-1} ≡ 1 (mod p).\n    32\t\n    33\t**Proof.** The map x ↦ ax is a bijection on {1, ..., p-1} (since gcd(a,p)=1). Consider the multiplicative group G = (Z/pZ)*, which has order p-1. Each element a ∈ G has a unique inverse a⁻¹ ∈ G. The equation a² ≡ 1 (mod p) means p | (a-1)(a+1), so by primality p | a-1 or p | a+1, giving a ≡ ±1 (mod p). Therefore in G, only 1 and p-1 are self-inverse. Pairing all other elements {2, 3, ..., p-2} with their distinct inverses, the product of each pair is 1. Hence (p-1)! ≡ 1·(p-1)·1 ≡ -1 (mod p). □\n    42\t\n    43\t**Proof (⇐).** Suppose (n-1)! ≡ -1 (mod n). If n = ab with 1 < a,b < n, then a | (n-1)! and a | n, so a | 1. Contradiction. Key properties:\n    82\t\n    83\t**Norm:** N(a + bi) = a² + b² = (a+bi)(a-bi). The norm is multiplicative: N(αβ) = N(α)N(β).\n    84\t\n    85\t**Units:** The units of Z[i] are exactly the elements with norm 1: {±1, ±i}.\n    86\t\n    87\t**Gaussian primes:** An element π ∈ Z[i] \\ {0} is a Gaussian prime if π = αβ implies α or β is a unit. The Gaussian primes are:\n    88\t- (1+i) and its associates (since N(1+i) = 2)\n    89\t- p + 0i for rational primes p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (inert primes)\n    90\t- a + bi where a² + b² = p for rational primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and p = 2 (split primes)\n    91\t\n    92\t**Unique factorization:** Z[i] is a Euclidean domain (division algorithm with Euclidean function N), hence a PID and UFD. This follows from N(αβ) = N(α)N(β) in Z[i].\n   102\t\n   103\t### 2.3 The Identity X⁴ + Y⁴ in Z[i]\n   104\t\n   105\tThe factorization X⁴ + Y⁴ = (X² + iY²)(X² - iY²) = (X²+iY²)·\\overline{(X²+iY²)} is fundamental to many olympiad problems involving fourth powers.\n   106\t\n   107\t**Key point:** X² + iY² and X² - iY² are complex conjugates. Their product is X⁴ + Y⁴ ∈ Z.\n   108\t\n   109\t**Coprimality condition:** gcd(X²+iY², X²-iY²) in Z[i] divides their difference 2iY² and their sum 2X². If gcd(X,Y) = 1 in Z, one must still carefully analyze which Gaussian primes can divide both X²+iY² and X²-iY².\n   110\t\n   111\t**UFD consequence:** If X²+iY² and X²-iY² are coprime in Z[i] and their product = α⁵ for some α ∈ Z[i], then each factor must itself be a fifth power (times a unit) in Z[i].\n   112\t\n   113\t**Critical subtlety:** Establishing coprimality of X²+iY² and X²-iY² requires checking that no Gaussian prime divides both. A common approach: any common divisor γ divides both (X²+iY²)+(X²-iY²) = 2X² and (X²+iY²)-(X²-iY²) = 2iY². If γ is not an associate of (1+i), then γ | X² and γ | Y², which combined with gcd(X,Y)=1 in Z gives a contradiction.\n   114\t\n   115\t**Evaluation criteria for Gaussian integer proofs:**\n   116\t- Must explicitly verify coprimality of the two conjugate factors, not just assert it\n   117\t- Must correctly enumerate all units in Z[i] (not just ±1)\n   118\t- Must carefully handle the case of the ramified prime (1+i)\n   119\t- Conclusions about when two expressions \"must be fifth powers\" require verified coprimality + UFD\n   120\t- The claim \"since they are coprime and their product is an nth power, each is an nth power (times a unit)\" is valid in any UFD and may be stated without proof in an olympiad context\n   121\t\n   122\t### 2.4 Quadratic Residues and the Legendre Symbol\n   123\t\n   124\tFor odd prime p and integer a with p ∤ a, a is a **quadratic residue** modulo p if there exists x with x² ≡ a (mod p).\n   125\t\n   126\t**Legendre symbol:** (a/p) = 1 if a is a QR mod p, -1 if not, 0 if p | a.\n   127\t\n   128\t**Euler's criterion:** (a/p) ≡ a^{(p-1)/2} (mod p).\n   129\t\n   130\t**Quadratic reciprocity (Gauss):** For distinct odd primes p, q:\n   131\t(p/q)(q/p) = (-1)^{(p-1)(q-1)/4}\n   132\t\n   133\tSupplements: (-1/p) = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} and (2/p) = (-1)^{(p²-1)/8}.\n   134\t\n   135\t**Applications:** Quadratic residues determine which integers are represented by binary quadratic forms. The form x² + y² represents n if and only if every prime factor p ≡ 3 (mod 4) appears to an even power in n. This is equivalent to the Gaussian integer factorization of n having no inert prime factors to odd powers.\n   136\t\n   137\t---\n   138\t\n   139\t## Part III: Diophantine Equations and p-adic Methods\n   140\t\n   141\t### 3.1 Linear Diophantine Equations\n   142\t\n   143\tax + by = c has integer solutions if and only if gcd(a,b) | c. When solutions exist, the general solution is x = x₀ + (b/d)t, y = y₀ - (a/d)t for t ∈ Z, where d = gcd(a,b) and (x₀,y₀) is any particular solution.\n   144\t\n   145\t### 3.2 Pythagorean Triples\n   146\t\n   147\tInteger solutions to x² + y² = z² with gcd(x,y,z) = 1 and x,z > 0, y even are:\n   148\tx = m² - n², y = 2mn, z = m² + n²\n   149\tfor positive integers m > n with gcd(m,n) = 1 and m ≢ n (mod 2).\n   150\t\n   151\t### 3.3 Fermat's Last Theorem Context\n   152\t\n   153\tFor n ≥ 3, the equation xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no solutions in positive integers. The proof for n = 4 (Fermat himself) and n = 3 (Euler) uses infinite descent. The general case is Wiles's theorem (1995). In olympiad contexts, fourth-power problems often use Gaussian integer factorizations.\n   154\t\n   155\t### 3.4 Valuation Theory\n   156\t\n   157\tThe p-adic valuation v_p(n) is the exponent of p in the prime factorization of n. Properties:\n   158\t- v_p(ab) = v_p(a) + v_p(b)\n   159\t- v_p(a+b) ≥ min(v_p(a), v_p(b)) with equality if v_p(a) ≠ v_p(b)\n   160\t- v_p(a^n) = n · v_p(a)\n   161\t\n   162\t**Divisibility by prime powers:** n | m if and only if v_p(n) ≤ v_p(m) for all primes p.\n   163\t\n   164\t**Common error:** Using v_p(a+b) = min(v_p(a), v_p(b)) when v_p(a) = v_p(b). In this case, v_p(a+b) could be strictly greater than min(v_p(a), v_p(b)).\n   165\t\n   166\t---\n   167\t\n   168\t## Part IV: Multiplicative Functions and Arithmetic Functions\n   169\t\n   170\t### 4.1 The Euler Totient Function\n   171\t\n   172\tφ(n) = |{1 ≤ k ≤ n : gcd(k,n)=1}|. Key properties:\n   173\t- φ(p) = p-1 for prime p\n   174\t- φ(p^k) = p^k - p^{k-1} = p^{k-1}(p-1) for prime power p^k\n   175\t- φ is multiplicative: gcd(m,n)=1 implies φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n)\n   176\t- Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n\n   177\t\n   178\t### 4.2 The Number and Sum of Divisors\n   179\t\n   180\tτ(n) = number of divisors of n, σ(n) = sum of divisors of n. Both are multiplicative. For prime power p^k: τ(p^k) = k+1, σ(p^k) = (p^{k+1}-1)/(p-1).\n   181\t\n   182\t### 4.3 Mobius Function and Inversion\n   183\t\n   184\tThe Möbius function: μ(1) = 1, μ(n) = (-1)^k if n is a product of k distinct primes, μ(n) = 0 if p² | n for some prime p.\n   185\t\n   186\t**Möbius inversion formula:** If f(n) = Σ_{d|n} g(d) then g(n) = Σ_{d|n} μ(n/d) f(d).\n   187\t\n   188\t---\n   189\t\n   190\t## Part V: Prime Distribution and Dirichlet's Theorem\n   191\t\n   192\t### 5.1 Dirichlet's Theorem on Primes in Arithmetic Progressions\n   193\t\n   194\tFor gcd(a,d) = 1, the arithmetic progression {a, a+d, a+2d, ...} contains infinitely many primes. Moreover, the primes are equidistributed among the φ(d) coprime residue classes modulo d.\n   195\t\n   196\t**Consequence:** If a property holds for all primes p > N, and it is asserted that only finitely many primes can satisfy a given fixed congruence condition, this requires careful use of Dirichlet's theorem or direct analysis of the fixed integer whose prime factors are at issue.\n   197\t\n   198\t**Key application:** If D is a fixed nonzero integer and we need p | D for all primes p in some infinite set, then D must be 0. This is because any nonzero integer has finitely many prime divisors. This principle is heavily used in the polynomial-prime divisibility problems.\n   199\t\n   200\t### 5.2 Chebyshev's Theorem\n   201\t\n   202\tThere is always a prime between n and 2n for n ≥ 1. This is weaker than PNT but sufficient for many olympiad applications.\n   203\t\n   204\t---\n   205\t\n   206\t## Part VI: Common Proof Structures in Number Theory Problems\n   207\t\n   208\t### 6.1 Infinite Descent\n   209\t\n   210\tUsed to show Diophantine equations have no positive integer solutions. Assume a minimal positive solution exists and derive a smaller solution, contradicting minimality.\n   211\t\n   212\t**Evaluation criterion:** The descent step must produce a strictly smaller (by well-ordering) solution. A proof that claims \"we can repeat this process\" without explicit minimality or termination is incomplete.\n   213\t\n   214\t### 6.2 Polynomial Congruences\n   215\t\n   216\tFor a polynomial f(x) ∈ Z[x] of degree d, the number of roots modulo prime p is at most d (by Lagrange's theorem). This is used to analyze when a polynomial vanishes at many primes.\n   217\t\n   218\t**Key lemma:** If f(p) ≡ 0 (mod p) for all primes p in an infinite set, and f has degree d < p for large p, then either f ≡ 0 or p | leading coefficient for infinitely many p (both impossible if leading coefficient is fixed nonzero). Hence f ≡ 0.\n   219\t\n   220\t**Stronger result:** If D(r) = 2(-1)^{r+1} + r! is a fixed integer and D(r) ≡ 0 (mod p) for all primes p > r, then D(r) = 0 (since only finitely many primes divide a fixed nonzero integer).\n   221\t\n   222\t### 6.3 Divisibility Chains\n   223\t\n   224\tWhen establishing p | f(n) for a prime p and fixed polynomial f, a common technique is:\n   225\t1. Write f(n) in terms of (n-1)! using Wilson's theorem\n   226\t2. Compute (n-r)! in terms of (n-1)! using the factorial identity\n   227\t3. Derive a fixed constant that must be ≡ 0 (mod p) for all large primes p\n   228\t4. Conclude the constant is 0\n   229\t\n   230\t**Evaluation criterion:** Step 4 requires the explicit argument that a fixed nonzero integer cannot be divisible by all sufficiently large primes. This is often stated as \"the only way infinitely many primes can divide a fixed integer is if that integer is zero.\" This argument is valid and may be stated briefly in a competition proof.\n   231\t\n   232\t### 6.4 Parameterization of Divisors\n   233\t\n   234\tWhen p^k | f(a,b) and p ∤ a and p ∤ b, we can sometimes factor f and analyze which prime power divides each factor separately. This often involves writing f(a,b) = g(a,b) · h(a,b) and showing gcd(g,h) | m for some explicit m.\n   235\t\n   236\t---\n   237\t\n   238\t## Part VII: Standard Techniques Specific to the Proofs in This Audit\n   239\t\n   240\t### 7.1 Polynomial Divisibility and Wilson's Theorem (proof_01 type)\n   241\t\n   242\t**Problem type:** Find all monic polynomials f ∈ Z[x] such that p | 2(f(p))!+1 for all large primes p.\n   243\t\n   244\t**Standard approach:**\n   245\t1. **Degree bound:** For deg f ≥ 2, f(p) ≥ p for large p, so p | (f(p))! and thus 2(f(p))!+1 ≡ 1 (mod p) ≠ 0. Eliminates deg ≥ 2.\n   246\t2. **Constant polynomials:** f ≡ 1 (monic degree 0) gives 2·1!+1 = 3, only finitely many primes divide 3. Contradiction.\n   247\t3. **Linear case:** f(x) = x+b. Positive b gives f(p) ≥ p → contradiction (same as deg ≥ 2). So b < 0, write b = -r, r > 0.\n   248\t4. **Wilson application:** (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)···(p-r)·(p-r-1)! ≡ (-1)^r r! · (p-r-1)! (mod p). Combined with (p-1)! ≡ -1: get (p-r-1)! ≡ (-1)^{r+1}/(r!) (mod p).\n   249\t5. **Fixed integer condition:** 2(p-r-1)!+1 ≡ 0 (mod p) translates to the fixed integer D_r = 2(-1)^{r+1} + r! ≡ 0 (mod p) for all large p. Hence D_r = 0.\n   250\t6. **Find r:** Check small r until D_r = 0. Only r = 3 works: 2(-1)^4 + 3! = 2+6? No wait, let me recheck.\n   251\t\n   252\tActually for D_r = 2(-1)^{r+1} + r! (before the multiply through by r!), the condition after multiplying is: r! · 2(-1)^{r+1} + (r!)² = 0, or ... let me be careful. The exact form of D_r depends on the precise derivation. The proof should arrive at a specific integer that must be zero, and then check r=1,2,3,...\n   253\t\n   254\t**Correctness check:** A correct proof must:\n   255\t- Correctly derive the exact fixed integer D_r involving r\n   256\t- Note that this being ≡ 0 (mod p) for all large p forces D_r = 0\n   257\t- Correctly compute the specific value of r that makes D_r = 0\n   258\t- Verify that this r gives a working polynomial f(x) = x - r\n   259\t\n   260\t**First error in flawed proofs:** If the proof arrives at the wrong equation for D_r (perhaps confusing (p-r-1)! with (p-r)!), the final equation to solve will be wrong and the claimed value of r will be incorrect.\n   261\t\n   262\t### 7.2 Gaussian Integer Factorization Problems (proof_06 type)\n   263\t\n   264\t**Problem type:** Given a⁴+b⁴ = c⁴+d⁴ = e⁵ with distinct positive integers, show ac+bd is composite (or more generally, analyze the algebraic structure).\n   265\t\n   266\t**Standard approach:**\n   267\t1. **Reduction:** By coprimality of a,b,c,d,e (if a common factor p existed, divide through and repeat), assume gcd = 1.\n   268\t2. **Factorization in Z[i]:** a⁴+b⁴ = (a²+ib²)(a²-ib²). Show these factors are coprime in Z[i].\n   269\t3. **UFD consequence:** Each factor is a fifth power times a unit: a²+ib² = ε·α⁵ for some α = u+vi ∈ Z[i] and unit ε.\n   270\t4. **Norm equation:** N(a²+ib²) = a⁴+b⁴ = e⁵. N(α⁵) = N(α)⁵ = (u²+v²)⁵. Hence e = u²+v².\n   271\t5. **Repeat for (c,d):** c²+id² = ε'·α⁵ for some unit ε'. Since both pairs factorize in terms of the same α = u+vi...\n   272\t\n   273\t**Critical subtlety:** At step 5, the claim that (c²+id²) must involve the SAME α as (a²+ib²) requires justification. Both (a²+ib²) and (c²+id²) equal fifth powers (times units) of Gaussian integers with norm e = u²+v². But different choices of unit ε could give genuinely different fifth-power Gaussian integers. The argument \"the assignment must swap because the pairs are distinct\" needs to be made rigorous.\n   274\t\n   275\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof that hand-waves the step \"hence the two factorizations must be related by swapping u+vi and u-vi\" without justifying why has a logical gap. Moreover, the conclusion c²=a², d²=-b² cannot hold for positive real a,b,c,d. If the proof DOES correctly derive a contradiction, the verdict is correct. If it makes an unjustified leap to derive this contradiction, the verdict is incorrect.\n   276\t\n   277\t### 7.3 Divisibility Congruences and Case Analysis (proof_10 type)\n   278\t\n   279\t**Problem type:** Prove or disprove that specific prime-power Diophantine equations have solutions.\n   280\t\n   281\t**Common structure:** Write the equation as p · f(q,b) = g(b) for primes p and q, then case-analyze on q = 2 vs q odd.\n   282\t\n   283\t**Evaluation criterion for case q=2:** The claim \"p | 4·7^b - 1 implies p = 3\" requires showing that 4·7^b ≡ 1 (mod p) has solutions only for p = 3. This requires either:\n   284\t(a) Computing ord_p(7) and checking divisibility conditions, OR\n   285\t(b) Direct case analysis for small primes\n   286\t\n   287\tSimply asserting the conclusion without either computation or case analysis is an unjustified gap.\n   288\t\n   289\t### 7.4 Algebraic Inequalities in Number Theory (proof_17 type)\n   290\t\n   291\t**Problem type:** Use algebraic inequalities to bound prime-related quantities.\n   292\t\n   293\t**Key principle:** When a proof uses an estimate like \"Kp^a < Mp^b\" for all positive p, both K and M must be explicitly computed, and the direction of the inequality must be verified for all relevant cases.\n   294\t\n   295\t**Common error:** Writing an inequality in the wrong direction (e.g., 27p² < 9p² is false for all positive p). This immediately invalidates any argument that depends on it.\n   296\t\n   297\t**Evaluation criterion:** Check every inequality claim. If any single inequality is in the wrong direction for the claimed values, the proof is incorrect at that step, regardless of whether the conclusion might be provable by other means.\n   298\t\n   299\t---\n   300\t\n   301\t## Part VIII: Evaluation Rubric Summary for Number Theory Proofs\n   302\t\n   303\tWhen evaluating a number theory proof in this audit, apply the following checklist:\n   304\t\n   305\t1. **Factual accuracy:** Are all theorems cited correctly? (Wilson, Fermat, Euler, LTE, QR)\n   306\t2. **Hypothesis completeness:** Are all hypotheses of each theorem explicitly verified before application?\n   307\t3. **Case completeness:** Are all cases covered? (Especially: what if q = 2? what if p = 2? what if the base case fails?)\n   308\t4. **Fixed-integer arguments:** When a fixed integer must be divisible by all large primes, is the conclusion \"hence the integer is 0\" correctly derived?\n   309\t5. **Coprimality:** When coprimality of two expressions is needed, is it proved or given?\n   310\t6. **UFD consequences:** When factoring in Z[i] or other number rings, is unique factorization correctly applied?\n   311\t7. **Direction of inequalities:** Are all stated inequalities in the correct direction for the claimed parameters?\n   312\t\n   313\tA proof with ANY false claim, unjustified transition, or missing critical case at any of these points should be marked **incorrect**, and the FIRST such occurrence is the first material issue.\n   314\t\n   315\t---\n   316\t\n   317\t## Part IX: Extended Examples of Correct and Incorrect Number Theory Reasoning\n   318\t\n   319\t### Example 1: Correct use of Wilson's Theorem\n   320\t\n   321\t**Claim:** For prime p > 5, p | (p-4)! + (p-3)·(p-4)!/p + ... \n   322\t\n   323\t**Approach:** Start from (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3)(p-4)! ≡ (-1)(-2)(-3)(p-4)! = -6(p-4)! (mod p). Since (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p), we get -6(p-4)! ≡ -1 (mod p), so (p-4)! ≡ (6)^{-1} ≡ (6)^{-1} (mod p). **This is a correct use of Wilson's theorem**, assuming the inverses exist (which they do for p > 3).\n   324\t\n   325\t### Example 2: Incorrect application — wrong formula\n   326\t\n   327\t**Claim:** (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)···(p-r) · (p-r)! (off-by-one error in factorial)\n   328\t\n   329\tThis is FALSE: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)···(p-r) · (p-r-1)!, not (p-r)!. An off-by-one error in the factorial formula would give a completely wrong value for D_r, leading to an incorrect determination of r.\n   330\t\n   331\t### Example 3: Correct coprimality argument in Z[i]\n   332\t\n   333\t**Claim:** gcd_{Z[i]}(a²+ib², a²-ib²) is a unit, given that a⁴+b⁴ = e⁵ and gcd(a,b) = 1.\n   334\t\n   335\t**Proof:** Let δ = gcd(a²+ib², a²-ib²). Then δ | (a²+ib²)-(a²-ib²) = 2ib². Also δ | (a²+ib²)+(a²-ib²) = 2a². So δ | gcd(2ib², 2a²) = 2·gcd(b², a²)·i. Since gcd(a,b) = 1, gcd(a²,b²) = 1 in Z, so δ | 2i. The only Gaussian prime dividing 2i = -i(1+i)² is (1+i). If (1+i) | (a²+ib²), then N(1+i)=2 | N(a²+ib²) = a⁴+b⁴ = e⁵, so 2 | e⁵, hence 2 | e. Then 2^5 | e⁵ = a⁴+b⁴. But if a and b are both odd, a⁴+b⁴ ≡ 1+1 = 2 (mod 4), not 0 (mod 32). Careful analysis shows (1+i) ∤ (a²+ib²) under the coprimality assumptions. **This is a correct argument.**\n   336\t\n   337\t### Example 4: Incorrect — overlooked unit ambiguity\n   338\t\n   339\t**Claim:** Since a²+ib² = (u+vi)⁵ and c²+id² = ε'(u+vi)⁵ for unit ε', and (a²,b²) ≠ (c²,d²), the unit ε' must be i or -i, forcing c² = -a², d² = b².\n   340\t\n   341\t**Error:** This doesn't follow. The unit ε' could be 1, -1, i, or -i. The case ε' = -1 gives c²+id² = -(u+vi)⁵ = (-u-vi)⁵... one needs to trace through each case systematically. Simply asserting \"it must be i or -i\" based on distinctness is an unjustified leap.\n   342\t\n   343\t### Example 5: Correct evaluation — catch the wrong inequality\n   344\t\n   345\t**Claim in proof:** \"Since 3(k+1)p² ≤ 9p² for k ≥ 2, we have...\"\n   346\t\n   347\t**Check:** 3(k+1) ≤ 9 iff k+1 ≤ 3 iff k ≤ 2. For k ≥ 2, we have k+1 ≥ 3 so 3(k+1) ≥ 9. The inequality is BACKWARDS for k ≥ 3. This is the first material issue.\n   348\t\n   349\t### Example 6: Correct handling of cases in divisibility\n   350\t\n   351\t**Claim:** For the equation 4p^k = 7^m + 1, analyzing case p = 2: we get 2^{k+2} = 7^m + 1. Modulo 4: 0 ≡ 7^m + 1 ≡ 3^m + 1 (mod 4). For m even: 3^m ≡ 1 (mod 4), so 3^m+1 ≡ 2 (mod 4), but 2^{k+2} ≡ 0 (mod 4) for k ≥ 0. Contradiction unless k+2 = 1 i.e. k = -1 (not valid). For m odd: 3^m ≡ 3 (mod 4), so 3^m+1 ≡ 0 (mod 4). OK so m must be odd. Continue: 2^{k+2} = 7^m+1 and m odd... **This is a correct case analysis approach** — systematically checking mod small numbers to constrain the variables.\n   352\t\n   353\t---\n   354\t\n   355\t## Part X: Summary of First Material Issues Commonly Found\n   356\t\n   357\tIn number theory proofs at olympiad level, the most common first material issues are:\n   358\t\n   359\t1. **Wrong inequality direction** — claimed \"a < b\" when actually a ≥ b for the values in question\n   360\t2. **Missing case** — analyzed case p odd but not p = 2 (or vice versa), or analyzed cases modulo 3 but missed a residue class\n   361\t3. **Unjustified divisibility claim** — said \"p | N implies p = q\" without showing why\n   362\t4. **Incorrect application of Wilson** — used wrong factorial or wrong parity of (-1)\n   363\t5. **Coprimality assumed, not proven** — applied UFD factoring without establishing coprimality\n   364\t6. **Wrong final value** — computed D_r = 0 for wrong r, claiming incorrect polynomial\n   365\t7. **Overlooked units in Z[i]** — in Gaussian integer arguments, forgot to account for all four units {1, -1, i, -i}\n   366\t8. **Circular case elimination** — \"proved\" case q=2 by assuming p=3 and checking consistency, rather than deriving p=3 from q=2\n   367\t\n   368\tAny of the above at the FIRST occurrence in a proof constitutes a material issue and should be reported as the first_material_issue_summary in your audit.\n   369\t\n   370\t---\n   371\t\n   372\t## Appendix A: Extended Worked Examples — Number Theory Proof Evaluation\n   373\t\n   374\t### A.1 Wilson's Theorem Applications — 20 Evaluation Scenarios\n   375\t\n   376\t**Scenario 1 (Correct).** Claim: \"For prime p > 3, p divides (p-2)! - 1.\"\n   377\tProof: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)! ≡ -1 (mod p). Also (p-1) ≡ -1 (mod p), so (-1)(p-2)! ≡ -1 (mod p), giving (p-2)! ≡ 1 (mod p). Hence p | (p-2)! - 1. Assessment: CORRECT. Uses Wilson properly, all steps valid.\n   378\t\n   379\t**Scenario 2 (Incorrect — wrong case boundary).** Claim: \"For prime p ≥ 2, p | (p-1)!+1.\"\n   380\tProof: By Wilson's theorem, (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p), so (p-1)!+1 ≡ 0 (mod p). Assessment: INCORRECT first material issue. For p = 2: (2-1)! = 1! = 1, and 1+1 = 2. 2|2 holds. But the proof works for all primes p ≥ 2. Actually CORRECT — Wilson holds for p=2: (2-1)! = 1 ≡ -1 ≡ 1 (mod 2), so (2-1)!+1 = 2 ≡ 0 (mod 2). So this proof is correct after all.\n   381\t\n   382\t**Scenario 3 (Incorrect — composite modulus).** Claim: \"15 | (15-1)! + 1 by Wilson's theorem.\"\n   383\tFirst material issue: Wilson's theorem requires p to be prime. 15 = 3×5 is not prime. In fact (14)! = 14·13·...·1 contains factors 3, 5, 6, 10, 15... wait, 15 ∤ {1,...,14}, but 3·5 = 15 ∤ any single element yet 3 and 5 are both in {1,...,14}. So 15 | 14! and 14!+1 ≡ 1 (mod 15) ≠ 0. INCORRECT: first issue is applying Wilson to non-prime 15.\n   384\t\n   385\t**Scenario 4 (Correct).** Claim: \"For prime p, ((p-1)/2)!² ≡ (-1)^{(p+1)/2} (mod p).\"\n   386\tProof: (p-1)! ≡ -1. Pair j with p-j for j=1,...,(p-1)/2. Product of each pair = j(p-j) ≡ j(-j) = -j² (mod p). Product of all pairs = Π_{j=1}^{(p-1)/2} (-j²) = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} · (((p-1)/2)!)². So (p-1)! = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} · (((p-1)/2)!)² ≡ -1. Hence (((p-1)/2)!)² ≡ (-1)^{(p+1)/2}. CORRECT.\n   387\t\n   388\t**Scenario 5 (Incorrect — off-by-one).** Claim: \"For prime p and r=3: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) · (p-3)!.\"\n   389\tFirst material issue: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3)(p-4)···1. Extracting the first 3 terms: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) · (p-4)!, NOT (p-3)!. The off-by-one error gives the wrong factorial: (p-3)! vs (p-4)!.\n   390\t\n   391\t**Scenario 6 (Correct).** Claim: \"Let D₃ = 2(-1)^4 + 3! = 2 + 6 = 8. Since D₃ ≠ 0, r = 3 is not a solution.\"\n   392\tThe correct formula is D_r = 2(-1)^r + (r-1)! and one checks r=3 gives D_3 = -2+2=0.\n   393\t\n   394\t**Scenario W7 (Correct — Wilson derivation step).** \"(p-1)! = product_{j=1}^{p-1} j = (product_{j=1}^{r} (p-j)) * (product_{j=1}^{p-r-1} j) = (product_{j=1}^r (-j) (mod p)) * (p-r-1)! = (-1)^r*r!*(p-r-1)! Key properties:\n    52\t- Simple graph: no multi-edges, no self-loops\n    53\t- Complete graph K_n: every pair of vertices connected\n    54\t- Bipartite graph K_{m,n}: vertices split into two groups, edges only between groups\n    55\t- Tree: connected graph with no cycles; has exactly n-1 edges for n vertices\n    56\t\n    57\t**Pigeonhole principle:** If n objects are placed in k bins and n > k, at least one bin has at least ⌈n/k⌉ objects.\n    58\t\n    59\t**Handshaking lemma:** Σ_{v∈V} deg(v) = 2|E|.\n    60\t\n    61\t### 2.2 Matchings and Hall's Theorem\n    62\t\n    63\tA **matching** in a bipartite graph is a set of edges with no shared vertices.\n    64\t\n    65\t**Hall's marriage theorem:** A bipartite graph G = (A∪B, E) has a matching saturating all of A if and only if for every subset S ⊆ A, |N(S)| ≥ |S| (where N(S) is the neighborhood of S in B).\n    66\t\n    67\t**Perfect matching:** Matches every vertex. In K_{n,n}, there are n! perfect matchings.\n    68\t\n    69\t**Evaluation criterion:** When a proof claims a matching or bijection exists, it must either exhibit one explicitly or invoke Hall's theorem with verification of the Hall condition.\n    70\t\n    71\t---\n    72\t\n    73\t## Part III: Boolean Lattice and Subset Systems\n    74\t\n    75\t### 3.1 The Boolean Lattice\n    76\t\n    77\tThe power set 2^S of a set S = {1,...,n} with the partial order of inclusion forms the Boolean lattice B_n. Key properties:\n    78\t- |B_n| = 2^n\n    79\t- Ranked by cardinality: rank k level has C(n,k) elements\n    80\t- Graded poset with n+1 ranks\n    81\t\n    82\t**Intervals in the Boolean lattice:** For A ⊆ B ⊆ S, the interval [A,B] = {C : A⊆C⊆B} is isomorphic to B_{|B|-|A|} and has 2^{|B|-|A|} elements.\n    83\t\n    84\t### 3.2 Chains and Antichains\n    85\t\n    86\tA **chain** is a totally ordered subset (any two elements comparable). A **antichain** is a set of mutually incomparable elements (no containments).\n    87\t\n    88\t**Dilworth's theorem:** The minimum number of chains needed to cover the poset equals the maximum antichain size.\n    89\t\n    90\t**Sperner's theorem:** The maximum antichain in B_n has size C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) (take all subsets of size ⌊n/2⌋).\n    91\t\n    92\t### 3.3 Multiplicative Functions on the Boolean Lattice\n    93\t\n    94\tA function f: 2^S → ℝ is **multiplicative** over (∪, ∩) if f(T₁)·f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·f(T₁∩T₂) for all T₁,T₂ ⊆ S.\n    95\t\n    96\tThis is a strong structural condition. Not every function satisfying this for \"many pairs\" satisfies it for all pairs.\n    97\t\n    98\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof that f satisfies the multiplicative condition must verify it for ALL pairs (T₁, T₂), not just specific families. The verification \"one checks by routine computation\" is a placeholder that must be backed by an actual argument. If the proof leaves this verification implicit and it is genuinely non-trivial, this constitutes a critical skipped step.\n    99\t\n   100\t**Characterization theorem:** The non-negative functions f: 2^S → ℝ satisfying f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) are exactly those of the form f(T) = 2^{|T∩A|} for some A⊆S (when f(∅)=1), or f(T) = χ_{[U,U∪A']}(T) extended multiplicatively (when f(∅)=0).\n   101\t\n   102\t### 3.4 Möbius Inversion on the Boolean Lattice\n   103\t\n   104\tThe Möbius function for the Boolean lattice B_n is μ(A,B) = (-1)^{|B|-|A|} for A ⊆ B.\n   105\t\n   106\t**Inversion formula:** If g(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} f(U) for all T, then f(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} g(U).\n   107\t\n   108\t**Application to blue-set counting:** If f(T) = #{blue subsets of T}, then the indicator of whether T itself is blue is:\n   109\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} f(U)\n   110\t\n   111\tThis is the Möbius inversion of f (where f(T) = Σ_{U∈B, U⊆T} 1 = Σ_{U⊆T} 1_B(U) is the cumulative count).\n   112\t\n   113\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof using Möbius inversion must correctly state and apply the inversion formula. An error in the formula (wrong signs, wrong indexing) is a material issue. However, the inversion step itself is \"routine\" and may be cited as a known fact without re-proof in a competition context.\n   114\t\n   115\t---\n   116\t\n   117\t## Part IV: Extremal Combinatorics\n   118\t\n   119\t### 4.1 Optimization with Distinct Elements\n   120\t\n   121\t**Basic setup:** Given n distinct positive integers a₁ < a₂ < ... < aₙ, find the minimum value of max(Σ_{i∈I} aᵢ) or other extremal quantities subject to conditions on subset sums.\n   122\t\n   123\t**Key principle:** For k-element subsets, the one with the largest sum consists of the k largest elements {a_{n-k+1}, ..., aₙ}. The one with the smallest sum consists of the k smallest elements {a₁, ..., aₖ}.\n   124\t\n   125\t**Common technique:** Set a_{m} = c (the \"median\" element), then use inequalities:\n   126\t- a_{m-1} ≤ c-1, a_{m-2} ≤ c-2, ..., a_{m-k} ≤ c-k\n   127\t- a_{m+1} ≥ c+1, a_{m+2} ≥ c+2, ..., a_{m+k} ≥ c+k\n   128\t\n   129\tThese give lower and upper bounds on partial sums, which then constrain the possible values of c.\n   130\t\n   131\t### 4.2 Minimality Arguments\n   132\t\n   133\t**Technique:** To show that a minimum value of some parameter is N:\n   134\t1. **Existence:** Construct a configuration achieving the value N\n   135\t2. **Lower bound:** Show no configuration achieves a value less than N\n   136\t\n   137\tFor (1), the construction must be verified to satisfy ALL the problem's conditions. For (2), the argument must work for GENERAL configurations satisfying the problem's conditions, not just special cases.\n   138\t\n   139\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof that omits the existence direction (just shows the lower bound) proves an upper bound on the minimum, not the minimum itself. A proof that omits the lower bound just gives an example. Both directions are REQUIRED for a complete proof.\n   140\t\n   141\t### 4.3 The Role of Strict vs Non-Strict Inequalities\n   142\t\n   143\tWhen bounding a sum sum_{i=1}^k a_i ≤ kc - k(k+1)/2 (where c is the (k+1)-th element and the elements are distinct integers), the bound comes from:\n   144\ta₁ ≤ c-k, a₂ ≤ c-k+1, ..., aₖ ≤ c-1, so sum ≤ Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ (c-k+i-1) = kc - k(k+1)/2.\n   145\t\n   146\tThis is a UPPER BOUND. The lower bound for a_{k+1},...,a_{2k} uses: a_{k+1+j} ≥ c+j for j=1,...,k.\n   147\t\n   148\t**Evaluation criterion:** Strict vs non-strict inequalities can change the answer by 1. In a minimality problem, if the minimum involves \"≥\" vs \">\" or \"=\" vs \"≤\", check that the proof's inequalities are of the right type.\n   149\t\n   150\t---\n   151\t\n   152\t## Part V: Combinatorial Designs and Constructions\n   153\t\n   154\t### 5.1 Existence Proofs via Explicit Construction\n   155\t\n   156\tWhen a problem asks to show a configuration exists with given properties, the proof must:\n   157\t1. Exhibit an explicit configuration\n   158\t2. Verify EVERY required property for that configuration\n   159\t3. (If asking for minimum) show no smaller/fewer configuration satisfies all properties\n   160\t\n   161\t**Common error:** Exhibiting a configuration and checking only a subset of the required properties, assuming the rest hold.\n   162\t\n   163\t### 5.2 General vs Special Case\n   164\t\n   165\tIf a problem asks to show that for all n (or all k), some property holds, the proof must work for GENERAL n (or k). A proof that only handles specific cases (e.g., n = 1, 2, 3) and extrapolates without justification has a critical gap.\n   166\t\n   167\t**Evaluation criterion:** If the proof shows existence/construction for specific values and claims \"similarly for other values\" or \"by analogous argument,\" check whether the argument is genuinely analogous. If the analogous argument requires non-trivial new ideas, citing it without providing it is a gap.\n   168\t\n   169\t### 5.3 Counting Configurations\n   170\t\n   171\tWhen counting configurations with multiple constraints:\n   172\t\n   173\t**Strategy 1 (Sequential):** Count the number of ways to make each choice in sequence, multiplying at each step (only if choices are independent or conditional counts are computed).\n   174\t\n   175\t**Strategy 2 (Characterize then count):** First show all valid configurations have a specific structural form, then count that form.\n   176\t\n   177\t**Evaluation criterion for Strategy 2:** The \"characterize\" step must be bidirectional:\n   178\t- (⇒) Every valid configuration has the claimed form\n   179\t- (⇐) Every configuration of the claimed form is valid\n   180\t\n   181\tMissing either direction means the count is wrong (either over-counting or under-counting).\n   182\t\n   183\t---\n   184\t\n   185\t## Part VI: Set Systems and Monotone Functions\n   186\t\n   187\t### 6.1 Intersecting Families\n   188\t\n   189\tA family F of sets is **intersecting** if any two members of F have a non-empty intersection. Equivalently, no two members are disjoint.\n   190\t\n   191\t**Key result:** Any intersecting antichain in 2^S has size ≤ C(n-1, ⌊(n-1)/2⌋) (Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem for uniform families).\n   192\t\n   193\tIn the context of proof evaluation, an intersecting family arises naturally from functional conditions like f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) with f(∅) = 0: this forces any two sets in the support of f to intersect.\n   194\t\n   195\t### 6.2 Upward-Closed and Downward-Closed Families\n   196\t\n   197\tA family F is **upward-closed (upset)** if whenever A ∈ F and A ⊆ B ⊆ S, then B ∈ F.\n   198\tA family F is **downward-closed (downset)** if whenever A ∈ F and B ⊆ A, then B ∈ F.\n   199\t\n   200\t**Evaluation criterion:** When a proof concludes that the support of a function is upward-closed from F = {T : T ⊇ U} for some minimal element U, this conclusion requires verifying:\n   201\t- U is indeed in F (f(U) > 0)\n   202\t- U is minimal in F (f(V) = 0 for all proper subsets V ⊊ U)\n   203\t- Any superset of U is in F (f(T) > 0 for all T ⊇ U)\n   204\t\n   205\tThe third point requires explicit verification from the functional condition.\n   206\t\n   207\t### 6.3 Chains in the Boolean Lattice and Order Ideals\n   208\t\n   209\tA **chain** A₀ ⊂ A₁ ⊂ ... ⊂ Aₙ with |Aᵢ| = i is called a **maximal chain** in B_n (since it has length n+1, the maximum possible). The number of maximal chains in B_n is n! (corresponding to the n! orderings of the elements of S).\n   210\t\n   211\t**Application:** When counting pairs of disjoint chains (A₀ ⊂ A₁ ⊂ ... ⊂ Aₙ) and (B₀ ⊂ B₁ ⊂ ... ⊂ Bₙ) with A_n ∩ B_n = ∅ in B_{2n}:\n   212\t1. Choose A_n: C(2n, n) ways (any n-element subset)\n   213\t2. B_n is forced (= complement of A_n since |B_n| = n and A_n ∩ B_n = ∅ and A_n ∪ B_n = {1,...,2n} when n+n = 2n)\n   214\t3. Build the chain inside A_n: n! ways\n   215\t4. Build the chain inside B_n: n! ways\n   216\tTotal: C(2n,n)·n!·n! = (2n)!\n   217\t\n   218\t---\n   219\t\n   220\t## Part VII: Common Proof Structures in Combinatorics Problems\n   221\t\n   222\t### 7.1 Greedy Arguments\n   223\t\n   224\tA greedy algorithm makes locally optimal choices. A greedy proof must:\n   225\t1. Define the greedy choice precisely\n   226\t2. Show the greedy choice doesn't preclude future valid choices (exchange argument or augmenting path argument)\n   227\t3. Show the result of the greedy algorithm has the required properties\n   228\t\n   229\t**Common error:** Assuming greedy is optimal without proving the exchange argument.\n   230\t\n   231\t### 7.2 Induction on Problem Parameters\n   232\t\n   233\t**Base case:** Verify the claim for the smallest valid parameter (n=1, k=0, etc.).\n   234\t\n   235\t**Inductive step:** Assume the claim for all values ≤ n-1, prove for n. The reduction from n to n-1 (or n-k) must be carefully justified.\n   236\t\n   237\t**Evaluation criterion:** If the inductive step says \"apply the induction hypothesis,\" verify that:\n   238\t- The hypothesis applies (the smaller problem satisfies the induction's hypotheses)\n   239\t- The conclusion for the smaller problem correctly implies the conclusion for the larger\n   240\t\n   241\t### 7.3 Extremal Arguments\n   242\t\n   243\t**Setup:** Take an element/configuration with a specific extremal property (minimal, maximal, etc.).\n   244\t\n   245\t**Technique:** Use the extremality to derive structural properties.\n   246\t\n   247\t**Evaluation criterion:** If a proof takes a \"minimal element U in the support of f\" (for example), it must verify that such a minimal element exists (the support is non-empty) and that minimality gives the claimed structure.\n   248\t\n   249\t### 7.4 Bijective Proofs\n   250\t\n   251\tA bijection between two sets proves they have the same cardinality. A bijective proof must:\n   252\t1. Define the map explicitly\n   253\t2. Show it is well-defined (maps valid objects to valid objects)\n   254\t3. Show it is injective (different inputs give different outputs)\n   255\t4. Show it is surjective (every valid output is achieved)\n   256\t\n   257\t**Alternative:** Show the map is a bijection by finding a two-sided inverse.\n   258\t\n   259\t---\n   260\t\n   261\t## Part VIII: Specific Problem Type Guidance\n   262\t\n   263\t### 8.1 Coloring Problems with Multiplicative Condition (proof_13 type)\n   264\t\n   265\t**Problem type:** Color subsets of S blue or red, count colorings where f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) for all T₁,T₂ ⊆ S.\n   266\t\n   267\t**Standard case split:** f(∅) = 1 (empty set is blue) vs f(∅) = 0 (empty set is red).\n   268\t\n   269\t**Case 1 (f(∅)=1):**\n   270\t- For i ∉ T: apply functional condition with T₁ = {i}, T₂ = T to get f({i})·f(T) = f(T∪{i})·f(∅) = f(T∪{i})\n   271\t- This gives f(T∪{i}) = λᵢ·f(T) where λᵢ = f({i})\n   272\t- By induction: f(T) = Π_{i∈T} λᵢ = Π_{i∈T} f({i})\n   273\t- Möbius inversion then recovers the blue sets exactly as subsets of A = {i : λᵢ = 2}\n   274\t- Converse: verify that coloring B = P(A) satisfies the multiplicativity for all T₁, T₂\n   275\t\n   276\t**Critical verification in Case 1 (often skipped):** The Möbius inversion step gives the blue set indicator, but one must verify that this formula gives 0 or 1 (not other values), and that the resulting B satisfies the original multiplicativity. This computation is:\n   277\t\n   278\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} f(U) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} · 2^{|U∩A|}\n   279\t\n   280\tLet T∩A = T_A and T\\A = T_B. For U ⊆ T: U = U_A ∪ U_B with U_A ⊆ T_A and U_B ⊆ T_B. Then:\n   281\t\n   282\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U_A⊆T_A, U_B⊆T_B} (-1)^{|T_A|+|T_B|-|U_A|-|U_B|} · 2^{|U_A|}\n   283\t        = [Σ_{U_A⊆T_A} (-1)^{|T_A|-|U_A|} 2^{|U_A|}] · [Σ_{U_B⊆T_B} (-1)^{|T_B|-|U_B|}]\n   284\t\n   285\tThe second factor = Σ_{k=0}^{|T_B|} C(|T_B|,k)(-1)^{|T_B|-k} = (1-1)^{|T_B|} = 0^{|T_B|}.\n   286\t\n   287\tSo 1_B(T) = 0 if |T_B| > 0, i.e., if T ⊄ A.\n   288\tIf T ⊆ A, then T_B = ∅, so 1_B(T) = Σ_{U_A⊆T_A} (-1)^{|T_A|-|U_A|} 2^{|U_A|} = (2-1)^{|T_A|} = 1.\n   289\t\n   290\tSo 1_B(T) = 1 if T ⊆ A and 0 otherwise, i.e., B = P(A). ✓\n   291\t\n   292\t**This computation verifies Case 1.** A proof that only claims \"one checks\" without this computation has a minor omission (the computation is straightforward).\n   293\t\n   294\t**Case 2 (f(∅)=0):** \n   295\t- Functional condition with T₂ disjoint from T₁: f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·f(∅) = 0\n   296\t- So for any T₁, T₂ in the support of f, T₁∩T₂ ≠ ∅ (support is intersecting)\n   297\t- Take minimal element U in support; show f(U) = 1, B∩P(U) = {U}, support = {T : T⊇U}\n   298\t- Reduce to Case 1 on S' = S\\U via g(W) = f(U∪W)\n   299\t- Converse: verify that any interval [U, U∪A'] satisfies multiplicativity for ALL pairs T₁, T₂ ⊆ S\n   300\t\n   301\t**Critical gap in Case 2 converse:** If the proof claims \"one checks that [U, U∪A'] satisfies the condition\" without doing the check, and the check is non-trivial, this is a critical skipped step.\n   302\t\n   303\t**The check:** For B = [U, U∪A'], we have f(T) = g(T\\U)·χ_{T⊇U}(T) where g(W) = 2^{|W∩A'|}. For arbitrary T₁, T₂ ⊆ S:\n   304\t- If T₁ ⊅ U or T₂ ⊅ U: then at least one of f(T₁), f(T₂) equals 0. Also T₁∪T₂ may or may not ⊇ U, and T₁∩T₂ ⊇ U only if both T₁,T₂ ⊇ U (which fails). So at least one of f(T₁∪T₂), f(T₁∩T₂) = 0. The condition 0·f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·0 becomes 0 = 0 or 0 = 0. ✓\n   305\t- If T₁ ⊇ U and T₂ ⊇ U: then T₁∪T₂ ⊇ U and T₁∩T₂ ⊇ U. Let W₁ = T₁\\U, W₂ = T₂\\U. Then f(Tᵢ) = g(Wᵢ) = 2^{|Wᵢ∩A'|} and similarly. The condition becomes g(W₁)g(W₂) = g(W₁∪W₂)g(W₁∩W₂), i.e., 2^{|W₁∩A'|}·2^{|W₂∩A'|} = 2^{|(W₁∪W₂)∩A'|}·2^{|(W₁∩W₂)∩A'|}. This holds because |W₁∩A'|+|W₂∩A'| = |(W₁∩A')∪(W₂∩A')|+|(W₁∩A')∩(W₂∩A')| = |(W₁∪W₂)∩A'|+|(W₁∩W₂)∩A'| (using |A|+|B| = |A∪B|+|A∩B| for any finite sets). ✓\n   306\t\n   307\tSo the converse IS valid and checkable — but it requires this computation. The proof's \"one checks by routine verification\" is in fact routine (as shown above). However, an auditor must distinguish between (a) \"the proof says one checks and the check is indeed routine/trivial\" (= minor omission, proof essentially correct) and (b) \"the proof says one checks and the check is non-trivial and was actually skipped\" (= critical gap).\n   308\t\n   309\t**Verdict guidance for this problem type:** If the converse verification is ONLY cited as \"one checks\" and similar phrases appear at multiple critical steps, the cumulative effect of all the skipped steps determines the verdict.\n   310\t\n   311\t### 8.2 Grid/Matrix Set Systems with Monotonicity (proof_15 type)\n   312\t\n   313\t**Problem type:** Count collections {S_{ij}} with |S_{ij}| = i+j and S_{ij} ⊆ S_{kl} when i≤k, j≤l.\n   314\t\n   315\t**Standard reduction:** Write A_i = S_{i,0} and B_j = S_{0,j}. By monotonicity:\n   316\t- A_i = S_{i,0} ⊆ S_{i,j}\n   317\t- B_j = S_{0,j} ⊆ S_{i,j}\n   318\t- Hence A_i ∪ B_j ⊆ S_{i,j}\n   319\t- |A_i∪B_j| ≤ |A_i|+|B_j| = i+j = |S_{ij}|\n   320\t\n   321\tThe conclusion S_{ij} = A_i ∪ B_j requires |A_i∪B_j| = i+j, which requires A_i ∩ B_j = ∅.\n   322\t\n   323\t**Critical point:** The argument \"|A_i∪B_j| ≤ i+j = |S_{ij}| implies S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j\" is INVALID without additionally knowing |A_i∪B_j| = i+j. The bound |A_i∪B_j| ≤ i+j combined with A_i∪B_j ⊆ S_{ij} and |S_{ij}| = i+j shows A_i∪B_j ⊆ S_{ij} with |A_i∪B_j| ≤ |S_{ij}|. But this does NOT imply equality — it only shows A_i∪B_j could be a proper subset of S_{ij}.\n   324\t\n   325\tTo CORRECTLY conclude S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j, one needs |A_i∪B_j| = i+j, which requires A_i∩B_j = ∅. But A_i∩B_j = ∅ is derived from S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j! This is CIRCULAR.\n   326\t\n   327\tA correct proof would avoid this circularity by first establishing A_n∩B_n = ∅ (using |S_{nn}| = 2n and A_n∪B_n ⊆ S_{nn}, with |A_n|+|B_n| = 2n, forcing |A_n∩B_n| = 0 IF |S_{nn}| = |A_n∪B_n| = 2n). But even this requires |S_{nn}| = |A_n∪B_n|, which again needs A_n∩B_n = ∅...\n   328\t\n   329\tThe correct resolution: since A_n∪B_n ⊆ S_{nn} and |S_{nn}| = 2n and |A_n|+|B_n| = n+n = 2n, we need |A_n∪B_n| ≤ 2n (trivially true). But for a proper subset A_n∪B_n ⊊ S_{nn}, we'd need |A_n∪B_n| < 2n, i.e., A_n∩B_n ≠ ∅. Conversely, S_{nn} ⊆ {1,...,2n} with |S_{nn}| = 2n means S_{nn} = {1,...,2n}. And |A_n∪B_n| ≤ |{1,...,2n}| = 2n with |A_n|+|B_n| = 2n implies |A_n∩B_n| ≥ 0, so possibly A_n∩B_n ≠ ∅.\n   330\t\n   331\tActually, since A_n∪B_n ⊆ S_{nn} = {1,...,2n} (ALL elements), we have |A_n∪B_n| ≤ 2n. And |A_n|+|B_n| = 2n. So |A_n∩B_n| = |A_n|+|B_n|-|A_n∪B_n| ≥ 2n-2n = 0. This gives no contradiction.\n   332\t\n   333\tThe proof IS circular unless there's additional structure. The correct proof would use a different approach (e.g., induction or direct construction from disjoint chains).\n   334\t\n   335\t### 8.3 Sum Optimization with Distinct Integers (proof_19 type)\n   336\t\n   337\t**Problem type:** Find minimum N such that there exist 2k+1 distinct positive integers with total sum > N but every k-element subset sums to ≤ N/2.\n   338\t\n   339\t**Key structural observations:**\n   340\t1. The condition \"every k-subset ≤ N/2\" is most constraining for the largest k elements\n   341\t2. The condition \"total sum > N\" is most constraining for the smallest k+1 elements\n   342\t3. A symmetric set around some center c is a natural candidate for the extremal configuration\n   343\t\n   344\t**Construction technique:** Take S = {c-k, c-k+1, ..., c, ..., c+k} for some c.\n   345\t- |S| = 2k+1 ✓ (distinct positive integers if c > k)\n   346\t- Largest k elements: {c+1,...,c+k}, sum = kc+k(k+1)/2\n   347\t- Set N = 2·(kc+k(k+1)/2) to make the largest k-subset sum exactly N/2\n   348\t- Then total sum = (2k+1)c + 0 = ? No, total = Σ_{j=-k}^k (c+j) = (2k+1)c\n   349\t\n   350\tWait: Σ_{j=-k}^k (c+j) = (2k+1)c + Σ_{j=-k}^k j = (2k+1)c + 0 = (2k+1)c.\n   351\t\n   352\tAnd N = 2(kc + k(k+1)/2) = 2kc + k(k+1).\n   353\t\n   354\tFor total sum > N: (2k+1)c > 2kc+k(k+1) iff c > k(k+1), i.e., c ≥ k(k+1)+1.\n   355\t\n   356\tWith c = k(k+1)+1: N = 2k·(k(k+1)+1)+k(k+1) = 2k²(k+1)+2k+k(k+1) = k(2k+3)(k+1)+2k... let me compute directly.\n   357\t\n   358\tc = k(k+1)+1 = k²+k+1.\n   359\tN = 2kc+k(k+1) = 2k(k²+k+1)+k(k+1) = 2k³+2k²+2k+k²+k = 2k³+3k²+3k ✓\n   360\t\n   361\tTotal sum = (2k+1)c = (2k+1)(k²+k+1).\n   362\t\n   363\tNeed: (2k+1)(k²+k+1) > 2k³+3k²+3k.\n   364\t\n   365\t(2k+1)(k²+k+1) = 2k³+2k²+2k+k²+k+1 = 2k³+3k²+3k+1. ✓ (Exceeds N=2k³+3k²+3k by 1.)\n   366\t\n   367\t**Minimality argument:** Must show N < 2k³+3k²+3k leads to contradiction. Set a_{k+1} = c (the (k+1)-th smallest element in sorted order). Using a_{k+1+j} ≥ c+j and a_{k+1-j} ≤ c-j (both strict since elements are distinct integers), derive c ≥ k(k+1)+1, hence S_k ≥ N/2.\n   368\t\n   369\t**Evaluation criterion for proof_19 type:** The proof must:\n   370\t(a) Correctly compute N = 2k³+3k²+3k\n   371\t(b) Exhibit the construction explicitly\n   372\t(c) Verify both sum conditions for the construction\n   373\t(d) Prove minimality through a general lower bound\n   374\t\n   375\tAny error in (a)-(d) is a material issue.\n   376\t\n   377\t### 8.4 Non-General Construction Problems (proof_12 type)\n   378\t\n   379\t**Problem type:** Construct a combinatorial object (e.g., a graph or set system) with given properties.\n   380\t\n   381\t**Common gap:** Proving existence for specific small cases (n=1,2,3) and claiming the general case follows \"by analogous construction\" without providing the general construction.\n   382\t\n   383\t**Evaluation criterion:** If the proof only handles specific cases, the verdict should be incorrect if the problem asks for a GENERAL construction. A construction that works for specific n values but doesn't generalize is not a valid proof of the general claim.\n   384\t\n   385\t---\n   386\t\n   387\t## Part IX: Combinatorics Proof Evaluation Rubric\n   388\t\n   389\t1. **Completeness of case analysis:** All cases must be covered. Especially: if splitting on f(∅) = 0 vs f(∅) = 1, both cases must be handled.\n   390\t\n   391\t2. **Converse direction:** When classifying all valid configurations, both directions of \"if and only if\" must be proved. A proof that only shows (⇒) has a gap.\n   392\t\n   393\t3. **Counting formula correctness:** Verify every counting formula. C(2n,n)·n!·n! = (2n)! by C(2n,n) = (2n)!/(n!·n!), multiplied by n!·n! = (2n)!/1 = (2n)!. ✓\n   394\t\n   395\t4. **Non-circularity:** The reduction to boundary chains must not assume what it is trying to prove. Establishing A_i∩B_j = ∅ requires a separate non-circular argument.\n   396\t\n   397\t5. **Generality:** Does the proof work for general n (or k, or S), not just specific values?\n   398\t\n   399\t6. **Verification of construction:** Every claimed construction must be verified to satisfy ALL the problem's conditions.\n   400\t\n   401\t7. **Skipped steps:** \"One checks\" and \"by routine verification\" are acceptable for genuinely routine computations (like Möbius inversion in specific cases), but NOT for non-trivial verifications. Assess whether the skipped step is truly routine or not.\n   402\t\n   403\t**Identifying the first material issue:** Work through the proof sequentially. The FIRST step that violates one of criteria 1-7 is the first material issue.\n   404\t\n   405\t\n   406\t---\n   407\t\n   408\t## Appendix A: Extended Examples for Combinatorics Proof Evaluation\n   409\t\n   410\t### A.1 The Coloring Classification Problem (proof_13 type) — Step-by-Step Audit Guide\n   411\t\n   412\t**Complete structure of valid colorings:**\n   413\t\n   414\tA coloring (B, set of blue subsets) satisfies f(T1)f(T2)=f(T1 cup T2)f(T1 cap T2) for all T1,T2 in P(S) iff B belongs to one of these families:\n   415\t\n   416\tFamily 1: B = P(A) for some A subset S (includes empty set = A=empty gives B={empty set})\n   417\tFamily 2: B = [U, U cup A'] for some nonempty U subset S and A' subset S\\U (interval in Boolean lattice)\n   418\tFamily 3: B = empty (all-red, the \"zero\" solution)\n   419\t\n   420\tNote: Family 3 corresponds to f equiv 0 which vacuously satisfies the equation.\n   421\tFamily 1 corresponds to f(empty)=1.\n   422\tFamily 2 corresponds to f(empty)=0 with some blue set.\n   423\t\n   424\t**Count:** |Family 1| = 2^n (one per A subset S). |Family 2| = sum_{nonempty U} 2^{n-|U|} = 3^n-2^n. |Family 3| = 1.\n   425\tTotal = 2^n + (3^n - 2^n) + 1 = 3^n + 1.\n   426\t\n   427\t**First audit step:** Verify the proof splits into f(empty)=1 vs f(empty)=0 cases.\n   428\t**Second audit step:** Verify Case 1 concludes B=P(A) for 2^n colorings.\n   429\t**Third audit step:** Verify Case 2 concludes B=[U, U cup A'] plus all-red for 3^n-2^n+1 colorings.\n   430\t**Fourth audit step:** Add: 2^n + 3^n - 2^n + 1 = 3^n + 1.\n   431\t\n   432\tAny error in these four steps is a material issue.\n   433\t\n   434\t### A.2 The S_{ij} Counting Problem (proof_15 type) — Audit Guide\n   435\t\n   436\t**Setup:** Count valid {S_{ij}: 0<=i,j<=n, S_{ij} subset {1,...,2n}} with |S_{ij}|=i+j and S_{ij} subset S_{kl} when i<=k, j<=l.\n   437\t\n   438\t**The claimed reduction:** Every valid collection {S_{ij}} arises from a pair of disjoint chains A_0 subset ... subset A_n and B_0 subset ... subset B_n with A_n cap B_n = empty, via S_{ij} = A_i cup B_j.\n   439\t\n   440\t**Circularity check:** The proof must establish A_i cap B_j = empty BEFORE claiming S_{ij} = A_i cup B_j. If it first claims equality then derives empty intersection, it is circular.\n   441\t\n   442\t**Non-circular approach outline:**\n   443\tStep 1: From A_n cup B_n subset S_{nn} and |S_{nn}|=2n, we get S_{nn}={1,...,2n}.\n   444\tStep 2: From inclusion-exclusion |A_n cup B_n| = |A_n|+|B_n|-|A_n cap B_n| = 2n-|A_n cap B_n|.\n   445\tStep 3: But A_n cup B_n is not necessarily {1,...,2n}; we only know it's a subset of size <=2n.\n   446\tStep 4: (Stuck — the above doesn't give A_n cap B_n = empty without additional work.)\n   447\t\n   448\tA correct proof uses a different approach, such as:\n   449\t- Working with the largest sets and their complements\n   450\t- Using induction on n\n   451\t- Constructing the chains directly from a valid {S_{ij}} by setting A_i = S_{i,0} and showing these form a chain (obvious from i<=k => S_{i,0} subset S_{k,0}) and similarly for B, then establishing disjointness by a non-circular argument\n   452\t\n   453\tThe specific difficulty: establishing S_{ij}=A_i cup B_j requires |A_i cup B_j|=i+j, which requires disjointness, which the proof assumes from the conclusion. This circularity is a first material issue in this type of proof: the characterization is unproven.\n   454\t\n   455\t### A.3 Combinatorial Optimization (proof_19 type) — Detailed Audit\n   456\t\n   457\t**Problem:** Find minimum N such that there exist 2k+1 distinct positive integers with sum > N and every k-subset sums to at most N/2.\n   458\t\n   459\t**Key lemmas:**\n   460\t\n   461\tLemma 1 (Largest k-subset): The maximum sum of a k-element subset of {a_1 < ... < a_{2k+1}} is a_{k+2} + ... + a_{2k+1} (the k largest elements).\n   462\tProof: Any k elements sum to at most the k largest. ✓\n   463\t\n   464\tLemma 2 (Lower bound on c): With c = a_{k+1} and the conditions, c >= k(k+1)+1.\n   465\tProof: From sum_{i=1}^{k+1} a_i > S_k (where S_k = sum of k largest):\n   466\t  sum_{i=1}^k a_i + c > S_k >= kc + k(k+1)/2\n   467\t  But sum_{i=1}^k a_i <= kc - k(k+1)/2 (since a_{k+1-j} <= c-j for j=1,...,k)\n   468\t  So kc - k(k+1)/2 >= sum_{i=1}^k a_i > kc + k(k+1)/2 - c = (k-1)c + k(k+1)/2\n   469\t  This gives kc - k(k+1)/2 > (k-1)c + k(k+1)/2\n   470\t  c > k(k+1). So c >= k(k+1)+1. ✓\n   471\t\n   472\tLemma 3 (Minimum N): N' >= 2k^3+3k^2+3k.\n   473\tProof: N' >= 2S_k >= 2(kc + k(k+1)/2) >= 2(k(k(k+1)+1) + k(k+1)/2) = 2k^2(k+1)+2k + k(k+1) = 2k^3+3k^2+3k. ✓\n   474\t\n   475\tLemma 4 (Construction achieves N=2k^3+3k^2+3k): Set c=k(k+1)+1, S={c-k,...,c+k}.\n   476\t- k-subset max sum: kc+k(k+1)/2 = N/2. ✓ (all k-subsets have sum <= N/2)\n   477\t- Total sum: (2k+1)c = N+1 > N. ✓\n   478\t\n   479\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof correctly establishing Lemmas 1-4 is CORRECT. The first error in any lemma is the first material issue.\n   480\t\n   481\t### A.4 Non-General Construction Problem (proof_12 type) — Audit Guide\n   482\t\n   483\t**Common structure of proof_12 type problems:** \"Construct [combinatorial object with property P for all n >= 1].\"\n   484\t\n   485\t**Required proof elements:**\n   486\t1. Description of a construction (for general n)\n   487\t2. Verification that the construction has property P\n   488\t\n   489\t**Common gap:** Construction given for small n (e.g., n=1,2,3) with \"similar for larger n\" or \"obvious generalization.\" Without specifying the general construction, this is incomplete.\n   490\t\n   491\t**Evaluation criterion:**\n   492\t- If the proof ONLY handles specific small cases: INCORRECT (first material issue = missing general construction)\n   493\t- If the proof gives a general construction but fails to verify P: INCORRECT (first material issue = missing verification)\n   494\t- If both are present: evaluate whether the verification is correct\n   495\t\n   496\t---\n   497\t\n   498\t## Appendix B: Additional Combinatorial Identities and Techniques\n   499\t\n   500\t### B.1 Key Subset Sum Identities\n   501\t\n   502\tFor S = {1,...,n} and A subset S with |A|=k:\n   503\tsum_{A subset S, |A|=k} sum_{i in A} i = C(n-1,k-1) * sum_{i=1}^n i = C(n-1,k-1) * n(n+1)/2\n   504\t\n   505\tThis counts pairs (i, A) with i in A and |A|=k: each i is in C(n-1,k-1) such sets.\n   506\t\n   507\t### B.2 Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion — Extended\n   508\t\n   509\tFor events A_1,...,A_m in sample space Omega:\n   510\tP(A_1 cup ... cup A_m) = sum P(A_i) - sum_{i<j} P(A_i cap A_j) + ... + (-1)^{m+1} P(A_1 cap ... cap A_m)\n   511\t\n   512\t**Sieve formula:** Number of elements with NO property = sum_{S subset [m]} (-1)^|S| * |cap_{i in S} A_i|\n   513\t\n   514\t**Derangement formula:** D(n) = n! * sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k / k!\n   515\t\n   516\t### B.3 Lattice Path Counting\n   517\t\n   518\tA lattice path from (0,0) to (m,n) using steps (1,0) and (0,1) has C(m+n,m) total paths.\n   519\t\n   520\t**Ballot problem:** Path from (0,0) to (m,n) with m>n that stays strictly above the diagonal: C(m+n,m) * (m-n)/(m+n).\n   521\t\n   522\t**Catalan numbers:** C_n = C(2n,n)/(n+1) counts Dyck paths (lattice paths from (0,0) to (2n,0) with steps +1,-1 staying >= 0).\n   523\t\n   524\t### B.4 Counting Chains in Boolean Lattice\n   525\t\n   526\tNumber of chains of length k+1 (k+1 elements including empty) in B_n:\n   527\t= sum over A_0 subset A_1 subset ... subset A_k (each proper containment and in S)\n   528\t= n! / (n-k)! * C(n,k) ... (complex formula)\n   529\t\n   530\tFor maximal chains (length n+1): exactly n! (orderings of S).\n   531\t\n   532\tFor chains A_0 subset A_1 subset ... subset A_n with |A_i|=i:\n   533\t= n! (one for each ordering/labeling of S as {s_1,...,s_n}, taking A_i = {s_1,...,s_i})\n   534\t\n   535\tThis is the bijection: chains of this type <-> permutations of S. Hence n! chains.\n   536\t\n   537\t### B.5 Counting Disjoint Chains\n   538\t\n   539\tTwo disjoint chains in B_{2n}: choose A-chain of length n+1 and B-chain of length n+1 with A_n cap B_n = empty.\n   540\t\n   541\tMethod 1 (direct count):\n   542\tChoose A_n: C(2n,n) ways. Key properties:\n    52\t- Simple graph: no multi-edges, no self-loops\n    53\t- Complete graph K_n: every pair of vertices connected\n    54\t- Bipartite graph K_{m,n}: vertices split into two groups, edges only between groups\n    55\t- Tree: connected graph with no cycles; has exactly n-1 edges for n vertices\n    56\t\n    57\t**Pigeonhole principle:** If n objects are placed in k bins and n > k, at least one bin has at least ⌈n/k⌉ objects.\n    58\t\n    59\t**Handshaking lemma:** Σ_{v∈V} deg(v) = 2|E|.\n    60\t\n    61\t### 2.2 Matchings and Hall's Theorem\n    62\t\n    63\tA **matching** in a bipartite graph is a set of edges with no shared vertices.\n    64\t\n    65\t**Hall's marriage theorem:** A bipartite graph G = (A∪B, E) has a matching saturating all of A if and only if for every subset S ⊆ A, |N(S)| ≥ |S| (where N(S) is the neighborhood of S in B).\n    66\t\n    67\t**Perfect matching:** Matches every vertex. Key properties:\n    78\t- |B_n| = 2^n\n    79\t- Ranked by cardinality: rank k level has C(n,k) elements\n    80\t- Graded poset with n+1 ranks\n    81\t\n    82\t**Intervals in the Boolean lattice:** For A ⊆ B ⊆ S, the interval [A,B] = {C : A⊆C⊆B} is isomorphic to B_{|B|-|A|} and has 2^{|B|-|A|} elements.\n    83\t\n    84\t### 3.2 Chains and Antichains\n    85\t\n    86\tA **chain** is a totally ordered subset (any two elements comparable). A **antichain** is a set of mutually incomparable elements (no containments).\n    87\t\n    88\t**Dilworth's theorem:** The minimum number of chains needed to cover the poset equals the maximum antichain size.\n    89\t\n    90\t**Sperner's theorem:** The maximum antichain in B_n has size C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) (take all subsets of size ⌊n/2⌋).\n    91\t\n    92\t### 3.3 Multiplicative Functions on the Boolean Lattice\n    93\t\n    94\tA function f: 2^S → ℝ is **multiplicative** over (∪, ∩) if f(T₁)·f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·f(T₁∩T₂) for all T₁,T₂ ⊆ S.\n    95\t\n    96\tThis is a strong structural condition. Not every function satisfying this for \"many pairs\" satisfies it for all pairs.\n    97\t\n    98\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof that f satisfies the multiplicative condition must verify it for ALL pairs (T₁, T₂), not just specific families. The verification \"one checks by routine computation\" is a placeholder that must be backed by an actual argument. If the proof leaves this verification implicit and it is genuinely non-trivial, this constitutes a critical skipped step.\n    99\t\n   100\t**Characterization theorem:** The non-negative functions f: 2^S → ℝ satisfying f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) are exactly those of the form f(T) = 2^{|T∩A|} for some A⊆S (when f(∅)=1), or f(T) = χ_{[U,U∪A']}(T) extended multiplicatively (when f(∅)=0).\n   101\t\n   102\t### 3.4 Möbius Inversion on the Boolean Lattice\n   103\t\n   104\tThe Möbius function for the Boolean lattice B_n is μ(A,B) = (-1)^{|B|-|A|} for A ⊆ B.\n   105\t\n   106\t**Inversion formula:** If g(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} f(U) for all T, then f(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} g(U).\n   107\t\n   108\t**Application to blue-set counting:** If f(T) = #{blue subsets of T}, then the indicator of whether T itself is blue is:\n   109\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} f(U)\n   110\t\n   111\tThis is the Möbius inversion of f (where f(T) = Σ_{U∈B, U⊆T} 1 = Σ_{U⊆T} 1_B(U) is the cumulative count).\n   112\t\n   113\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof using Möbius inversion must correctly state and apply the inversion formula.
