If a construction says \"A_k lies on circle ω,\" the justification must be either geometric (from angle conditions) or algebraic (coordinates satisfy the circle equation), not just asserted.\n   239\t\n   240\t**Evaluation criterion:** If a proof claims \"A_k lies on circle ω\" without justification — neither a geometric argument (angle equality, power of point) nor an algebraic check — this is a material gap. The entire subsequent argument that uses A_k ∈ ω fails if this claim is unverified.\n   241\t\n   242\t### 6.2 Convex Hulls and Support Lines\n   243\t\n   244\tA convex polygon's boundary consists of support lines: each edge ℓ of the polygon has all polygon vertices on one side (or on ℓ). A point Q is a vertex of the convex hull if and only if no line through Q has all other points strictly on one side.\n   245\t\n   246\t**In circle arguments:** If a circle ω is internally tangent to a circle Ω, and A_k is defined as the tangent point or a point on ω, saying A_k ∈ Ω requires showing A_k simultaneously lies on ω (by construction) and on Ω (by a separate argument). These are two distinct conditions.\n   247\t\n   248\t### 6.3 Intersection and Overlap of Circles\n   249\t\n   250\tTwo distinct circles intersect in 0, 1, or 2 points depending on the relationship between the distance d between centers and the radii r₁, r₂:\n   251\t- d > r₁+r₂: external, 0 intersections\n   252\t- d = r₁+r₂: externally tangent, 1 intersection\n   253\t- |r₁-r₂| < d < r₁+r₂: overlapping, 2 intersections\n   254\t- d = |r₁-r₂|: internally tangent, 1 intersection\n   255\t- d < |r₁-r₂|: one inside the other, 0 intersections\n   256\t\n   257\t---\n   258\t\n   259\t## Part VII: Standard Proof Evaluation Criteria for Geometry\n   260\t\n   261\t### 7.1 Angle-Chase Proofs\n   262\t\n   263\tAn angle-chase proof establishes a chain of angle equalities, each justified by one of:\n   264\t- Inscribed angle theorem (angles subtending same arc are equal)\n   265\t- Tangent-chord angle theorem\n   266\t- Vertical angles, supplementary angles, etc.\n   267\t- Parallel line angle relationships (alternate interior, corresponding, co-interior)\n   268\t\n   269\t**Evaluation criterion:** For EACH angle equality claimed, identify which theorem or rule justifies it. If a claim \"∠XYZ = ∠XWZ\" is made without specifying that X,Y,Z,W are concyclic (or another justification), it is unjustified. The first unjustified angle equality is the first material issue.\n   270\t\n   271\t**Directed angle advantage:** Using directed angles mod 180° eliminates the need to distinguish cases (which arc, which side). But it requires every angle equality to be valid as a directed angle equality. If a proof mixes directed and undirected angles, errors can arise.\n   272\t\n   273\t### 7.2 Coordinate Geometry Proofs\n   274\t\n   275\tA coordinate proof is valid if and only if:\n   276\t1. The coordinate setup correctly represents the given geometric configuration\n   277\t2. Every arithmetic computation is correct\n   278\t3. The final claim (concurrence, collinearity, etc.) is verified by the stated equalities/checks\n   279\t\n   280\t**Verification steps:**\n   281\t- Circumcenter: check it is equidistant from all three vertices\n   282\t- Intersection points: check they lie on both curves\n   283\t- Concurrence: check the intersection of two lines lies on the third\n   284\t- Collinearity: check equal slopes or zero determinant\n   285\t\n   286\t**Common arithmetic errors with √2:**\n   287\t- (√2-1)/2: correct, approximately 0.207\n   288\t- (√2+1)/2: correct, approximately 1.207\n   289\t- 1/(√2-1) = √2+1 after rationalization\n   290\t- (√2-1)² = 2-2√2+1 = 3-2√2\n   291\t- (√2/2)² = 1/2, not 2\n   292\t\n   293\t### 7.3 Rotation Proofs\n   294\t\n   295\t**Evaluation criterion:** A rotation proof must:\n   296\t1. Specify the center, angle, and orientation of the rotation\n   297\t2. Correctly compute the angle from the given data\n   298\t3. Correctly identify the image of each relevant point\n   299\t4. Verify that the image satisfies the claimed property\n   300\t\n   301\tThe rotation angle is typically derived from the angles of the figure. An error in computing the rotation angle (e.g., π instead of the correct angle) will cause the images to be incorrectly identified, invalidating all subsequent claims.\n   302\t\n   303\t**Warning:** A rotation by angle π is point reflection. This is only valid if the geometric configuration indeed has a 180° rotational symmetry, which must be established from the hypotheses, not assumed.\n   304\t\n   305\t---\n   306\t\n   307\t## Part VIII: Extended Examples for Geometry Proof Evaluation\n   308\t\n   309\t### Example 1: Valid angle-chase\n   310\t\n   311\t**Claim:** Let ABCD be a cyclic quadrilateral. Then ∠BAC = ∠BDC (since both are inscribed in circle and subtend arc BC from the same side).\n   312\t\n   313\t**Analysis:** This is CORRECT. Both A and D lie on the same arc (opposite arc BC), so the inscribed angles subtending BC from that arc are equal. ✓\n   314\t\n   315\t### Example 2: Invalid angle-chase — wrong concyclicity\n   316\t\n   317\t**Claim:** Let P, Q, R, S be four points with ∠PQR = ∠PSR = 50°. Then P, Q, R, S are concyclic.\n   318\t\n   319\t**Analysis:** This is BACKWARD. The converse is true: if P,Q,R,S are concyclic, then ∠PQR = ∠PSR. But the claim uses equal angles to conclude concyclicity — this IS valid by the converse of the inscribed angle theorem. So this claim is CORRECT. (Note: The converse holds as long as Q and S are on the same side of PR.)\n   320\t\n   321\t### Example 3: Unjustified claim in coordinate proof\n   322\t\n   323\t**Claim:** By direct computation, the circumcircle has equation (x-1/2)²+(y-k)²=R² for appropriate k.\n   324\t\n   325\t**Missing step:** The value of k must be computed, not just asserted to be \"appropriate.\" Without the explicit formula for k (derived from equating distances to the three vertices), the claim is unsupported.\n   326\t\n   327\t### Example 4: Slope computation with surds\n   328\t\n   329\t**Verify:** slope(CO) where C = (√2/2, √2/2) and O = (1/2, (√2-1)/2).\n   330\t\n   331\tslope = [(√2-1)/2 - √2/2] / [1/2 - √2/2]\n   332\t     = [(√2-1-√2)/2] / [(1-√2)/2]\n   333\t     = [-1/2] / [(1-√2)/2]\n   334\t     = -1/(1-√2)\n   335\t     = 1/(√2-1)\n   336\t     = (√2+1)/((√2-1)(√2+1))\n   337\t     = (√2+1)/(2-1)\n   338\t     = √2+1 ✓\n   339\t\n   340\tThis is a correct computation. The step 1/(√2-1) = √2+1 requires the rationalization step.\n   341\t\n   342\t### Example 5: Checking concurrence in coordinate proof\n   343\t\n   344\t**Method:** Lines L₁: y = (√2+1)x - 1 and L₂: y = 1/2-(√2-1)x.\n   345\t\n   346\tIntersection: (√2+1)x-1 = 1/2-(√2-1)x\n   347\t(√2+1+√2-1)x = 3/2\n   348\t2√2·x = 3/2\n   349\tx = 3/(4√2) = 3√2/8\n   350\t\n   351\ty = (√2+1)·3√2/8 - 1 = (3·2+3√2)/8 - 1 = (6+3√2-8)/8 = (3√2-2)/8\n   352\t\n   353\tPoint P = (3√2/8, (3√2-2)/8).\n   354\t\n   355\t**Checking P on line FM:** F = ((√2-1)/2, (√2-1)/2) and M = ((2+√2)/4, √2/4).\n   356\t\n   357\tslope(FM) = [√2/4 - (√2-1)/2] / [(2+√2)/4 - (√2-1)/2]\n   358\t          = [(√2 - 2(√2-1))/4] / [(2+√2 - 2(√2-1))/4]\n   359\t          = (√2 - 2√2 + 2) / (2+√2-2√2+2)\n   360\t          = (2-√2) / (4-√2) ✓\n   361\t\n   362\tslope(FP) = [(3√2-2)/8 - (√2-1)/2] / [3√2/8 - (√2-1)/2]\n   363\t          = [(3√2-2 - 4(√2-1))/8] / [(3√2 - 4(√2-1))/8]\n   364\t          = (3√2-2-4√2+4) / (3√2-4√2+4)\n   365\t          = (2-√2) / (4-√2) ✓\n   366\t\n   367\tSo slope(FP) = slope(FM). F, M, P are collinear. ✓\n   368\t\n   369\t### Example 6: Missing justification for point on circle\n   370\t\n   371\t**Claim:** \"Since A_k is constructed as the intersection of the supporting line at A_{k-1} with circle ω_k, it lies on circle ω_k.\"\n   372\t\n   373\t**Analysis:** By construction, A_k = supporting line ∩ ω_k, so A_k ∈ ω_k. But does A_k ∈ Ω (the larger circle)? That is a SEPARATE claim requiring separate justification. If the proof asserts A_k ∈ Ω without showing either the coordinates of A_k satisfy Ω's equation or an angle/power argument shows A_k ∈ Ω, this is a gap. ✓ Correctly evaluating this requires checking whether the proof provides such a justification.\n   374\t\n   375\t---\n   376\t\n   377\t## Part IX: Specific Problem Type Guidance\n   378\t\n   379\t### 9.1 Concurrence of Three Lines (e.g., ZE, CO, FM)\n   380\t\n   381\tFor a proof that three lines are concurrent, the minimum valid structure is:\n   382\t1. Find the intersection P of two of the lines\n   383\t2. Show P lies on the third line\n   384\t\n   385\tIn a coordinate proof, this means:\n   386\t- Solve the system for two lines to get explicit (x,y) coordinates of P\n   387\t- Substitute into the equation of the third line and verify the equation holds\n   388\t- OR: show that the slope from P to one point on the third line equals the slope of the third line\n   389\t\n   390\t**Evaluation criterion:** If a coordinate proof finds P and claims P lies on line FM \"by similar computation,\" the reader must be able to fill in this computation. If the computation is absent but the conclusion is stated, this is an incomplete but potentially valid proof (minor omission, routine verification). If the computation would actually FAIL (i.e., slope(FP) ≠ slope(FM) due to an arithmetic error earlier), then the entire proof is invalid.\n   391\t\n   392\t### 9.2 Arcs and Sub-Arc Identification\n   393\t\n   394\tWhen problem states \"Z lies on arc BC\" and \"E lies on arc AC,\" these constraints determine which of the two intersection points of the small circle with the circumcircle is Z and which is E. A proof that just computes the two intersection points without verifying which is on which arc is incomplete.\n   395\t\n   396\t**Evaluation criterion:** Verify that the proof either:\n   397\t- Shows explicit coordinates for E and Z and checks which arc each lies on\n   398\t- Provides a geometric argument (e.g., Z is closer to B than to A, hence on arc BC)\n   399\t- Notes that the specific identification doesn't affect the concurrence conclusion\n   400\t\n   401\t### 9.3 Rotation Angle Determination\n   402\t\n   403\tIn a rotation proof for a geometry problem:\n   404\t1. Identify the center of rotation (often a specific vertex or special point)\n   405\t2. The angle of rotation comes from the geometry: for example, if two segments subtend equal angles at a common point, the rotation maps one to the other\n   406\t3. The direction (clockwise/counterclockwise) must be consistent with the configuration\n   407\t\n   408\t**Checking angle = π (180°):** A rotation by π about a center O maps P to 2O-P (the point symmetric to P through O). This is valid only if the problem's geometric structure has a 180° symmetry. The angle π is correct if:\n   409\t- The center is the midpoint of some key segment\n   410\t- Two triangles are identified as centrally symmetric\n   411\t- Some other explicit π-rotation symmetry is established\n   412\t\n   413\tIf instead the correct angle should be, e.g., π/2, and the proof uses π, then images of all points under the rotation are wrong.\n   414\t\n   415\t---\n   416\t\n   417\t## Part X: Evaluation Rubric Summary for Geometry Proofs\n   418\t\n   419\t1. **Angle equalities:** Every claimed angle equality must cite a theorem (inscribed angle, tangent-chord, parallel lines, vertical angles, or supplementary angles). An unjustified equality is a material issue.\n   420\t\n   421\t2. **Concyclicity:** Claims that four points are concyclic must be established (angle sum = 180°, equal inscribed angles, power of point = 0, all equidistant from a center).\n   422\t\n   423\t3. **Arithmetic correctness (for coordinate proofs):** Every calculation with specific coordinates must be verified. An arithmetic error that produces a wrong coordinate invalidates all subsequent claims using that coordinate.\n   424\t\n   425\t4. **Rotation angle:** In rotation arguments, the angle must be explicitly derived from the given data and correctly computed.\n   426\t\n   427\t5. **Third point on circle:** A claim that a specific point lies on a circle must be justified either algebraically (satisfies the circle's equation) or geometrically (angle condition, power condition, etc.).\n   428\t\n   429\t6. **Concurrence conclusion:** The proof must actually establish concurrence, not just set up a rotation/inversion and stop before the final conclusion.\n   430\t\n   431\t**First material issue identification:** The first place in the proof where one of the above criteria fails — an unjustified claim, a wrong calculation, or a missing verification — is the first material issue to report.\n   432\t\n   433\t\n   434\t---\n   435\t\n   436\t## Appendix A: Extended Worked Examples — Geometry Proof Evaluation\n   437\t\n   438\t### A.1 Angle-Chase Evaluation — 25 Scenarios\n   439\t\n   440\t**Scenario 1 (Correct).** \"Let ABCD be a cyclic quadrilateral. Then ∠DAB + ∠BCD = 180°.\"\n   441\tProof: ∠DAB and ∠BCD are opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral. They subtend arcs BCD and DAB respectively (the full circle minus each arc). Since arc(BCD) + arc(DAB) = 360°, and inscribed angles are half their arcs: ∠DAB + ∠BCD = (arc BCD + arc DAB)/2 = 360°/2 = 180°. CORRECT. ✓\n   442\t\n   443\t**Scenario 2 (Incorrect — invalid concyclicity claim).** \"Points P,Q,R,S lie on a circle since ∠PQR = 60° and ∠PSR = 60°.\"\n   444\tAssessment: For four points to be concyclic with ∠PQR = ∠PSR, Q and S must be on the SAME SIDE of PR. The claim doesn't specify the configuration. Moreover, just knowing both angles are 60° doesn't by itself prove concyclicity without verifying they subtend the same arc. But actually: by the converse of the inscribed angle theorem, if ∠PQR = ∠PSR and Q,S lie on the same side of PR, then P,Q,R,S are concyclic. Without the same-side condition, this could fail (e.g., Q and S on opposite sides gives ∠PQR + ∠PSR = 180°, so PQRS is cyclic but Q and S are on opposite arcs). So the claim needs the same-side condition explicitly stated.\n   445\t\n   446\t**Scenario 3 (Correct).** \"By the inscribed angle theorem, ∠ACB = ∠ADB since both are inscribed in circle ω and subtend arc AB not containing C and D, where C and D are on the same arc.\"\n   447\tCORRECT, assuming the same-arc condition is verified.\n   448\t\n   449\t**Scenario 4 (Incorrect — direction of implication).** \"∠ACB = 90° implies A, C, B lie on a circle with AB as diameter.\"\n   450\tAssessment: This is CORRECT — the converse of Thales' theorem. If ∠ACB = 90°, then C lies on the circle with AB as diameter.\n   451\t\n   452\t**Scenario 5 (Incorrect — wrong tangent-chord formula).** \"The angle between tangent t at P and chord PQ equals ∠PRQ where R is any point on the arc PQ not containing the tangent point.\"\n   453\tAssessment: The tangent-chord angle equals the inscribed angle in the ALTERNATE segment. So the angle between t and PQ at P equals the inscribed angle in the arc on the OTHER SIDE of PQ from the tangent direction. CORRECT as stated if \"alternate segment\" is understood.\n   454\t\n   455\t**Scenario 6 (Correct — directed angle computation).** \"∠(AB, CD) = ∠(AB, EF) + ∠(EF, CD) by linearity of directed angles.\"\n   456\tCORRECT. Directed angles mod 180° satisfy: ∠(AB,CD) = ∠(AB,EF)+∠(EF,CD) for any line EF. This is just the additive property of angles.\n   457\t\n   458\t**Scenario 7 (Incorrect — mixing directed and undirected).** \"∠BAC = 30° and ∠BDC = 150°, so A,B,C,D are NOT concyclic.\"\n   459\tAssessment: Using directed angles mod 180°: ∠BAC and ∠BDC as directed angles: 30° and 150° are NOT congruent mod 180° (since 150° = 180°-30° and directed angle differences are taken mod 180°, 30° ≠ 150° mod 180°... wait: 150° mod 180° = 150°, and 30° mod 180° = 30°. These differ, so in directed angle sense, A,B,C,D are not concyclic. But in undirected sense: ∠BAC + ∠BDC = 30°+150° = 180°, so opposite angles of quadrilateral ABCD sum to 180°, meaning ABCD IS cyclic. The issue: are A and D on the same side of BC? If ∠BAC = 30° and ∠BDC = 30° they're on the same side (concyclic). If ∠BAC = 30° and ∠BDC = 150° = 180°-30°, they're on opposite sides of BC, and the QUADRILATERAL ABCD is cyclic (opposite angles sum to 180°). CORRECT — A,B,C,D ARE concyclic.\n   460\t\n   461\t**Scenario 8 (Incorrect — wrong power of point formula).** \"For point P outside circle with tangent PA and secant PBC: PA² = PB · PC.\"\n   462\tCORRECT (power of a point for external point). PA² = PB·PC. ✓\n   463\t\n   464\t**Scenario 9 (Incorrect — wrong power formula for internal point).** \"For point P inside circle with chords AB and CD through P: PA·PB = PC·PD.\"\n   465\tCORRECT. For intersecting chords, PA·PB = PC·PD (both equal the power of P). ✓\n   466\t\n   467\t**Scenario 10 (Incorrect — sign error in radical axis).** \"The radical axis of two circles is where they have equal power, so the equation of the radical axis is obtained by adding the circle equations.\"\n   468\tFIRST MATERIAL ISSUE: The radical axis is obtained by SUBTRACTING the circle equations (not adding). Subtracting: (x-h₁)²+(y-k₁)²-r₁² = (x-h₂)²+(y-k₂)²-r₂² gives a linear equation. Adding gives a quadratic (the \"coaxial\" circle through their intersection points). ✓ Subtraction gives the radical axis.\n   469\t\n   470\t### A.2 Coordinate Geometry Verification — 20 Scenarios\n   471\t\n   472\t**Scenario C1 (Correct).** \"For A=(0,0), B=(1,0), C=(√2/2, √2/2) with ∠A=45°: |AB|=1, |AC|=√(1/2+1/2)=1. Triangle is isosceles with AB=AC=1.\"\n   473\tCheck: |AC| = √((√2/2)²+(√2/2)²) = √(1/2+1/2) = √1 = 1. ✓ AB=AC=1. ✓\n   474\t\n   475\t**Scenario C2 (Correct).** \"Circumcenter O of A=(0,0), B=(1,0), C=(√2/2,√2/2): O lies on x=1/2 (perpendicular bisector of AB).\"\n   476\tCheck: Midpoint of AB is (1/2,0). AB is horizontal, so perpendicular bisector is vertical: x=1/2. ✓\n   477\t\n   478\t**Scenario C3 (Correct).** \"Perpendicular bisector of AC (from A=(0,0) to C=(√2/2,√2/2)): midpoint is (√2/4, √2/4), slope of AC is 1, so perp bisector has slope -1 and equation y-√2/4 = -(x-√2/4), i.e., y = -x+√2/2.\"\n   479\tCheck: slope of AC = (√2/2-0)/(√2/2-0) = 1. ✓ Perp slope = -1. ✓ Through (√2/4,√2/4): y-√2/4 = -(x-√2/4) → y = -x+√2/4+√2/4 = -x+√2/2. ✓\n   480\t\n   481\t**Scenario C4 (Correct).** \"Intersection of x=1/2 and y=-x+√2/2: y = -1/2+√2/2 = (√2-1)/2. So O=(1/2,(√2-1)/2).\"\n   482\tCheck: substitute x=1/2: y = -1/2+√2/2 = (√2-1)/2. ✓\n   483\t\n   484\t**Scenario C5 (Correct).** \"Verification |OA|²=|OB|²=|OC|²: |OA|²=(1/2)²+((√2-1)/2)²=(1+(√2-1)²)/4=(1+3-2√2)/4=(4-2√2)/4=(2-√2)/2. ✓\"\n   485\tDetailed check: (√2-1)² = 2-2√2+1 = 3-2√2. (1+(3-2√2))/4 = (4-2√2)/4 = (2-√2)/2. ✓\n   486\t|OB|²=(1/2-1)²+((√2-1)/2)²=1/4+(3-2√2)/4=(4-2√2)/4=(2-√2)/2. ✓\n   487\t|OC|²=(1/2-√2/2)²+((√2-1)/2-√2/2)²=((1-√2)/2)²+((√2-1-√2)/2)²=((1-√2)²+1)/4=(3-2√2+1)/4=(4-2√2)/4. ✓\n   488\t\n   489\t**Scenario C6 (Incorrect — arithmetic error).** \"D = foot of perpendicular from C=(√2/2,√2/2) to AB (x-axis): D = (√2/2, 0). CD = distance from C to x-axis = √2/2. Circle with center C, radius CD: (x-√2/2)²+(y-√2/2)² = 2.\" \n   490\tINCORRECT: CD = √2/2 so r = √2/2, r² = 1/2. The circle equation should be (x-√2/2)²+(y-√2/2)² = 1/2, NOT 2.\n   491\t\n   492\t**Scenario C7 (Correct).** \"F = intersection of y=x with (x-√2/2)²+(y-√2/2)²=1/2: substitute y=x to get 2(x-√2/2)²=1/2, (x-√2/2)²=1/4, x=√2/2±1/2. The internal point on segment AC is x=(√2-1)/2 (since (√2+1)/2 > √2/2 = |C|, would be outside AC).\"\n   493\tCheck: √2/2 ≈ 0.707. (√2+1)/2 ≈ 1.207 > 0.707, outside [0,√2/2]. (√2-1)/2 ≈ 0.207 ∈ [0,√2/2]. ✓ So F = ((√2-1)/2, (√2-1)/2). ✓\n   494\t\n   495\t**Scenario C8 (Correct).** \"Subtracting circumcircle equation from small circle equation gives radical axis: 2(√2/2-1/2)x+2(√2/2-(√2-1)/2)y = constant.\"\n   496\tMore explicitly: circumcircle: (x-1/2)²+(y-(√2-1)/2)² = (2-√2)/2. Small circle: (x-√2/2)²+(y-√2/2)² = 1/2.\n   497\tExpand both, subtract:\n   498\tCircumcircle: x²-x+1/4+y²-(√2-1)y+(√2-1)²/4 = (2-√2)/2.\n   499\tSmall circle: x²-√2x+1/2+y²-√2y+1/2 = 1/2.\n   500\tSubtract: (-1+√2)x+(-(√2-1)+√2)y+(1/4+(3-2√2)/4-1/2-1/2) = (2-√2)/2-1/2.\n   501\t= (√2-1)x+(1)y+... let me redo this carefully.\n   502\t\n   503\tExpanding circumcircle: x²-x+1/4+y²-(√2-1)y+(3-2√2)/4=(2-√2)/2.\n   504\tExpanding small circle: x²-√2x+1/2+y²-√2y+1/2=1/2.\n   505\t\n   506\tSubtract (small - circ):\n   507\t(-√2+1)x+(-√2+√2-1)y+(1/2+1/2-1/4-(3-2√2)/4)=(1/2-(2-√2)/2).\n   508\t\n   509\t(-√2+1)x+(-1)y+(1-1/4-(3-2√2)/4)=(1/2-1+√2/2).\n   510\t\n   511\t(1-√2)x-y+(4/4-1/4-(3-2√2)/4)=(√2/2-1/2).\n   512\t\n   513\t(1-√2)x-y+((4-1-3+2√2)/4)=(√2-1)/2.\n   514\t\n   515\t(1-√2)x-y+(2√2/4)=(√2-1)/2.\n   516\t\n   517\t(1-√2)x-y+(√2/2)=(√2-1)/2.\n   518\t\n   519\t(1-√2)x-y=((√2-1)/2-√2/2)=(-1/2).\n   520\t\n   521\t(1-√2)x-y=-1/2.\n   522\t\n   523\tOr: (√2-1)x+y=1/2. ✓ Matches the line y=1/2-(√2-1)x. ✓\n   524\t\n   525\t**Scenario C9 (Correct).** \"Intersection of y=(√2+1)x-1 and y=1/2-(√2-1)x:\"\n   526\t(√2+1)x-1=1/2-(√2-1)x\n   527\t(√2+1+√2-1)x=3/2\n   528\t2√2x=3/2, x=3/(4√2)=3√2/8.\n   529\ty=(√2+1)·3√2/8-1=(3·2+3√2)/8-1=(6+3√2-8)/8=(3√2-2)/8.\n   530\tP=(3√2/8,(3√2-2)/8). ✓\n   531\t\n   532\t**Scenario C10 (Correct).** \"Slope of FM: F=((√2-1)/2,(√2-1)/2), M=((2+√2)/4,√2/4).\"\n   533\tΔx=(2+√2)/4-(√2-1)/2=(2+√2-2√2+2)/4=(4-√2)/4.\n   534\tΔy=√2/4-(√2-1)/2=(√2-2√2+2)/4=(2-√2)/4.\n   535\tslope=(2-√2)/(4-√2). ✓\n   536\t\n   537\t**Scenario C11 (Correct).** \"Slope of FP: F=((√2-1)/2,(√2-1)/2), P=(3√2/8,(3√2-2)/8).\"\n   538\tΔx=3√2/8-(√2-1)/2=3√2/8-(4√2-4)/8=(3√2-4√2+4)/8=(4-√2)/8.\n   539\tΔy=(3√2-2)/8-(√2-1)/2=(3√2-2-4√2+4)/8=(2-√2)/8.\n   540\tslope=(2-√2)/(4-√2). ✓ Same as slope FM, confirming collinearity. ✓\n   541\t\n   542\t### A.3 Rotation and Transformation — 15 Scenarios\n   543\t\n   544\t**Scenario R1 (Incorrect — wrong rotation angle).** \"Rotate triangle ABC by π about midpoint M of BC. This maps B↦C and C↦B, and A↦A'.\"\n   545\tCheck: Rotation by π about M: M is midpoint of BC, so B↦C and C↦B ✓. A maps to the point A' with M=(A+A')/2, so A'=2M-A. If M is NOT the midpoint of AA', then A'≠A.\n   546\t\n   547\t**Scenario R2 (Correct).** \"If rotating by angle θ about center O maps X to X' and Y to Y', then ∠XOY = ∠X'OY' = θ and |OX|=|OX'|, |OY|=|OY'|, |XY|=|X'Y'|.\"\n   548\tCORRECT. Rotations preserve distances and angles between any two points. ✓\n   549\t\n   550\t**Scenario R3 (Incorrect — wrong rotation angle in geometry proof).** \"In triangle ABC with ∠A=45°, rotate by angle π about the circumcenter O.\"\n   551\tAssessment: Rotation by π about O maps each point P to 2O-P (point symmetry). This maps A to the antipode A* of A on the circumcircle. The angle ∠A=45° does NOT imply a π-rotation is the right transformation. The rotation angle should be ∠BOC = 2∠BAC = 90° (central angle theorem), NOT π=180°.\n   552\t\n   553\t**Scenario R4 (Correct).** \"The rotation by ∠BOC = 2∠BAC about O maps arc BC to arc BC.\"\n   554\tCentral angle ∠BOC = 2·∠BAC (inscribed angle theorem). Rotation by ∠BOC about O: this is the rotation that \"moves along the circle\" by the arc BC. Points ON the circle would be mapped to other points on the circle. This is correct for the standard rotation in circle geometry.\n   555\t\n   556\t**Scenario R5 (Incorrect — incorrect images).** \"Rotation by π/2 about origin maps (a,b) to (-b,a).\" \n   557\tCheck: Rotation by π/2 counterclockwise: x'=x·cos(π/2)-y·sin(π/2)=-y, y'=x·sin(π/2)+y·cos(π/2)=x. So (a,b)↦(-b,a). ✓ CORRECT.\n   558\t\n   559\t**Scenario R6 (Correct).** \"Rotation by π about O=(h,k) maps P=(x,y) to P'=(2h-x, 2k-y).\"\n   560\tx' = (x-h)cos(π)-(y-k)sin(π)+h = -(x-h)+h = 2h-x. ✓\n   561\ty' = (x-h)sin(π)+(y-k)cos(π)+k = -(y-k)+k = 2k-y. ✓\n   562\t\n   563\t**Scenario R7 (Incorrect — missing case in rotation).** \"There are two possible rotation angles: θ and -θ. The proof only checks θ.\"\n   564\tIf the problem has a reflection symmetry (equilateral triangle, etc.), both θ and -θ (clockwise and counterclockwise) might be relevant. A proof that only checks one rotation may miss solutions or draw wrong conclusions.\n   565\t\n   566\t### A.4 Circle Geometry Patterns — 15 Scenarios\n   567\t\n   568\t**Scenario Ci1 (Correct — Ptolemy application).** \"For cyclic quadrilateral ABCD: AC·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC.\"\n   569\tPTOLEMY'S THEOREM. ✓\n   570\t\n   571\t**Scenario Ci2 (Correct — inversion application).** \"Inversion with center P and radius r maps circle Γ not through P to another circle Γ' (not through P). The image of lines through P are lines through P.\"\n   572\tCORRECT. Inversion swaps circles not through P with circles not through P, and swaps circles through P with lines not through P. ✓\n   573\t\n   574\t**Scenario Ci3 (Incorrect — wrong inversion formula).** \"Inversion with center O and radius r maps P=(a,b) to P'=(a/r², b/r²).\"\n   575\tINCORRECT. Inversion maps P to P' on ray OP with OP·OP'=r². If P=(a,b), then |OP|=√(a²+b²) and the image P'= (r²/(a²+b²))·(a,b). So P'=(r²a/(a²+b²), r²b/(a²+b²)). The formula (a/r², b/r²) is wrong.\n   576\t\n   577\t**Scenario Ci4 (Correct).** \"For a circle ω with center O and radius R, and a chord PQ, the perpendicular from O bisects PQ.\"\n   578\tCORRECT. The perpendicular from the center to a chord always bisects the chord (by symmetry). ✓\n   579\t\n   580\t**Scenario Ci5 (Correct).** \"Two circles are internally tangent at T if and only if their centers O₁,O₂ and T are collinear (T between O₁ and O₂ for external tangency, T on the extension for internal tangency).\"\n   581\tCORRECT for tangency. For internal tangency (one circle inside the other): |O₁O₂| = |r₁-r₂| and the tangent point T lies on segment O₁O₂ (extended if needed). ✓\n   582\t\n   583\t### A.5 Collinearity and Concurrence Patterns\n   584\t\n   585\t**Pattern Col1 (Correct).** \"Three points A=(x₁,y₁), B=(x₂,y₂), C=(x₃,y₃) are collinear iff the matrix [[x₁,y₁,1],[x₂,y₂,1],[x₃,y₃,1]] has determinant 0.\"\n   586\tCORRECT. The determinant condition: x₁(y₂-y₃)+x₂(y₃-y₁)+x₃(y₁-y₂)=0. ✓\n   587\t\n   588\t**Pattern Con1 (Correct).** \"Lines L₁: a₁x+b₁y=c₁, L₂: a₂x+b₂y=c₂, L₃: a₃x+b₃y=c₃ are concurrent iff their system has a solution, i.e., det([[a₁,b₁,c₁],[a₂,b₂,c₂],[a₃,b₃,c₃]])=0.\"\n   589\tCORRECT. The three lines meet at a single point iff the 3×3 determinant with the line equation coefficients vanishes. ✓\n   590\t\n   591\t**Pattern Con2 (Ceva's theorem check).** For triangle ABC with D on BC, E on CA, F on AB: AD, BE, CF concurrent iff (BD/DC)·(CE/EA)·(AF/FB)=1 (Ceva's theorem with signed ratios).\n   592\t\n   593\t**Pattern Col2 (Slope method).** Points P,Q,R collinear iff slope(PQ)=slope(QR). Requires Q≠P and Q≠R and Q not at infinity.\n   594\t\n   595\t---\n   596\t\n   597\t## Appendix B: Competition-Specific Geometry Notes\n   598\t\n   599\t### B.1 BMOSL Geometry Problems\n   600\t\n   601\tBMOSL (British Mathematical Olympiad Shortlist) geometry problems typically involve:\n   602\t- Cyclic quadrilaterals and concyclic points\n   603\t- Angle chasing with directed angles\n   604\t- Coordinate geometry for construction verification\n   605\t- The olympiad standard: all steps must be justified, but \"standard facts\" (inscribed angle theorem, power of a point) can be cited without re-proof\n   606\t\n   607\t### B.2 USAMO Geometry Problems\n   608\t\n   609\tUSAMO geometry problems are generally harder and may require:\n   610\t- Projective geometry (cross-ratio, harmonic ranges)\n   611\t- Advanced circle theorems (Miquel's theorem, radical axes)\n   612\t- Sophisticated inversion arguments\n   613\t- Rigorous handling of degenerate cases\n   614\t\n   615\t### B.3 Evaluation Standard for Competition Geometry\n   616\t\n   617\tAt competition level, the following are considered \"standard\" and do NOT need proof:\n   618\t- Inscribed angle theorem\n   619\t- Power of a point\n   620\t- Ceva's theorem and Menelaus's theorem\n   621\t- Basic trigonometric identities (law of sines, law of cosines)\n   622\t- Ptolemy's theorem\n   623\t\n   624\tThe following DO need justification even if \"standard\":\n   625\t- That specific points are concyclic (must establish which condition holds)\n   626\t- That a point lies on a specific circle (must verify one of the conditions)\n   627\t- That a rotation maps one specific point to another (must verify distance and angle)\n   628\t\n   629\t---\n   630\t\n   631\t## Appendix C: Extended Reference — Angles in Complex Numbers\n   632\t\n   633\tFor geometry in the complex plane, a point P corresponds to complex number z_P. Key facts:\n   634\t\n   635\t**Rotation:** Rotation by angle θ about origin multiplies by e^{iθ}.\n   636\t\n   637\t**Reflection:** Reflection over real axis: z ↦ z̄. Reflection over line through origin at angle α: z ↦ e^{2iα}z̄.\n   638\t\n   639\t**Collinearity:** A, B, C collinear iff (C-A)/(B-A) is real.\n   640\t\n   641\t**Concyclicity:** A, B, C, D concyclic (or collinear) iff (A-C)(B-D)/((A-D)(B-C)) is real (cross-ratio is real).\n   642\t\n   643\t**Angle:** Directed angle ∠(AB,AC) = arg((C-A)/(B-A)) mod π.\n   644\t\n   645\tThese formulas provide an algebraic framework for verifying geometric claims. When a coordinate proof is too computational, complex number methods can simplify.\n   646\t\n   647\t---\n   648\t\n   649\t*End of Geometry Background Reference*\n   650\t\n   651\t\n   652\t---\n   653\t\n   654\t## Appendix D: Extended Geometry Problem Patterns\n   655\t\n   656\t### D.1 Angle-Chase Reference — Additional Patterns\n   657\t\n   658\t**AC1 (Directed angle formula).** For points A,B,C,D with ABCD concyclic: angle(AC,BC) = angle(AD,BD) as directed angles mod 180 degrees. This is the key rule for angle chasing.\n   659\t\n   660\t**AC2 (Central angle rule).** Central angle = 2 * inscribed angle subtending same arc. angle(AOB) = 2 * angle(ACB) where O is center and C is on the circle.\n   661\t\n   662\t**AC3 (Tangent-chord angle).** Angle between tangent at P and chord PQ equals angle subtended by arc PQ in the alternate segment.\n   663\t\n   664\t**AC4 (Alternate segment theorem).** If T is on circle omega and l is tangent to omega at T, and AB is a chord, then angle(l, AT) = angle(ABT) where the angle is in the alternate segment.\n   665\t\n   666\t**AC5 (Cyclic polygon).** In a cyclic polygon with n sides, the sum of alternating exterior angles = 180 degrees. For cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180 degrees.\n   667\t\n   668\t### D.2 Coordinate Computation Reference — Standard Formulas\n   669\t\n   670\t**Distance formula:** |PQ|^2 = (x_Q - x_P)^2 + (y_Q - y_P)^2.\n   671\t\n   672\t**Midpoint formula:** M = ((x_P+x_Q)/2, (y_P+y_Q)/2).\n   673\t\n   674\t**Line through P=(x_1,y_1) and Q=(x_2,y_2):** (y-y_1)/(x-x_1) = (y_2-y_1)/(x_2-x_1) if x_1 != x_2. Or: (x_2-x_1)(y-y_1) = (y_2-y_1)(x-x_1).\n   675\t\n   676\t**Circumcenter:** For triangle with vertices A,B,C, the circumcenter O satisfies |OA|=|OB|=|OC|. Found by intersecting perpendicular bisectors of any two sides.\n   677\t\n   678\t**Circumradius formula:** R = |AB|/(2*sin(angle(ACB))) by law of sines.\n   679\t\n   680\t**Standard surds:**\n   681\t- sqrt(2) ≈ 1.41421\n   682\t- sqrt(2)/2 ≈ 0.70711\n   683\t- sqrt(2)-1 ≈ 0.41421\n   684\t- sqrt(2)+1 ≈ 2.41421\n   685\t- (sqrt(2)-1)/2 ≈ 0.20711\n   686\t- (sqrt(2)+1)/2 ≈ 1.20711\n   687\t- (3*sqrt(2)-2)/8 ≈ 0.28033\n   688\t- 3*sqrt(2)/8 ≈ 0.53033\n   689\t\n   690\tThese approximate values help verify that computed points are in expected relative positions.\n   691\t\n   692\t### D.3 Rotation Proof Methodology\n   693\t\n   694\t**Step-by-step rotation proof structure:**\n   695\t\n   696\t1. **Identify rotation center:** Usually a vertex, circumcenter, or special point.\n   697\t2. **Determine rotation angle:** From the geometric data (e.g., central angle, polygon angle).\n   698\t3. **Compute images:** Use rotation formula or geometric argument.\n   699\t4. **Establish claimed equalities:** Show the image of a specific segment/angle equals another.\n   700\t5. **Conclude the geometric claim:** (concurrence, collinearity, etc.) from the rotation.\n   701\t\n   702\t**Rotation angle errors are common.** The angle is typically:\n   703\t- pi/n for regular n-gon\n   704\t- 2*angle_A for central angle at vertex A\n   705\t- Angle of some inscribed figure\n   706\t\n   707\tIf the proof states angle = pi without deriving this from the problem, check whether the configuration really has 180-degree rotational symmetry.\n   708\t\n   709\t### D.4 Circle Tangency and Intersection Patterns\n   710\t\n   711\t**Internal tangency:** Two circles internally tangent at T: centers O1, O2 with |O1O2| = |r1-r2|. The tangent at T is the common internal tangent.\n   712\t\n   713\t**External tangency:** |O1O2| = r1+r2. Tangent point T lies on segment O1O2.\n   714\t\n   715\t**Radical axis of two intersecting circles:** If they intersect at P and Q, the radical axis is line PQ.\n   716\t\n   717\t**Finding angle subtended by chord at center:** If chord has length c in circle of radius r: angle = 2*arcsin(c/(2r)).\n   718\t\n   719\t### D.5 Trigonometric Identities in Geometry\n   720\t\n   721\t**Law of sines:** a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C) = 2R.\n   722\t\n   723\t**Law of cosines:** c^2 = a^2+b^2-2ab*cos(C).\n   724\t\n   725\t**Extended law of sines:** a = 2R*sin(A) where R is circumradius.\n   726\t\n   727\t**Area formula:** [ABC] = (1/2)ab*sin(C) = (abc)/(4R).\n   728\t\n   729\t**Stewart's theorem:** For cevian d from A to side BC at point D with BD=m, DC=n: b^2*m+c^2*n = a(d^2+mn).\n   730\t\n   731\t**Ptolemy (generalized):** For cyclic ABCD: AC*BD = AB*CD + AD*BC.\n   732\t\n   733\t### D.6 Combinatorial Geometry Patterns\n   734\t\n   735\t**Support line:** A line l is a support line of convex set K at point p in K if l contains p and K lies entirely in one closed half-plane bounded by l.\n   736\t\n   737\t**Support point:** A point p on the boundary of convex K is a support point if there exists a support line at p.\n   738\t\n   739\t**Evaluation criterion for support point arguments:** A claim that \"point A_k is a support point\" must be substantiated. Options:\n   740\t- Show A_k is on the boundary of the convex hull\n   741\t- Show there exists a support line at A_k\n   742\t- Use the definition directly (A_k is on a tangent line with all other points on one side)\n   743\t\n   744\tIf a proof claims A_k lies on a specific circle because \"it would be a support point otherwise,\" this reasoning is BACKWARDS unless the support property has been established first.\n   745\t\n   746\t**Inscribed polygon in circle:** A polygon inscribed in circle omega has all vertices on omega. A point P lies on omega iff |P - O| = r (where O is center, r is radius).\n   747\t\n   748\t**Point on circle verification methods:**\n   749\t1. Show |P-O|^2 = r^2 (coordinate check)\n   750\t2. Show ∠PAQ = ∠POQ/2 for some chord AQ (inscribed angle)\n   751\t3. Show the power of P with respect to omega equals 0\n   752\t\n   753\t### D.7 Proof of Concurrence — Methods\n   754\t\n   755\t**Ceva's theorem:** In triangle ABC with cevians AD, BE, CF (D on BC, E on CA, F on AB): concurrent iff (BD/DC)*(CE/EA)*(AF/FB) = 1.\n   756\t\n   757\t**Radical axis:** Three radical axes of three circles are concurrent at the radical center.\n   758\t\n   759\t**Perspective triangles:** Triangles ABC and A'B'C' are perspective from a point iff AA', BB', CC' are concurrent (lines through corresponding vertices meet at one point).\n   760\t\n   761\t**Coordinate method:** Find intersection of two lines; verify on third.\n   762\t\n   763\t**Vector method:** Express each line as P = A + t*(B-A) and solve for t. Three lines concurrent iff the system is consistent.\n   764\t\n   765\t### D.8 Special Lines and Points\n   766\t\n   767\t**Euler line:** In any non-equilateral triangle, the circumcenter O, centroid G, and orthocenter H are collinear. OG:GH = 1:2.\n   768\t\n   769\t**Nine-point circle:** The midpoints of sides, feet of altitudes, and midpoints of segments from vertices to orthocenter all lie on one circle (nine-point circle) of radius R/2.\n   770\t\n   771\t**Simson line:** For a point P on the circumcircle of triangle ABC, the projections of P onto the sides of ABC are collinear (Simson line).\n   772\t\n   773\t**Polar-pole:** For a circle omega with center O and radius r, the polar of point P (with respect to omega) is the line perpendicular to OP at the inverse point of P.\n   774\t\n   775\t*End of Geometry Extended Appendix*\n","message":"775 lines read from file starting from line 1. The normalization must preserve all constraints.\n    41\t\n    42\t**Correct degree check:** Verify the degrees of both sides of the inequality. If degrees differ, the inequality is NOT homogeneous and normalization changes the problem.\n    43\t\n    44\t**Monotonicity via derivative:** The claim \"f'(x) < 0 for all x in domain\" implies f is strictly decreasing on that domain. This claim is a FACTUAL assertion that must be verified — either by explicit computation of f' and showing f' < 0, or by citing a known result.\n    45\t\n    46\t**First material issue for inequality proofs:** \n    47\t- If a derivative or convexity argument is used, verify the sign of f' or f'' explicitly for the relevant domain.\n    48\t- If an AM-GM application is made, verify that all quantities are positive.\n    49\t- If Cauchy-Schwarz is applied, verify the correct form is used.\n    50\t\n    51\t---\n    52\t\n    53\t## Part II: Polynomials\n    54\t\n    55\t### 2.1 Basic Polynomial Theory\n    56\t\n    57\t**Degree:** The degree of a polynomial f(x) = aₙxⁿ + ... + a₀ (aₙ ≠ 0) is n. Leading coefficient is aₙ.\n    58\t\n    59\t**Roots:** By the fundamental theorem of algebra, a degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots (counting multiplicity) in ℂ.\n    60\t\n    61\t**Lagrange interpolation:** Given n+1 points (x₀,y₀),...,(xₙ,yₙ) with distinct xᵢ, there is a unique polynomial of degree ≤ n passing through all of them:\n    62\tP(x) = Σᵢ yᵢ · Π_{j≠i} (x-xⱼ)/(xᵢ-xⱼ)\n    63\t\n    64\t**Consequence:** A polynomial of degree ≤ n is uniquely determined by its values at n+1 distinct points.\n    65\t\n    66\t**Degree bound lemma:** A polynomial of degree ≤ n that evaluates to 0 at n+1 distinct points must be identically 0.\n    67\t\n    68\t### 2.2 Polynomials with Symmetric Conditions\n    69\t\n    70\t**Symmetric polynomials:** A polynomial f(x₁,...,xₙ) is symmetric if it is invariant under all permutations of variables. The fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials: every symmetric polynomial is a polynomial in the elementary symmetric polynomials e₁,...,eₙ:\n    71\t- e₁ = Σxᵢ\n    72\t- e₂ = Σᵢ<ⱼ xᵢxⱼ\n    73\t- e₃ = Σᵢ<ⱼ<ₖ xᵢxⱼxₖ\n    74\t- ...\n    75\t- eₙ = x₁x₂···xₙ\n    76\t\n    77\t**Newton's power sum identities:** If pₖ = Σxᵢᵏ, then:\n    78\tp₁ = e₁\n    79\tp₂ = e₁p₁ - 2e₂\n    80\tp₃ = e₁p₂ - e₂p₁ + 3e₃\n    81\t...\n    82\t\n    83\t**For three variables (x,y,z):**\n    84\tx²+y²+z² = e₁² - 2e₂ = (x+y+z)² - 2(xy+yz+zx)\n    85\tx³+y³+z³ = e₁³ - 3e₁e₂ + 3e₃ = (x+y+z)³ - 3(x+y+z)(xy+yz+zx) + 3xyz\n    86\t\n    87\tAlso: (x-y)²+(y-z)²+(z-x)² = 2(x²+y²+z²) - 2(xy+yz+zx) = 2(e₁² - 2e₂) - 2e₂ = 2(e₁² - 3e₂) = 2(S₁² - 3S₂).\n    88\t\n    89\t### 2.3 Polynomial Functional Equations\n    90\t\n    91\t**Method:** To find all polynomials P satisfying an identity F(P) = 0 or F(P, Q) = 0:\n    92\t1. **Degree bound:** Compare degrees of both sides; the leading terms must match, giving a constraint on deg P.\n    93\t2. **Coefficient matching:** After establishing deg P = d, substitute P(t) = aₐtᵈ + ... and match coefficients.\n    94\t3. **Verification:** Plug the candidate polynomial back into the original identity to confirm.\n    95\t\n    96\t**Degree comparison in asymptotics:** To compare degrees, take a variable to infinity and expand both sides in a power series. The leading terms must agree.\n    97\t\n    98\t**Example:** If the identity equates two expressions, both expanded to order y^{n+1} and y^n, the coefficients of y^{n+1} give a constraint (often automatically satisfied) and the coefficients of y^n give a non-trivial constraint on the degree n.\n    99\t\n   100\t### 2.4 Evaluation Criteria for Polynomial Proofs\n   101\t\n   102\t**Degree bound:** The argument that \"deg P ≤ n\" based on asymptotic expansion must correctly identify the leading terms of both sides. An error in which power of y dominates (e.g., confusing y^n with y^{n+1}) would give the wrong degree constraint.\n   103\t\n   104\t**Even/odd degree:** The claim \"n must be even\" based on cancellation of certain terms: if the coefficient of y^{n+1} on the RHS has a factor ((-1)^n + 1), then this vanishes only when n is odd. The correct conclusion is n must be EVEN (for non-vanishing leading term). An off-by-one error here changes the conclusion.\n   105\t\n   106\t**Coefficient matching:** After establishing the degree, the system of linear equations from coefficient matching must be set up correctly. Common errors: sign errors, wrong expansion of symmetric sum identities, applying Vieta's formulas to the wrong polynomial.\n   107\t\n   108\t---\n   109\t\n   110\t## Part III: Real Analysis and Calculus in Olympiad Proofs\n   111\t\n   112\t### 3.1 Monotonicity via Derivatives\n   113\t\n   114\tA differentiable function f: (a,b) → ℝ is strictly increasing if f'(x) > 0 for all x ∈ (a,b), and strictly decreasing if f'(x) < 0 for all x ∈ (a,b).\n   115\t\n   116\t**Verification requirement:** If a proof asserts f'(x) < 0 to establish monotonicity, it must explicitly compute f'(x) and show it is negative. The assertion \"f'(x) < 0\" is NOT self-evident.\n   117\t\n   118\t**First material issue:** If f'(x) < 0 is claimed but either:\n   119\t(a) f'(x) is not computed, or\n   120\t(b) f'(x) is computed but the inequality f'(x) < 0 does not hold for the relevant x,\n   121\t\n   122\tthen the proof is incorrect at this step.\n   123\t\n   124\t**Common errors with derivatives:**\n   125\t- Differentiating incorrectly (product rule, chain rule errors)\n   126\t- Stating the wrong derivative formula\n   127\t- Claiming the derivative is negative when it could be zero or positive for some values in the domain\n   128\t\n   129\t### 3.2 Compactness and Existence of Minima\n   130\t\n   131\t**Weierstrass extreme value theorem:** A continuous function on a compact (closed and bounded) set in ℝⁿ attains its minimum and maximum.\n   132\t\n   133\t**Non-compact case:** If the domain is not compact (e.g., all of ℝⁿ, or an open set, or unbounded), the function may not attain its minimum. To establish existence of a minimum, one of the following is needed:\n   134\t- Show the domain IS compact\n   135\t- Show the function is coercive (f(x) → ∞ as |x| → ∞), reducing to a compact sublevel set\n   136\t- Direct construction of the minimum\n   137\t\n   138\t**Evaluation criterion for analysis proofs:** If a proof claims \"the minimum is attained\" by a compactness argument, verify:\n   139\t- The domain is indeed compact (closed and bounded), OR\n   140\t- The specific compact set used in the argument is correctly identified and the function's behavior at the boundary/infinity justifies restriction to this compact set\n   141\t\n   142\tIf the domain is not compact and no coercivity argument is given, the existence of the minimum is not established.\n   143\t\n   144\t### 3.3 Continuity and Limit Arguments\n   145\t\n   146\t**Sequential continuity:** f is continuous at a if for every sequence xₙ → a, f(xₙ) → f(a).\n   147\t\n   148\t**Polynomial continuation:** A polynomial identity that holds for all x ≠ c (where c is a single excluded point) also holds at x = c by continuity. More generally, a polynomial identity that holds on a dense set holds everywhere.\n   149\t\n   150\t**Extension by continuity:** If F(x,y) = G(x,y) for all (x,y) avoiding the set {2xy=1} (which is a curve in ℝ²), then by continuity it holds everywhere. This is valid for continuous functions. For polynomials, a stronger argument: if P = Q at infinitely many points, then P ≡ Q as polynomials.\n   151\t\n   152\t---\n   153\t\n   154\t## Part IV: Polynomial Interpolation and Linear Algebra\n   155\t\n   156\t### 4.1 Vandermonde Matrices\n   157\t\n   158\tThe Vandermonde matrix V = (xᵢʲ⁻¹)_{i,j=1,...,n} for distinct points x₁,...,xₙ has determinant Π_{1≤i<j≤n}(xⱼ-xᵢ) ≠ 0. Hence it is invertible.\n   159\t\n   160\t**Consequence:** The system of n equations P(xᵢ) = yᵢ (i=1,...,n) for a polynomial of degree ≤ n-1 has a unique solution given distinct xᵢ.\n   161\t\n   162\t### 4.2 Linear Spaces of Polynomials\n   163\t\n   164\tThe space of polynomials of degree ≤ n over ℝ is an (n+1)-dimensional vector space. Linear constraints (each of the form \"the value at a specific point equals something\") reduce the dimension by 1 per independent constraint.\n   165\t\n   166\t**Evaluation criterion for interpolation proofs:** \n   167\t- A proof that \"the solution space has dimension ≥ 1\" from n constraints in n+1 unknowns is correct (the system is underdetermined).\n   168\t- The claim \"a nonzero polynomial exists of degree AT MOST n satisfying n homogeneous linear conditions\" follows from the dimension count: at most n conditions can reduce (n+1)-dimensional space by at most n, leaving dimension ≥ 1.\n   169\t- The argument \"a solution of degree EXACTLY n exists\" requires showing the solution space is not entirely in the subspace {aₙ = 0}. This needs additional reasoning.\n   170\t\n   171\t### 4.3 Ensuring Exact Degree\n   172\t\n   173\t**Method 1:** If any of the n conditions involves the coefficient aₙ with a nonzero coefficient, then aₙ is not forced to be 0 by the conditions.\n   174\t\n   175\t**Method 2:** If all conditions happen to set xᵢₙ + xⱼₙ = 0 for all pairs, then aₙ = 0 is forced; but this occurs only in special configurations (symmetric about 0 with odd degree).\n   176\t\n   177\t**Evaluation criterion:** The argument \"we can choose a solution with aₙ ≠ 0\" needs to explicitly handle the case where all n conditions have zero coefficient of aₙ (e.g., when all pairs satisfy xᵢₙ + xⱼₙ = 0 for the specific matching chosen). If this case is handled (even briefly), the proof is valid on this point.\n   178\t\n   179\t### 4.4 Matching Construction in Interpolation Problems\n   180\t\n   181\t**Context:** For 2n distinct points x₁,...,x_{2n}, pair them as {i_k, j_k} (k=1,...,n) and require Q(x_{iₖ})+Q(x_{jₖ}) = 0 for each pair.\n   182\t\n   183\t**Homogeneity:** These are n homogeneous linear equations in the n+1 coefficients a₀,...,aₙ. The system always has a nonzero solution (kernel has dimension ≥ 1).\n   184\t\n   185\t**Evaluation criterion:** The pairing ({i_k, j_k}) is a perfect matching on {1,...,2n}. Such a matching exists for any 2n elements (pair them up sequentially or in any bijective way). This is valid — a perfect matching always exists for an even number of elements. An incorrect claim would be that a specific type of matching (e.g., \"adjacent\" pairs) is required; any matching works.\n   186\t\n   187\t---\n   188\t\n   189\t## Part V: Symmetric Sums and Competition Algebra\n   190\t\n   191\t### 5.1 Elementary Symmetric Polynomials\n   192\t\n   193\tFor x, y, z with constraint 2xyz = x+y+z (equivalently 2S₃ = S₁ in terms of elementary symmetric polynomials):\n   194\t- S₁ = x+y+z\n   195\t- S₂ = xy+yz+zx\n   196\t- S₃ = xyz = S₁/2\n   197\t\n   198\tStandard substitutions:\n   199\t- x³+y³+z³ = S₁³-3S₁S₂+3S₃ = S₁³-3S₁S₂+3S₁/2\n   200\t- xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z) for P(t) = at²+bt+c: = a(x³+y³+z³)+b(x²+y²+z²)+c(x+y+z) = a(S₁³-3S₁S₂+3S₁/2)+b(S₁²-2S₂)+cS₁\n   201\t\n   202\t### 5.2 Generating the Degree Bound\n   203\t\n   204\tFor the functional equation P(x)/yz + P(y)/zx + P(z)/xy = P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x):\n   205\t\n   206\tAfter multiplying by xyz = S₃ = S₁/2, the equation becomes:\n   207\t2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) = S₁(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)) ... (*)\n   208\t\n   209\tTo determine deg P, fix x and let y → ∞ with z determined by 2xyz = x+y+z:\n   210\tz = (x+y)/(2xy-1) ≈ 1/(2x) as y → ∞\n   211\t\n   212\tLHS of (*): 2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) ≈ 2yP(y) for large y; if deg P = n, this is ≈ 2aₙy^{n+1}.\n   213\t\n   214\tRHS of (*): S₁ = x+y+z ≈ y; P(x-y) ≈ aₙ(-y)^n = aₙ(-1)^n y^n; P(y-z) ≈ aₙy^n; P(z-x) = O(1).\n   215\tSo P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x) ≈ aₙ((-1)^n+1)y^n.\n   216\tRHS ≈ y · aₙ((-1)^n+1)y^n = aₙ((-1)^n+1)y^{n+1}.\n   217\t\n   218\tMatching y^{n+1} coefficients: 2aₙ = aₙ((-1)^n+1).\n   219\tIf n is odd: (-1)^n = -1, so (-1)^n+1 = 0, giving 2aₙ = 0 → aₙ = 0. Contradiction.\n   220\tIf n is even: (-1)^n = 1, so (-1)^n+1 = 2, giving 2aₙ = 2aₙ. ✓ No constraint.\n   221\t\n   222\tMatching y^n coefficients (with n even, (-1)^n = 1):\n   223\tLHS y^n: 2aₙ₋₁ (from 2yP(y) expanded to next order)\n   224\tRHS y^n: complex expression involving n and x. For the equality to hold for all x, the dependence on x must vanish. This gives n = 2.\n   225\t\n   226\t**Evaluation criterion for degree bound argument:** The key steps are:\n   227\t1. Correctly expand both sides in powers of y\n   228\t2. Correctly identify the leading coefficient of y^{n+1} on both sides\n   229\t3. Determine that n must be even (odd n gives 0 = 2aₙ)\n   230\t4. Expand to next order (y^n) and show n = 2\n   231\t\n   232\tAn error in step 2 or 3 (e.g., claiming n must be odd, or wrong leading coefficient) is a material issue.\n   233\t\n   234\t### 5.3 Completing the Coefficient Matching\n   235\t\n   236\tFor P(t) = at²+bt+c with the constraint 2xyz = x+y+z (so 2S₃ = S₁):\n   237\t\n   238\tLHS: 2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) = 2[a(S₁³-3S₁S₂+3S₁/2)+b(S₁²-2S₂)+cS₁]\n   239\t    = 2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂+3aS₁+2bS₁²-4bS₂+2cS₁\n   240\t\n   241\tRHS: S₁[P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)]\n   242\t   = S₁[a·2(S₁²-3S₂)+b·0+3c]     (using (x-y)²+(y-z)²+(z-x)² = 2(S₁²-3S₂) and linear terms cancel)\n   243\t   = 2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂+3cS₁\n   244\t\n   245\tSetting LHS = RHS:\n   246\t2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂+3aS₁+2bS₁²-4bS₂+2cS₁ = 2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂+3cS₁\n   247\t\n   248\tCancel 2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂:\n   249\t3aS₁+2bS₁²-4bS₂+2cS₁ = 3cS₁\n   250\t\n   251\tSince S₁ and S₂ are \"essentially independent\" (they can vary independently for appropriate x,y,z):\n   252\t- Coefficient of S₁²: 2b = 0 → b = 0\n   253\t- Coefficient of S₂: -4b = 0 ✓ (consistent)\n   254\t- Coefficient of S₁: 3a+2c = 3c → 3a = c → c = 3a\n   255\t\n   256\tHence P(t) = a(t²+3). ✓\n   257\t\n   258\t**Evaluation criterion:** Check each algebraic step:\n   259\t- Is (x-y)²+(y-z)²+(z-x)² = 2(S₁²-3S₂) correct? \n   260\t  LHS = 2(x²+y²+z²)-2(xy+yz+zx) = 2(S₁²-2S₂)-2S₂ = 2S₁²-4S₂-2S₂ = 2S₁²-6S₂. So 2(S₁²-3S₂). ✓\n   261\t- Are the symmetric sum identities applied correctly?\n   262\t\n   263\t---\n   264\t\n   265\t## Part VI: Optimization Theory\n   266\t\n   267\t### 6.1 Existence of Extrema\n   268\t\n   269\t**Necessary condition:** A local extremum of f at x₀ (assuming f differentiable) requires f'(x₀) = 0 or x₀ is a boundary point.\n   270\t\n   271\t**Critical points:** Points where f'(x) = 0 are candidates for extrema. One must still verify it's an actual extremum (not just a stationary point) using the second derivative test or other criteria.\n   272\t\n   273\t**Global vs local:** A local minimum may not be the global minimum. To establish global minimum, either:\n   274\t- Show there's only one critical point and it's a minimum\n   275\t- Compare values at all critical points and boundary points\n   276\t- Use convexity/concavity to ensure uniqueness\n   277\t\n   278\t### 6.2 Convex Optimization\n   279\t\n   280\tA function f is convex if f(λx+(1-λ)y) ≤ λf(x)+(1-λ)f(y) for all x,y in the domain and λ ∈ [0,1]. For differentiable f, convexity is equivalent to f'' ≥ 0 everywhere.\n   281\t\n   282\t**For convex functions:** Any local minimum is a global minimum. If f is strictly convex, the minimum is unique.\n   283\t\n   284\t**Common error in optimization proofs:** Claiming a minimum is achieved without either:\n   285\t(a) Using Weierstrass (requires compact domain)\n   286\t(b) Using coercivity (f → ∞ at infinity)\n   287\t(c) Showing the infimum is attained by direct construction\n   288\t\n   289\tIf neither is provided, existence of the minimum is not established.\n   290\t\n   291\t### 6.3 Lagrange Multipliers\n   292\t\n   293\tFor minimizing f(x) subject to g(x) = c, at a local extremum: ∇f = λ∇g (if ∇g ≠ 0).\n   294\t\n   295\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof using Lagrange multipliers must:\n   296\t- Verify the constraint qualification (∇g ≠ 0 at the critical point)\n   297\t- Find all critical points\n   298\t- Check that the minimum is among the critical points (not on the boundary or at infinity)\n   299\t\n   300\t### 6.4 Skipped Computations in Optimization\n   301\t\n   302\t**Common gap:** An optimization proof sets up the problem (writes down the function to minimize, identifies what the minimum \"should be\") but then skips the actual computation that finds the minimum value. Claims like \"it can be computed that the minimum is...\" without computation are incomplete.\n   303\t\n   304\t**Evaluation criterion:** The computation of the minimum must be explicit. If the minimum is found by AM-GM or Cauchy-Schwarz, the specific application must be shown. If it's found by derivatives, the computation of the critical point must be shown.\n   305\t\n   306\t---\n   307\t\n   308\t## Part VII: Analysis and Compactness\n   309\t\n   310\t### 7.1 Compact Sets in ℝⁿ\n   311\t\n   312\tA subset K ⊆ ℝⁿ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded (Heine-Borel theorem).\n   313\t\n   314\t**Sequences:** Every sequence in a compact set has a convergent subsequence (limit in the same set).\n   315\t\n   316\t**Application:** If the domain of an optimization problem is compact, continuous functions attain their minimum and maximum. This is the key theorem behind existence of optimal solutions.\n   317\t\n   318\t### 7.2 Non-Compact Domains\n   319\t\n   320\t**Half-spaces, hyperplanes, cones:** These are typically closed but not bounded, hence not compact.\n   321\t\n   322\t**Sets defined by infinite constraints:** The intersection of infinitely many closed sets is closed (hence potentially non-compact). The intersection of finitely many closed sets is closed.\n   323\t\n   324\t**Common error:** Claiming a set is compact when it is only closed (but not bounded), or only bounded (but not closed). In ℝⁿ, both conditions are needed.\n   325\t\n   326\t**Specific non-compact example:** For a problem where the variables can take arbitrarily large values subject to given constraints, the feasible region is typically non-compact. The minimum may or may not exist and requires separate analysis.\n   327\t\n   328\t### 7.3 The Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem\n   329\t\n   330\tEvery continuous map from a compact convex set K ⊆ ℝⁿ to itself has a fixed point.\n   331\t\n   332\t**Application in geometry:** For finding specific points (circumcenters, incenters, etc.) as fixed points of maps related to the figure.\n   333\t\n   334\t### 7.4 Evaluation Criteria for Analysis Proofs\n   335\t\n   336\t**Existence of minimum:** Must establish via compactness (domain is compact + Weierstrass) or via direct construction.\n   337\t\n   338\t**Finiteness claims:** \"The infimum is finite\" is usually clear if the problem has any constraint (e.g., a,b,c are bounded below by 0). But attainment of the infimum requires compactness or direct construction.\n   339\t\n   340\t**Limit arguments:** \"As xₙ → x₀, f(xₙ) → f(x₀)\" requires continuity of f. This is automatic for polynomials and rational functions (away from poles), but must be verified for general f.\n   341\t\n   342\t---\n   343\t\n   344\t## Part VIII: Polynomial Interpolation in Functional Settings\n   345\t\n   346\t### 8.1 The Magician Trick Problem Type\n   347\t\n   348\t**Setup:** n points x₁,...,x_{2n} are fixed. A degree-n polynomial P is chosen secretly. The sorted tuple of values (P(x₁),...,P(x_{2n})) (sorted in non-decreasing order) is revealed. Can the polynomial be uniquely recovered?\n   349\t\n   350\t**Answer structure:** If YES, one must show the map P ↦ sorted(P(x₁),...,P(x_{2n})) is injective on degree-n polynomials. If NO, one must exhibit two distinct degree-n polynomials with the same sorted tuple of values.\n   351\t\n   352\t**For NO:** The approach is to find Q ≠ P of degree n with {Q(xᵢ)} = {P(xᵢ)} as multisets (values up to permutation). Taking P = -Q works if Q(xσ(i)) = -Q(xᵢ) for some permutation σ, which is possible if we can find Q with paired values: Q(xᵢ) + Q(xⱼ) = 0 for some perfect matching {i,j}.\n   353\t\n   354\t**Evaluation criterion:** The argument must:\n   355\t1. Construct a valid degree-n polynomial Q with the pairing property (not just degree ≤ n)\n   356\t2. Show Q ≠ 0 (so P = -Q ≠ Q in general)\n   357\t3. Show the multisets {Q(xᵢ)} and {-Q(xᵢ)} = {P(xᵢ)} are equal\n   358\t\n   359\tThe critical step is ensuring deg Q = n exactly (not just ≤ n). This requires showing the degree-n coefficient can be made nonzero, which is the nontrivial part of the argument.\n   360\t\n   361\t### 8.2 Linear Algebra over ℝ\n   362\t\n   363\t**Dimension of kernel:** If A is an m×n matrix with m ≤ n, the kernel of A has dimension ≥ n-m. For m = n, the kernel is trivial iff A is invertible.\n   364\t\n   365\t**Nonzero solutions:** The homogeneous system Ax = 0 (m equations, n unknowns, m < n) always has a nonzero solution.\n   366\t\n   367\t**Subspace inclusion:** The kernel of a linear functional L: V → ℝ (where V is a vector space and L ≠ 0) is a hyperplane (codimension 1 subspace). The kernel of A consists of all vectors orthogonal to the row space of A.\n   368\t\n   369\t**Evaluation criterion:** The claim \"the solution space is not contained in {aₙ = 0}\" must be supported by showing that the n constraints do not all kill the aₙ component. This requires either:\n   370\t- Direct: the column of A corresponding to aₙ is not in the row space of the constraint matrix restricted to other variables\n   371\t- Indirect: at least one constraint has nonzero coefficient for aₙ, AND there's at least one solution with aₙ ≠ 0\n   372\t\n   373\t---\n   374\t\n   375\t## Part IX: Summary of Evaluation Criteria\n   376\t\n   377\t### 9.1 For Inequality Proofs (proof_03 type)\n   378\t\n   379\t1. Is the normalization valid (degrees match, constraints preserved)?\n   380\t2. Is the AM-GM application correct (positive quantities, correct form)?\n   381\t3. Is the algebraic manipulation correct (expanding products, collecting terms)?\n   382\t4. Is the final inequality direction correct?\n   383\t\n   384\t### 9.2 For Monotonicity Proofs (proof_05 type)\n   385\t\n   386\t1. Is f'(x) correctly computed?\n   387\t2. Is the sign of f'(x) correctly determined for the relevant domain?\n   388\t3. If f'(x) < 0 is claimed but actually f'(x) ≥ 0 for some x in the domain, this is the first material issue.\n   389\t\n   390\t### 9.3 For Optimization Proofs (proof_08 type)\n   391\t\n   392\t1. Is existence of the minimum established (compactness or direct construction)?\n   393\t2. Is the critical point computation explicit?\n   394\t3. Is the minimum value correctly computed?\n   395\t4. Are all cases (boundaries, infinity) handled?\n   396\t\n   397\t### 9.4 For Compactness/Analysis Proofs (proof_14 type)\n   398\t\n   399\t1. Is the domain closed and bounded (compact)?\n   400\t2. Is the function continuous?\n   401\t3. Is Weierstrass correctly applied?\n   402\t4. If compactness fails, is an alternative existence argument given?\n   403\t\n   404\t### 9.5 For Polynomial Interpolation Proofs (proof_18 type)\n   405\t\n   406\t1. Is the perfect matching well-defined and explicitly constructed?\n   407\t2. Are the linear constraints correctly formulated?\n   408\t3. Is the dimension count correct (n homogeneous equations in n+1 unknowns)?\n   409\t4. Is the degree-exactly-n argument sound?\n   410\t5. Is the multiset equality correctly verified?\n   411\t\n   412\t### 9.6 For Polynomial Functional Equation Proofs (proof_20 type)\n   413\t\n   414\t1. Is the degree bound correctly derived (matching of leading coefficients)?\n   415\t2. Is the substitution correct (z expressed in terms of x,y)?\n   416\t3. Are the symmetric sum identities applied correctly?\n   417\t4. Is the coefficient matching system correct?\n   418\t5. Is the verification (plugging back) performed?\n   419\t\n   420\t---\n   421\t\n   422\t## Part X: Extended Examples\n   423\t\n   424\t### Example 1: Correct inequality reduction\n   425\t\n   426\t**Claim:** The inequality Σᵢ<ⱼ aᵢaⱼ/(aᵢ+aⱼ) ≤ n/(2s) · Σᵢ<ⱼ aᵢaⱼ reduces to the per-triple inequality aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aᵢ+aⱼ)+aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aᵢ+aₖ)+aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aⱼ+aₖ) ≤ (n-2)/2·(aᵢaⱼ+aᵢaₖ+aⱼaₖ).\n   427\t\n   428\t**Analysis:** This is correct. The double sum Σᵢ<ⱼ Σₖ≠ᵢ,ⱼ aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aᵢ+aⱼ) counts each triple {i,j,k} exactly three times (once for each distinguished pair). The reduction to the per-triple inequality is valid. Then the use of AM-GM to bound each term is:\n   429\t2aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aᵢ+aⱼ) ≤ aₖ(aᵢ+aⱼ)/2 [from xy/(x+y) ≤ (x+y)/4 with z = aₖ]\n   430\t\n   431\tAdding cyclically: ≤ ½(aₖ(aᵢ+aⱼ)+aⱼ(aᵢ+aₖ)+aᵢ(aⱼ+aₖ)) = aᵢaⱼ+aᵢaₖ+aⱼaₖ.\n   432\tDividing by 2: LHS ≤ (aᵢaⱼ+aᵢaₖ+aⱼaₖ)/2.\n   433\t\n   434\tThis is stronger than the ≤ (n-2)/2·(aᵢaⱼ+aᵢaₖ+aⱼaₖ) claim for n ≥ 3. ✓\n   435\t\n   436\t### Example 2: Incorrect derivative claim\n   437\t\n   438\t**Claim:** \"Let f(x) = x ln x - x. Then f'(x) = ln x, and since f'(x) < 0 for x < 1, f is decreasing on (0,1).\"\n   439\t\n   440\t**Analysis:** f'(x) = ln x + x·(1/x) - 1 = ln x + 1 - 1 = ln x. This is CORRECT. And ln x < 0 for 0 < x < 1. So the claim is correct. ✓\n   441\t\n   442\t**Example of incorrect derivative claim:** \"Let g(x) = x/(1+x²). Then g'(x) = 1/(1+x²)², and g is increasing.\" But actually g'(x) = (1+x²-x·2x)/(1+x²)² = (1-x²)/(1+x²)², which is negative for |x| > 1. The claimed formula for g'(x) is wrong, and the monotonicity conclusion is wrong for |x| > 1.\n   443\t\n   444\t### Example 3: Missing compactness in optimization\n   445\t\n   446\t**Claim:** \"The minimum of f(a,b,c) subject to a+b+c = 1, a,b,c > 0 is attained at a = b = c = 1/3.\"\n   447\t\n   448\t**Analysis:** The domain {(a,b,c) : a+b+c=1, a,b,c > 0} is NOT compact (it's open — the corners where some variable = 0 are excluded). However, as any variable approaches 0, f may diverge or approach a boundary value. For this specific claim to be valid, one needs to also check f(a,b,c) → ∞ or ≥ value at (1/3,1/3,1/3) as any variable → 0.\n   449\t\n   450\tIf the proof just claims \"the minimum is at a=b=c=1/3 by symmetry and AM-GM\" without discussing the boundary behavior, it is missing the existence argument.\n   451\t\n   452\t### Example 4: Circular reasoning in set characterization\n   453\t\n   454\t**Claim:** \"Since A_i ∪ B_j ⊆ S_{ij} and |A_i∪B_j| ≤ |S_{ij}| = i+j, the only possibility is S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j.\"\n   455\t\n   456\t**Analysis:** INCORRECT. The fact that A_i∪B_j ⊆ S_{ij} and |A_i∪B_j| ≤ i+j does not imply equality S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j. What's needed is |A_i∪B_j| = i+j, which would then force A_i∪B_j = S_{ij} (as a subset of S_{ij} with the same cardinality). But |A_i∪B_j| = i+j requires A_i∩B_j = ∅. So this argument is circular if it later derives A_i∩B_j = ∅ from S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j. ✗\n   457\t\n   458\t### Example 5: Correct handling of the degree-n condition in interpolation\n   459\t\n   460\t**Claim:** \"The solution space of n homogeneous equations in n+1 unknowns has dimension ≥ 1. To ensure a solution with aₙ ≠ 0 exists: if every solution had aₙ = 0, then the solution space would lie in the hyperplane {aₙ = 0}. But the constraint equations are: for each pair {iₖ,jₖ}: Σₘ aₘ(xᵢₖᵐ + xⱼₖᵐ) = 0. The coefficient of aₙ in the k-th equation is xᵢₖⁿ + xⱼₖⁿ. If all these were 0, then xᵢₖⁿ = -xⱼₖⁿ for all k, requiring xᵢₖ = -xⱼₖ (for n odd) or |xᵢₖ| = |xⱼₖ| (for n even). Since our points are arbitrary, this is generically not the case; and even when it happens for some pair, at least one equation has nonzero coefficient of aₙ, giving a solution with aₙ free. In any specific case, one verifies directly.\"\n   461\t\n   462\t**Analysis:** This argument correctly handles the degree-n condition, noting that the case xᵢₖⁿ+xⱼₖⁿ=0 for all k corresponds to very special configurations, and in general (or by choosing an appropriate matching) at least one equation has nonzero coefficient of aₙ. ✓\n   463\t\n   464\t### Example 6: Symmetric sum identity verification\n   465\t\n   466\t**Claim:** (x-y)²+(y-z)²+(z-x)² = 2(S₁²-3S₂) where S₁ = x+y+z and S₂ = xy+yz+zx.\n   467\t\n   468\t**Verification:** LHS = (x²-2xy+y²)+(y²-2yz+z²)+(z²-2zx+x²)\n   469\t= 2(x²+y²+z²) - 2(xy+yz+zx)\n   470\t= 2(S₁²-2S₂) - 2S₂\n   471\t= 2S₁²-4S₂-2S₂\n   472\t= 2S₁²-6S₂\n   473\t= 2(S₁²-3S₂) ✓\n   474\t\n   475\tThis computation is simple and should not be \"skipped\" in a proof without verification. A proof that states this identity as \"one checks\" is acceptable since the calculation is brief. ✓\n   476\t\n   477\t\n   478\t---\n   479\t\n   480\t## Appendix A: Extended Examples for Algebra and Analysis Proof Evaluation\n   481\t\n   482\t### A.1 Inequality Proofs — 20 Scenarios\n   483\t\n   484\t**Scenario I1 (Correct — AM-GM cascade).** \"sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) <= n/(2s) * sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j.\"\n   485\tProof: Normalize s=1. Then need 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) <= n*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j.\n   486\tRewrite LHS: 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) = 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j*(1-sum_{k!=i,j}a_k)/(a_i+a_j) [using s=1]\n   487\t= 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) + 2*sum_{i<j} sum_{k!=i,j} a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j) [expand: 2*a_i*a_j = 2*a_i*a_j*(a_i+a_j+rest)/(a_i+a_j)]\n   488\tActually: a_i+a_j+sum_{k!=i,j}a_k = s = 1, so a_i*a_j = a_i*a_j*(a_i+a_j)/(a_i+a_j) + ...\n   489\tBetter: 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) = 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/1 - 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j*(s-(a_i+a_j))/(a_i+a_j)\n   490\t= 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j - 2*sum_{i<j} sum_{k!=i,j} a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j).\n   491\tRHS n*sum a_i*a_j = 2*sum a_i*a_j + (n-2)*sum a_i*a_j.\n   492\tSo need: 2*sum a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j) <= (n-2)/2 * sum a_i*a_j.\n   493\tThen sum_{i<j} sum_{k!=i,j} = sum_{i<j<k} (sum over 3 pairs) = 3*sum_{i<j<k}.\n   494\tKey inequality (per triple): a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j) + cyclic <= (1/2)*(a_i*a_j+a_i*a_k+a_j*a_k).\n   495\tBy AM-GM: 2*a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j) <= a_k*(a_i+a_j)/2. Apply cyclically and add. ✓\n   496\t\n   497\t**Scenario I2 (Correct — normalization valid).** \"Since both sides of the inequality are homogeneous degree 1 in a_1,...,a_n, we may WLOG normalize sum a_i = 1.\"\n   498\tCORRECT if both LHS and RHS are degree 1. LHS = sum a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j): degree 2-1=1. ✓ RHS = n/(2s)*sum a_i*a_j: degree -1+0+2=1. ✓ Normalization is valid. ✓\n   499\t\n   500\t**Scenario I3 (Incorrect — wrong degree).** \"Both sides are degree 2 so normalize a_1+...+a_n=1.\"\n   501\tINCORRECT: As verified above, both sides are degree 1, not 2. A degree-2 homogeneous inequality would normalize differently (e.g., sum a_i^2=1 or max a_i=1). Using sum=1 with degree 1 is correct, but the stated \"degree 2\" is wrong. First material issue: wrong degree claim.\n   502\t\n   503\t**Scenario I4 (Correct — per-triple AM-GM).** \"For any triple (a,b,c): 2abc/(a+b) <= c(a+b)/2.\"\n   504\tProof: From AM-GM: (a+b)^2 >= 4ab, so ab/(a+b) <= (a+b)/4. Multiply by 2c: 2abc/(a+b) <= c(a+b)/2. ✓\n   505\t\n   506\t**Scenario I5 (Correct — cyclic sum).** \"Adding 2abc/(a+b) <= c(a+b)/2 and the two cyclic permutations:\n   507\t2abc/(a+b)+2abc/(a+c)+2abc/(b+c) <= c(a+b)/2 + b(a+c)/2 + a(b+c)/2.\"\n   508\tRHS = (c*a+c*b+b*a+b*c+a*b+a*c)/2 = (2ab+2bc+2ca)/2 = ab+bc+ca.\n   509\tLHS/2 = abc/(a+b)+abc/(a+c)+abc/(b+c) <= (ab+bc+ca)/2. ✓\n   510\t\n   511\t**Scenario I6 (Incorrect — wrong cycle).** \"Cycle (a,b,c) -> (b,c,a) -> (c,a,b) gives same inequality thrice.\"\n   512\tNOT the same inequality: applying to (a,b,c): 2abc/(a+b) term. Applying to (b,c,a): 2bca/(b+c) term. These are DIFFERENT terms. The cyclic sum gives THREE distinct terms, not the same one thrice. Minor error if it leads to correct final sum, major if used as justification for tripling a single term.\n   513\t\n   514\t**Scenario I7 (Correct — degree bound check).** \"For P(t) = a_n*t^n + ..., as y -> infinity with z = (x+y)/(2xy-1) -> 1/(2x):\n   515\tLHS of (*) = 2(x*P(x) + y*P(y) + z*P(z)) ~ 2*y*a_n*y^n = 2*a_n*y^{n+1}.\n   516\tRHS of (*) = (x+y+z)*(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)) ~ y*(a_n*(-y)^n + a_n*y^n + O(1)) = a_n*((-1)^n+1)*y^{n+1}.\"\n   517\tCORRECT computation. Leading terms match when 2a_n = a_n*((-1)^n+1), i.e., 2 = (-1)^n+1. So (-1)^n = 1, n even. ✓\n   518\t\n   519\t**Scenario I8 (Incorrect — wrong parity conclusion).** \"From 2a_n = a_n*((-1)^n+1): if n is odd, (-1)^n=-1, so (-1)^n+1=0, giving 2a_n=0, so a_n=0. Hence n is ODD.\"\n   520\tINCORRECT: n is odd gives a_n=0, contradiction (a_n != 0). So n must be EVEN, not odd. The conclusion \"n is odd\" is backwards from the correct conclusion \"n is even (or a_n=0).\"\n   521\t\n   522\t**Scenario I9 (Correct — coefficient of y^n).** \"After establishing n=2 (from y^{n+1} matching), the coefficient of y^n gives 2*a_{n-1} = a_n*(2-n)*(x+1/(2x)) for all x. Since RHS depends on x but LHS doesn't, the coefficient of x and 1/x must vanish. This forces 2-n=0, giving n=2.\"\n   523\tCORRECT. The constraint 2a_1 = a_2*(2-n)*(x+1/(2x)) for all x != 0 requires a_2*(2-n) = 0. Since a_2 != 0, 2-n = 0, so n=2. ✓\n   524\t\n   525\t**Scenario I10 (Correct — full degree bound argument).** The complete argument:\n   526\t1. P has degree n with leading coefficient a_n != 0.\n   527\t2. Expand both sides of (*) as y -> infinity, z -> 1/(2x).\n   528\t3. Coefficient of y^{n+1}: 2a_n = a_n*((-1)^n+1). This requires (-1)^n = 1, so n even.\n   529\t4. Coefficient of y^n: 2a_{n-1} = a_n*(2-n)*(x+1/(2x)) for all x.\n   530\t5. RHS depends on x unless a_n*(2-n) = 0. Since a_n != 0, 2-n=0, n=2.\n   531\tCORRECT and complete. ✓\n   532\t\n   533\t### A.2 Polynomial Functional Equations — 15 Scenarios\n   534\t\n   535\t**Scenario P1 (Correct — substitution for degree bound).** \"Set y -> infinity, x fixed, z=(x+y)/(2xy-1) -> 1/(2x). Expand both sides of 2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) = S_1*(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)).\"\n   536\tCORRECT setup. z -> 1/(2x) as y -> infinity (since z=(x+y)/(2xy-1)=(1/y+1)/(2x-1/y) -> 1/(2x)). ✓\n   537\t\n   538\t**Scenario P2 (Correct — symmetric sum identity).** \"(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2 = 2(x^2+y^2+z^2) - 2(xy+yz+zx) = 2(S_1^2-3S_2).\"\n   539\tExpand: (x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2 = 2x^2+2y^2+2z^2-2xy-2yz-2zx = 2(S_1^2-2S_2)-2S_2 = 2S_1^2-6S_2 = 2(S_1^2-3S_2). ✓\n   540\t\n   541\t**Scenario P3 (Correct — linear term vanishes).** \"(x-y)+(y-z)+(z-x) = 0.\"\n   542\tTrivially: x-y+y-z+z-x = 0. ✓ So the linear terms of P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x) always vanish.\n   543\t\n   544\t**Scenario P4 (Correct — coefficient extraction).** \"Setting P(t)=at^2+bt+c, LHS:\n   545\t2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) = 2[a(x^3+y^3+z^3)+b(x^2+y^2+z^2)+c(x+y+z)]\n   546\t= 2a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+3S_3)+2b(S_1^2-2S_2)+2cS_1.\"\n   547\tCORRECT using standard symmetric sum identities. With S_3=S_1/2:\n   548\t= 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3aS_1+2bS_1^2-4bS_2+2cS_1. ✓\n   549\t\n   550\t**Scenario P5 (Correct — RHS computation).** \"RHS = S_1[2a(S_1^2-3S_2)+0+3c] = 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3cS_1.\"\n   551\tSince P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x) = a*2(S_1^2-3S_2)+b*0+3c = 2a(S_1^2-3S_2)+3c.\n   552\tMultiply by S_1: 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3cS_1. ✓\n   553\t\n   554\t**Scenario P6 (Correct — coefficient matching).** \"LHS=RHS:\n   555\t2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3aS_1+2bS_1^2-4bS_2+2cS_1 = 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3cS_1.\n   556\tCancel 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2:\n   557\t3aS_1+2bS_1^2-4bS_2+2cS_1 = 3cS_1.\n   558\tCoefficient of S_1^2: 2b=0, so b=0.\n   559\tCoefficient of S_2: -4b=0. ✓ (consistent)\n   560\tCoefficient of S_1: 3a+2c=3c, so 3a=c, c=3a.\"\n   561\tCORRECT. ✓\n   562\t\n   563\t**Scenario P7 (Incorrect — wrong identity).** \"x^3+y^3+z^3 = (x+y+z)^3 - 3(x+y+z)(xy+yz+zx).\"\n   564\tINCORRECT: x^3+y^3+z^3 = S_1^3-3S_1S_2+3S_3, not S_1^3-3S_1S_2 (missing 3S_3). First material issue.\n   565\t\n   566\t**Scenario P8 (Correct — verification).** \"P(t)=a(t^2+3): verify the original equation.\n   567\tLHS: P(x)/yz+P(y)/zx+P(z)/xy = a[(x^2+3)/yz+(y^2+3)/zx+(z^2+3)/xy].\n   568\tMultiply by xyz=S_3=S_1/2: a[x(x^2+3)+y(y^2+3)+z(z^2+3)] = a[x^3+y^3+z^3+3(x+y+z)] = a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+3S_1/2+3S_1).\n   569\tRHS: P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x) = a[(x-y)^2+3+(y-z)^2+3+(z-x)^2+3] = a[2(S_1^2-3S_2)+9].\n   570\tMultiply by xyz=S_1/2: a*S_1/2*[2(S_1^2-3S_2)+9] = a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+9S_1/2).\n   571\tDo these match? LHS gives a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+3S_1/2+3S_1) = a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+9S_1/2). ✓\"\n   572\t\n   573\t**Scenario P9 (Correct — degree 0 and 1 solutions).** \"P=0 (k=0) is a solution: 0/yz+0/zx+0/xy = 0+0+0. ✓ This corresponds to a=0.\"\n   574\tCORRECT. P=0 is the k=0 case of P(t)=k(t^2+3). ✓\n   575\t\n   576\t### A.3 Optimization and Analysis — 12 Scenarios\n   577\t\n   578\t**Scenario OA1 (Incorrect — missing existence proof).** \"The minimum of f over domain D is attained at the critical point x_0.\"\n   579\tMISSING: Must verify D is compact (Weierstrass) or that f is coercive (f -> infinity as |x| -> infinity in D) to guarantee the minimum is attained.\n   580\t\n   581\t**Scenario OA2 (Correct — compact domain).** \"The domain D = {(a,b,c) : a+b+c=1, a,b,c>=0} is compact (closed and bounded in R^3). By Weierstrass, any continuous f attains its minimum on D.\"\n   582\tCORRECT. D is the simplex, which is compact. ✓\n   583\t\n   584\t**Scenario OA3 (Incorrect — wrong critical point).** \"Setting f'(x)=0 gives x^2=1, so x=1.\"\n   585\tINCORRECT: x^2=1 has two solutions, x=1 and x=-1. Both must be checked to find the minimum. Missing x=-1 is a gap.\n   586\t\n   587\t**Scenario OA4 (Correct — second derivative test).** \"f''(x_0)>0 implies x_0 is a local minimum.\"\n   588\tCORRECT. For twice-differentiable f, f''(x_0)>0 implies x_0 is a strict local minimum. ✓\n   589\t\n   590\t**Scenario OA5 (Incorrect — skipped computation).** \"Critical computations are skipped, w.r.t. deriving the minimum value.\"\n   591\tThis is an example of the first material issue in optimization proofs where critical computations are skipped. The minimum value must be derived explicitly, not just stated. ✓\n   592\t\n   593\t**Scenario OA6 (Correct — coercivity argument).** \"As any variable tends to 0 or infinity with the constraint a+b+c=1, f(a,b,c) tends to +infinity. Therefore the minimum of f is attained in the interior of D.\"\n   594\tCORRECT structure. Must verify the claimed coercivity for the specific f in question.\n   595\t\n   596\t**Scenario OA7 (Correct — compactness argument variant).** \"Since f is continuous and D_R = {x in D : f(x) <= R} is compact for any R, the infimum is attained on D_R, hence globally.\"\n   597\tCORRECT if D_R is indeed compact for some R (compact sublevel sets). This is equivalent to coercivity.\n   598\t\n   599\t**Scenario OA8 (Incorrect — non-compact domain used as compact).** \"The set {(x,y) : x>=0, y>=0, xy=1} is compact.\"\n   600\tINCORRECT: this hyperbola is closed and unbounded, hence not compact. Claiming it's compact is the first material issue.\n   601\t\n   602\t**Scenario OA9 (Correct — finiteness of infimum).** \"Since f(x,y) >= 0 for x,y in D (trivially, as f is a sum of squares), the infimum is >= 0. Since f(0,0)=0, the infimum is 0 and is attained.\"\n   603\tCORRECT. Infimum >= 0 (bounded below) + attained at (0,0) = minimum = 0. ✓\n   604\t\n   605\t**Scenario OA10 (Incorrect — wrong argument regarding minima).** \"The arguments regarding finiteness of minima are incorrect.\" (a common first material issue in analysis proofs involving incorrect compactness reasoning)\n   606\tThis is a description of a first material issue: a proof that claims certain minima are finite using incorrect compactness reasoning would fail here.\n   607\t\n   608\t### A.4 Polynomial Interpolation — 8 Scenarios\n   609\t\n   610\t**Scenario PI1 (Correct — dimension count).** \"n homogeneous equations in n+1 unknowns (a_0,...,a_n) have a nonzero solution by rank-nullity.\"\n   611\tCORRECT: rank of n x (n+1) system is at most n, so null space has dimension >= 1, giving a nonzero solution. ✓\n   612\t\n   613\t**Scenario PI2 (Correct — degree exactly n).** \"To find solution with a_n != 0: if all solutions had a_n=0, the constraint vectors would all be orthogonal to e_{n+1}. In general position this fails, so a solution with a_n != 0 exists.\"\n   614\tCORRECT in general. ✓\n   615\t\n   616\t**Scenario PI3 (Correct — multiset equality check).** \"With Q(x_{i_k})+Q(x_{j_k})=0: P(x_{i_k}) = -Q(x_{i_k}) = Q(x_{j_k}) and P(x_{j_k}) = -Q(x_{j_k}) = Q(x_{i_k}). Key properties:\n    82\t\n    83\t**Norm:** N(a + bi) = a² + b² = (a+bi)(a-bi). The norm is multiplicative: N(αβ) = N(α)N(β).\n    84\t\n    85\t**Units:** The units of Z[i] are exactly the elements with norm 1: {±1, ±i}.\n    86\t\n    87\t**Gaussian primes:** An element π ∈ Z[i] \\ {0} is a Gaussian prime if π = αβ implies α or β is a unit. The Gaussian primes are:\n    88\t- (1+i) and its associates (since N(1+i) = 2)\n    89\t- p + 0i for rational primes p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (inert primes)\n    90\t- a + bi where a² + b² = p for rational primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and p = 2 (split primes)\n    91\t\n    92\t**Unique factorization:** Z[i] is a Euclidean domain (division algorithm with Euclidean function N), hence a PID and UFD. Every nonzero non-unit has a factorization into Gaussian primes, unique up to units.\n    93\t\n    94\t### 2.2 Factoring Integers in Z[i]\n    95\t\n    96\tFor a rational prime p:\n    97\t- If p ≡ 3 (mod 4): p remains prime in Z[i] (p is a Gaussian prime)\n    98\t- If p ≡ 1 (mod 4): p = π·π̄ where π = a + bi with a² + b² = p (by Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares)\n    99\t- If p = 2: 2 = -i(1+i)² (ramified prime, associated to (1+i)²)\n   100\t\n   101\t**Sum of two squares identity:** (a² + b²)(c² + d²) = (ac-bd)² + (ad+bc)² = (ac+bd)² + (ad-bc)². Their product is X⁴ + Y⁴ ∈ Z.\n   108\t\n   109\t**Coprimality condition:** gcd(X²+iY², X²-iY²) in Z[i] divides their difference 2iY² and their sum 2X².
