When solutions exist, the general solution is x = x₀ + (b/d)t, y = y₀ - (a/d)t for t ∈ Z, where d = gcd(a,b) and (x₀,y₀) is any particular solution.\n   144\t\n   145\t### 3.2 Pythagorean Triples\n   146\t\n   147\tInteger solutions to x² + y² = z² with gcd(x,y,z) = 1 and x,z > 0, y even are:\n   148\tx = m² - n², y = 2mn, z = m² + n²\n   149\tfor positive integers m > n with gcd(m,n) = 1 and m ≢ n (mod 2).\n   150\t\n   151\t### 3.3 Fermat's Last Theorem Context\n   152\t\n   153\tFor n ≥ 3, the equation xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no solutions in positive integers. The proof for n = 4 (Fermat himself) and n = 3 (Euler) uses infinite descent. The general case is Wiles's theorem (1995). In olympiad contexts, fourth-power problems often use Gaussian integer factorizations.\n   154\t\n   155\t### 3.4 Valuation Theory\n   156\t\n   157\tThe p-adic valuation v_p(n) is the exponent of p in the prime factorization of n. Properties:\n   158\t- v_p(ab) = v_p(a) + v_p(b)\n   159\t- v_p(a+b) ≥ min(v_p(a), v_p(b)) with equality if v_p(a) ≠ v_p(b)\n   160\t- v_p(a^n) = n · v_p(a)\n   161\t\n   162\t**Divisibility by prime powers:** n | m if and only if v_p(n) ≤ v_p(m) for all primes p.\n   163\t\n   164\t**Common error:** Using v_p(a+b) = min(v_p(a), v_p(b)) when v_p(a) = v_p(b). In this case, v_p(a+b) could be strictly greater than min(v_p(a), v_p(b)).\n   165\t\n   166\t---\n   167\t\n   168\t## Part IV: Multiplicative Functions and Arithmetic Functions\n   169\t\n   170\t### 4.1 The Euler Totient Function\n   171\t\n   172\tφ(n) = |{1 ≤ k ≤ n : gcd(k,n)=1}|. Key properties:\n   173\t- φ(p) = p-1 for prime p\n   174\t- φ(p^k) = p^k - p^{k-1} = p^{k-1}(p-1) for prime power p^k\n   175\t- φ is multiplicative: gcd(m,n)=1 implies φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n)\n   176\t- Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n\n   177\t\n   178\t### 4.2 The Number and Sum of Divisors\n   179\t\n   180\tτ(n) = number of divisors of n, σ(n) = sum of divisors of n. Both are multiplicative. For prime power p^k: τ(p^k) = k+1, σ(p^k) = (p^{k+1}-1)/(p-1).\n   181\t\n   182\t### 4.3 Mobius Function and Inversion\n   183\t\n   184\tThe Möbius function: μ(1) = 1, μ(n) = (-1)^k if n is a product of k distinct primes, μ(n) = 0 if p² | n for some prime p.\n   185\t\n   186\t**Möbius inversion formula:** If f(n) = Σ_{d|n} g(d) then g(n) = Σ_{d|n} μ(n/d) f(d).\n   187\t\n   188\t---\n   189\t\n   190\t## Part V: Prime Distribution and Dirichlet's Theorem\n   191\t\n   192\t### 5.1 Dirichlet's Theorem on Primes in Arithmetic Progressions\n   193\t\n   194\tFor gcd(a,d) = 1, the arithmetic progression {a, a+d, a+2d, ...} contains infinitely many primes. Moreover, the primes are equidistributed among the φ(d) coprime residue classes modulo d.\n   195\t\n   196\t**Consequence:** If a property holds for all primes p > N, and it is asserted that only finitely many primes can satisfy a given fixed congruence condition, this requires careful use of Dirichlet's theorem or direct analysis of the fixed integer whose prime factors are at issue.\n   197\t\n   198\t**Key application:** If D is a fixed nonzero integer and we need p | D for all primes p in some infinite set, then D must be 0. This is because any nonzero integer has finitely many prime divisors. This principle is heavily used in the polynomial-prime divisibility problems.\n   199\t\n   200\t### 5.2 Chebyshev's Theorem\n   201\t\n   202\tThere is always a prime between n and 2n for n ≥ 1. This is weaker than PNT but sufficient for many olympiad applications.\n   203\t\n   204\t---\n   205\t\n   206\t## Part VI: Common Proof Structures in Number Theory Problems\n   207\t\n   208\t### 6.1 Infinite Descent\n   209\t\n   210\tUsed to show Diophantine equations have no positive integer solutions. Assume a minimal positive solution exists and derive a smaller solution, contradicting minimality.\n   211\t\n   212\t**Evaluation criterion:** The descent step must produce a strictly smaller (by well-ordering) solution. A proof that claims \"we can repeat this process\" without explicit minimality or termination is incomplete.\n   213\t\n   214\t### 6.2 Polynomial Congruences\n   215\t\n   216\tFor a polynomial f(x) ∈ Z[x] of degree d, the number of roots modulo prime p is at most d (by Lagrange's theorem). This is used to analyze when a polynomial vanishes at many primes.\n   217\t\n   218\t**Key lemma:** If f(p) ≡ 0 (mod p) for all primes p in an infinite set, and f has degree d < p for large p, then either f ≡ 0 or p | leading coefficient for infinitely many p (both impossible if leading coefficient is fixed nonzero). Hence f ≡ 0.\n   219\t\n   220\t**Stronger result:** If D(r) = 2(-1)^{r+1} + r! is a fixed integer and D(r) ≡ 0 (mod p) for all primes p > r, then D(r) = 0 (since only finitely many primes divide a fixed nonzero integer).\n   221\t\n   222\t### 6.3 Divisibility Chains\n   223\t\n   224\tWhen establishing p | f(n) for a prime p and fixed polynomial f, a common technique is:\n   225\t1. Write f(n) in terms of (n-1)! using Wilson's theorem\n   226\t2. Compute (n-r)! in terms of (n-1)! using the factorial identity\n   227\t3. Derive a fixed constant that must be ≡ 0 (mod p) for all large primes p\n   228\t4. Conclude the constant is 0\n   229\t\n   230\t**Evaluation criterion:** Step 4 requires the explicit argument that a fixed nonzero integer cannot be divisible by all sufficiently large primes. This is often stated as \"the only way infinitely many primes can divide a fixed integer is if that integer is zero.\" This argument is valid and may be stated briefly in a competition proof.\n   231\t\n   232\t### 6.4 Parameterization of Divisors\n   233\t\n   234\tWhen p^k | f(a,b) and p ∤ a and p ∤ b, we can sometimes factor f and analyze which prime power divides each factor separately. This often involves writing f(a,b) = g(a,b) · h(a,b) and showing gcd(g,h) | m for some explicit m.\n   235\t\n   236\t---\n   237\t\n   238\t## Part VII: Standard Techniques Specific to the Proofs in This Audit\n   239\t\n   240\t### 7.1 Polynomial Divisibility and Wilson's Theorem (proof_01 type)\n   241\t\n   242\t**Problem type:** Find all monic polynomials f ∈ Z[x] such that p | 2(f(p))!+1 for all large primes p.\n   243\t\n   244\t**Standard approach:**\n   245\t1. **Degree bound:** For deg f ≥ 2, f(p) ≥ p for large p, so p | (f(p))! and thus 2(f(p))!+1 ≡ 1 (mod p) ≠ 0. Eliminates deg ≥ 2.\n   246\t2. **Constant polynomials:** f ≡ 1 (monic degree 0) gives 2·1!+1 = 3, only finitely many primes divide 3. Contradiction.\n   247\t3. **Linear case:** f(x) = x+b. Positive b gives f(p) ≥ p → contradiction (same as deg ≥ 2). So b < 0, write b = -r, r > 0.\n   248\t4. **Wilson application:** (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)···(p-r)·(p-r-1)! ≡ (-1)^r r! · (p-r-1)! (mod p). Combined with (p-1)! ≡ -1: get (p-r-1)! ≡ (-1)^{r+1}/(r!) (mod p).\n   249\t5. **Fixed integer condition:** 2(p-r-1)!+1 ≡ 0 (mod p) translates to the fixed integer D_r = 2(-1)^{r+1} + r! ≡ 0 (mod p) for all large p. Hence D_r = 0.\n   250\t6. **Find r:** Check small r until D_r = 0. Only r = 3 works: 2(-1)^4 + 3! = 2+6? No wait, let me recheck.\n   251\t\n   252\tActually for D_r = 2(-1)^{r+1} + r! (before the multiply through by r!), the condition after multiplying is: r! · 2(-1)^{r+1} + (r!)² = 0, or ... let me be careful. The exact form of D_r depends on the precise derivation. The proof should arrive at a specific integer that must be zero, and then check r=1,2,3,...\n   253\t\n   254\t**Correctness check:** A correct proof must:\n   255\t- Correctly derive the exact fixed integer D_r involving r\n   256\t- Note that this being ≡ 0 (mod p) for all large p forces D_r = 0\n   257\t- Correctly compute the specific value of r that makes D_r = 0\n   258\t- Verify that this r gives a working polynomial f(x) = x - r\n   259\t\n   260\t**First error in flawed proofs:** If the proof arrives at the wrong equation for D_r (perhaps confusing (p-r-1)! with (p-r)!), the final equation to solve will be wrong and the claimed value of r will be incorrect.\n   261\t\n   262\t### 7.2 Gaussian Integer Factorization Problems (proof_06 type)\n   263\t\n   264\t**Problem type:** Given a⁴+b⁴ = c⁴+d⁴ = e⁵ with distinct positive integers, show ac+bd is composite (or more generally, analyze the algebraic structure).\n   265\t\n   266\t**Standard approach:**\n   267\t1. **Reduction:** By coprimality of a,b,c,d,e (if a common factor p existed, divide through and repeat), assume gcd = 1.\n   268\t2. **Factorization in Z[i]:** a⁴+b⁴ = (a²+ib²)(a²-ib²). Show these factors are coprime in Z[i].\n   269\t3. **UFD consequence:** Each factor is a fifth power times a unit: a²+ib² = ε·α⁵ for some α = u+vi ∈ Z[i] and unit ε.\n   270\t4. **Norm equation:** N(a²+ib²) = a⁴+b⁴ = e⁵. N(α⁵) = N(α)⁵ = (u²+v²)⁵. Hence e = u²+v².\n   271\t5. **Repeat for (c,d):** c²+id² = ε'·α⁵ for some unit ε'. Since both pairs factorize in terms of the same α = u+vi...\n   272\t\n   273\t**Critical subtlety:** At step 5, the claim that (c²+id²) must involve the SAME α as (a²+ib²) requires justification. Both (a²+ib²) and (c²+id²) equal fifth powers (times units) of Gaussian integers with norm e = u²+v². But different choices of unit ε could give genuinely different fifth-power Gaussian integers. The argument \"the assignment must swap because the pairs are distinct\" needs to be made rigorous.\n   274\t\n   275\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof that hand-waves the step \"hence the two factorizations must be related by swapping u+vi and u-vi\" without justifying why has a logical gap. Moreover, the conclusion c²=a², d²=-b² cannot hold for positive real a,b,c,d. If the proof DOES correctly derive a contradiction, the verdict is correct. If it makes an unjustified leap to derive this contradiction, the verdict is incorrect.\n   276\t\n   277\t### 7.3 Divisibility Congruences and Case Analysis (proof_10 type)\n   278\t\n   279\t**Problem type:** Prove or disprove that specific prime-power Diophantine equations have solutions.\n   280\t\n   281\t**Common structure:** Write the equation as p · f(q,b) = g(b) for primes p and q, then case-analyze on q = 2 vs q odd.\n   282\t\n   283\t**Evaluation criterion for case q=2:** The claim \"p | 4·7^b - 1 implies p = 3\" requires showing that 4·7^b ≡ 1 (mod p) has solutions only for p = 3. This requires either:\n   284\t(a) Computing ord_p(7) and checking divisibility conditions, OR\n   285\t(b) Direct case analysis for small primes\n   286\t\n   287\tSimply asserting the conclusion without either computation or case analysis is an unjustified gap.\n   288\t\n   289\t### 7.4 Algebraic Inequalities in Number Theory (proof_17 type)\n   290\t\n   291\t**Problem type:** Use algebraic inequalities to bound prime-related quantities.\n   292\t\n   293\t**Key principle:** When a proof uses an estimate like \"Kp^a < Mp^b\" for all positive p, both K and M must be explicitly computed, and the direction of the inequality must be verified for all relevant cases.\n   294\t\n   295\t**Common error:** Writing an inequality in the wrong direction (e.g., 27p² < 9p² is false for all positive p). This immediately invalidates any argument that depends on it.\n   296\t\n   297\t**Evaluation criterion:** Check every inequality claim. If any single inequality is in the wrong direction for the claimed values, the proof is incorrect at that step, regardless of whether the conclusion might be provable by other means.\n   298\t\n   299\t---\n   300\t\n   301\t## Part VIII: Evaluation Rubric Summary for Number Theory Proofs\n   302\t\n   303\tWhen evaluating a number theory proof in this audit, apply the following checklist:\n   304\t\n   305\t1. **Factual accuracy:** Are all theorems cited correctly? (Wilson, Fermat, Euler, LTE, QR)\n   306\t2. **Hypothesis completeness:** Are all hypotheses of each theorem explicitly verified before application?\n   307\t3. **Case completeness:** Are all cases covered? (Especially: what if q = 2? what if p = 2? what if the base case fails?)\n   308\t4. **Fixed-integer arguments:** When a fixed integer must be divisible by all large primes, is the conclusion \"hence the integer is 0\" correctly derived?\n   309\t5. **Coprimality:** When coprimality of two expressions is needed, is it proved or given?\n   310\t6. **UFD consequences:** When factoring in Z[i] or other number rings, is unique factorization correctly applied?\n   311\t7. **Direction of inequalities:** Are all stated inequalities in the correct direction for the claimed parameters?\n   312\t\n   313\tA proof with ANY false claim, unjustified transition, or missing critical case at any of these points should be marked **incorrect**, and the FIRST such occurrence is the first material issue.\n   314\t\n   315\t---\n   316\t\n   317\t## Part IX: Extended Examples of Correct and Incorrect Number Theory Reasoning\n   318\t\n   319\t### Example 1: Correct use of Wilson's Theorem\n   320\t\n   321\t**Claim:** For prime p > 5, p | (p-4)! + (p-3)·(p-4)!/p + ... \n   322\t\n   323\t**Approach:** Start from (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3)(p-4)! ≡ (-1)(-2)(-3)(p-4)! = -6(p-4)! (mod p). Since (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p), we get -6(p-4)! ≡ -1 (mod p), so (p-4)! ≡ (6)^{-1} ≡ (6)^{-1} (mod p). **This is a correct use of Wilson's theorem**, assuming the inverses exist (which they do for p > 3).\n   324\t\n   325\t### Example 2: Incorrect application — wrong formula\n   326\t\n   327\t**Claim:** (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)···(p-r) · (p-r)! (off-by-one error in factorial)\n   328\t\n   329\tThis is FALSE: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)···(p-r) · (p-r-1)!, not (p-r)!. An off-by-one error in the factorial formula would give a completely wrong value for D_r, leading to an incorrect determination of r.\n   330\t\n   331\t### Example 3: Correct coprimality argument in Z[i]\n   332\t\n   333\t**Claim:** gcd_{Z[i]}(a²+ib², a²-ib²) is a unit, given that a⁴+b⁴ = e⁵ and gcd(a,b) = 1.\n   334\t\n   335\t**Proof:** Let δ = gcd(a²+ib², a²-ib²). Then δ | (a²+ib²)-(a²-ib²) = 2ib². Also δ | (a²+ib²)+(a²-ib²) = 2a². So δ | gcd(2ib², 2a²) = 2·gcd(b², a²)·i. Since gcd(a,b) = 1, gcd(a²,b²) = 1 in Z, so δ | 2i. The only Gaussian prime dividing 2i = -i(1+i)² is (1+i). If (1+i) | (a²+ib²), then N(1+i)=2 | N(a²+ib²) = a⁴+b⁴ = e⁵, so 2 | e⁵, hence 2 | e. Then 2^5 | e⁵ = a⁴+b⁴. But if a and b are both odd, a⁴+b⁴ ≡ 1+1 = 2 (mod 4), not 0 (mod 32). Careful analysis shows (1+i) ∤ (a²+ib²) under the coprimality assumptions. **This is a correct argument.**\n   336\t\n   337\t### Example 4: Incorrect — overlooked unit ambiguity\n   338\t\n   339\t**Claim:** Since a²+ib² = (u+vi)⁵ and c²+id² = ε'(u+vi)⁵ for unit ε', and (a²,b²) ≠ (c²,d²), the unit ε' must be i or -i, forcing c² = -a², d² = b².\n   340\t\n   341\t**Error:** This doesn't follow. The unit ε' could be 1, -1, i, or -i. The case ε' = -1 gives c²+id² = -(u+vi)⁵ = (-u-vi)⁵... one needs to trace through each case systematically. Simply asserting \"it must be i or -i\" based on distinctness is an unjustified leap.\n   342\t\n   343\t### Example 5: Correct evaluation — catch the wrong inequality\n   344\t\n   345\t**Claim in proof:** \"Since 3(k+1)p² ≤ 9p² for k ≥ 2, we have...\"\n   346\t\n   347\t**Check:** 3(k+1) ≤ 9 iff k+1 ≤ 3 iff k ≤ 2. For k ≥ 2, we have k+1 ≥ 3 so 3(k+1) ≥ 9. The inequality is BACKWARDS for k ≥ 3. This is the first material issue.\n   348\t\n   349\t### Example 6: Correct handling of cases in divisibility\n   350\t\n   351\t**Claim:** For the equation 4p^k = 7^m + 1, analyzing case p = 2: we get 2^{k+2} = 7^m + 1. Modulo 4: 0 ≡ 7^m + 1 ≡ 3^m + 1 (mod 4). For m even: 3^m ≡ 1 (mod 4), so 3^m+1 ≡ 2 (mod 4), but 2^{k+2} ≡ 0 (mod 4) for k ≥ 0. Contradiction unless k+2 = 1 i.e. k = -1 (not valid). For m odd: 3^m ≡ 3 (mod 4), so 3^m+1 ≡ 0 (mod 4). OK so m must be odd. Continue: 2^{k+2} = 7^m+1 and m odd... **This is a correct case analysis approach** — systematically checking mod small numbers to constrain the variables.\n   352\t\n   353\t---\n   354\t\n   355\t## Part X: Summary of First Material Issues Commonly Found\n   356\t\n   357\tIn number theory proofs at olympiad level, the most common first material issues are:\n   358\t\n   359\t1. **Wrong inequality direction** — claimed \"a < b\" when actually a ≥ b for the values in question\n   360\t2. **Missing case** — analyzed case p odd but not p = 2 (or vice versa), or analyzed cases modulo 3 but missed a residue class\n   361\t3. **Unjustified divisibility claim** — said \"p | N implies p = q\" without showing why\n   362\t4. **Incorrect application of Wilson** — used wrong factorial or wrong parity of (-1)\n   363\t5. **Coprimality assumed, not proven** — applied UFD factoring without establishing coprimality\n   364\t6. **Wrong final value** — computed D_r = 0 for wrong r, claiming incorrect polynomial\n   365\t7. **Overlooked units in Z[i]** — in Gaussian integer arguments, forgot to account for all four units {1, -1, i, -i}\n   366\t8. **Circular case elimination** — \"proved\" case q=2 by assuming p=3 and checking consistency, rather than deriving p=3 from q=2\n   367\t\n   368\tAny of the above at the FIRST occurrence in a proof constitutes a material issue and should be reported as the first_material_issue_summary in your audit.\n   369\t\n   370\t---\n   371\t\n   372\t## Appendix A: Extended Worked Examples — Number Theory Proof Evaluation\n   373\t\n   374\t### A.1 Wilson's Theorem Applications — 20 Evaluation Scenarios\n   375\t\n   376\t**Scenario 1 (Correct).** Claim: \"For prime p > 3, p divides (p-2)! - 1.\"\n   377\tProof: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)! ≡ -1 (mod p). Also (p-1) ≡ -1 (mod p), so (-1)(p-2)! ≡ -1 (mod p), giving (p-2)! ≡ 1 (mod p). Hence p | (p-2)! - 1. Assessment: CORRECT. Uses Wilson properly, all steps valid.\n   378\t\n   379\t**Scenario 2 (Incorrect — wrong case boundary).** Claim: \"For prime p ≥ 2, p | (p-1)!+1.\"\n   380\tProof: By Wilson's theorem, (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p), so (p-1)!+1 ≡ 0 (mod p). Assessment: INCORRECT first material issue. For p = 2: (2-1)! = 1! = 1, and 1+1 = 2. 2|2 holds. But the proof works for all primes p ≥ 2. Actually CORRECT — Wilson holds for p=2: (2-1)! = 1 ≡ -1 ≡ 1 (mod 2), so (2-1)!+1 = 2 ≡ 0 (mod 2). So this proof is correct after all.\n   381\t\n   382\t**Scenario 3 (Incorrect — composite modulus).** Claim: \"15 | (15-1)! + 1 by Wilson's theorem.\"\n   383\tFirst material issue: Wilson's theorem requires p to be prime. 15 = 3×5 is not prime. In fact (14)! = 14·13·...·1 contains factors 3, 5, 6, 10, 15... wait, 15 ∤ {1,...,14}, but 3·5 = 15 ∤ any single element yet 3 and 5 are both in {1,...,14}. So 15 | 14! and 14!+1 ≡ 1 (mod 15) ≠ 0. INCORRECT: first issue is applying Wilson to non-prime 15.\n   384\t\n   385\t**Scenario 4 (Correct).** Claim: \"For prime p, ((p-1)/2)!² ≡ (-1)^{(p+1)/2} (mod p).\"\n   386\tProof: (p-1)! ≡ -1. Pair j with p-j for j=1,...,(p-1)/2. Product of each pair = j(p-j) ≡ j(-j) = -j² (mod p). Product of all pairs = Π_{j=1}^{(p-1)/2} (-j²) = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} · (((p-1)/2)!)². So (p-1)! = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} · (((p-1)/2)!)² ≡ -1. Hence (((p-1)/2)!)² ≡ (-1)^{(p+1)/2}. CORRECT.\n   387\t\n   388\t**Scenario 5 (Incorrect — off-by-one).** Claim: \"For prime p and r=3: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) · (p-3)!.\"\n   389\tFirst material issue: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3)(p-4)···1. Extracting the first 3 terms: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) · (p-4)!, NOT (p-3)!. The off-by-one error gives the wrong factorial: (p-3)! vs (p-4)!.\n   390\t\n   391\t**Scenario 6 (Correct).** Claim: \"Let D₃ = 2(-1)^4 + 3! = 2 + 6 = 8. Since D₃ ≠ 0, r = 3 is not a solution.\"\n   392\tThe correct formula is D_r = 2(-1)^r + (r-1)! and one checks r=3 gives D_3 = -2+2=0.\n   393\t\n   394\t**Scenario W7 (Correct — Wilson derivation step).** \"(p-1)! = product_{j=1}^{p-1} j = (product_{j=1}^{r} (p-j)) * (product_{j=1}^{p-r-1} j) = (product_{j=1}^r (-j) (mod p)) * (p-r-1)! = (-1)^r*r!*(p-r-1)! (mod p).\" ✓\n   395\t\n   396\t**Scenario W8 (Correct — fixed integer argument).** \"The quantity 2(-1)^r + (r-1)! is a fixed integer independent of p. If this integer is nonzero, it has finitely many prime divisors, so only finitely many primes p can satisfy the congruence. Hence it must equal 0.\" ✓\n   397\t\n   398\t**Scenario W9 (Incorrect — r=2 claimed as solution).** Suppose someone computes D_2 = 2(-1)^2 + 1! = 2+1 = 3 ≠ 0, yet claims r=2 is a solution. INCORRECT: D_2 = 3 ≠ 0 means p | 3 for all large p, which fails for p > 3. Not a solution.\n   399\t\n   400\t**Scenario W10 (Correct — verification for r=3).** \"f(x)=x-3. For prime p > 3: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3)*(p-4)!... wait, (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3)*(p-3-1)! hmm. Let me use: (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) ≡ (-1)(-2)(-3) = -6 (mod p). And (p-1)! = (-6)*(p-4)!. But (p-1)! ≡ -1. So (-6)*(p-4)! ≡ -1, giving (p-4)! ≡ 1/6 (mod p). Hmm, this doesn't directly give 2(p-3)!+1. Better: (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3)*(p-3-1)! hmm again. Let me think. Actually (p-3)! * (p-2) * (p-1) = (p-1)! but that's wrong too. (p-3)! * 1 = (p-3)! and we need to get from (p-3)! to (p-1)!. \n   401\t\n   402\t(p-1)! = (p-3)! * (p-2) * (p-1) ≡ (p-3)! * (-2)(-1) = 2*(p-3)! (mod p). So 2*(p-3)! ≡ (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p). Hence 2*(p-3)!+1 ≡ 0 (mod p). ✓\"\n   403\t\n   404\tThis is the cleanest verification for r=3. Note: the key step is (p-1)! = (p-3)! * (p-2) * (p-1) ≡ (p-3)! * (-2)(-1) = 2*(p-3)! (mod p). The formula is (p-r-1)! going from (p-1)! by stripping the r=3 terms: \n   405\t\n   406\tActually: f(p)! = (p-3)!. And (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) * (p-4)!. \n   407\tHmm: p-3 terms from (p-1) to (p-3) are: (p-1)(p-2)(p-3). And (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3)(p-4)!.\n   408\tBut (p-3)! = (p-3)(p-4)! ... no, (p-3)! = 1*2*...*p-3 = (p-4)! * (p-3).\n   409\tSo (p-4)! = (p-3)! / (p-3).\n   410\t\n   411\t(p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) * (p-4)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) * (p-3)!/(p-3) = (p-1)(p-2) * (p-3)!.\n   412\t\n   413\tWait: (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) * (p-4)! = (p-1)! means (p-3)! = (p-3)(p-4)! (by definition). So (p-4)! = (p-3)!/(p-3). And (p-1)! = (p-1)(p-2)(p-3) * (p-3)!/(p-3) = (p-1)(p-2)*(p-3)!.\n   414\t\n   415\t(p-1)(p-2) ≡ (-1)(-2) = 2 (mod p). So (p-1)! ≡ 2*(p-3)! (mod p). By Wilson: -1 ≡ 2*(p-3)! (mod p). Hence 2*(p-3)! ≡ -1, so 2*(p-3)!+1 ≡ 0 (mod p). ✓\n   416\t\n   417\t### D.2 Gaussian Integer Arguments — 20 Additional Scenarios\n   418\t\n   419\t**GI1 (Correct — basic arithmetic in Z[i]).** \"(2+3i) * (1-i) = 2 - 2i + 3i - 3i^2 = 2 - 2i + 3i + 3 = 5 + i.\" N(2+3i) = 13. N(1-i) = 2. N(5+i) = 26 = 13*2. ✓\n   420\t\n   421\t**GI2 (Correct — Gaussian prime check).** \"Is 3 a Gaussian prime? 3 ≡ 3 (mod 4). Primes p ≡ 3 (mod 4) remain prime in Z[i]. So 3 is a Gaussian prime.\" ✓\n   422\t\n   423\t**GI3 (Correct — Gaussian prime factorization).** \"Factor 5 in Z[i]: 5 = (2+i)(2-i). N(2+i) = 5 prime in Z. 5 ≡ 1 (mod 4). This claim is a FACTUAL assertion that must be verified — either by explicit computation of f' and showing f' < 0, or by citing a known result.\n    45\t\n    46\t**First material issue for inequality proofs:** \n    47\t- If a derivative or convexity argument is used, verify the sign of f' or f'' explicitly for the relevant domain.\n    48\t- If an AM-GM application is made, verify that all quantities are positive.\n    49\t- If Cauchy-Schwarz is applied, verify the correct form is used.\n    50\t\n    51\t---\n    52\t\n    53\t## Part II: Polynomials\n    54\t\n    55\t### 2.1 Basic Polynomial Theory\n    56\t\n    57\t**Degree:** The degree of a polynomial f(x) = aₙxⁿ + ... + a₀ (aₙ ≠ 0) is n. Leading coefficient is aₙ.\n    58\t\n    59\t**Roots:** By the fundamental theorem of algebra, a degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots (counting multiplicity) in ℂ.\n    60\t\n    61\t**Lagrange interpolation:** Given n+1 points (x₀,y₀),...,(xₙ,yₙ) with distinct xᵢ, there is a unique polynomial of degree ≤ n passing through all of them:\n    62\tP(x) = Σᵢ yᵢ · Π_{j≠i} (x-xⱼ)/(xᵢ-xⱼ)\n    63\t\n    64\t**Consequence:** A polynomial of degree ≤ n is uniquely determined by its values at n+1 distinct points.\n    65\t\n    66\t**Degree bound lemma:** A polynomial of degree ≤ n that evaluates to 0 at n+1 distinct points must be identically 0.\n    67\t\n    68\t### 2.2 Polynomials with Symmetric Conditions\n    69\t\n    70\t**Symmetric polynomials:** A polynomial f(x₁,...,xₙ) is symmetric if it is invariant under all permutations of variables. The fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials: every symmetric polynomial is a polynomial in the elementary symmetric polynomials e₁,...,eₙ:\n    71\t- e₁ = Σxᵢ\n    72\t- e₂ = Σᵢ<ⱼ xᵢxⱼ\n    73\t- e₃ = Σᵢ<ⱼ<ₖ xᵢxⱼxₖ\n    74\t- ...\n    75\t- eₙ = x₁x₂···xₙ\n    76\t\n    77\t**Newton's power sum identities:** If pₖ = Σxᵢᵏ, then:\n    78\tp₁ = e₁\n    79\tp₂ = e₁p₁ - 2e₂\n    80\tp₃ = e₁p₂ - e₂p₁ + 3e₃\n    81\t...\n    82\t\n    83\t**For three variables (x,y,z):**\n    84\tx²+y²+z² = e₁² - 2e₂ = (x+y+z)² - 2(xy+yz+zx)\n    85\tx³+y³+z³ = e₁³ - 3e₁e₂ + 3e₃ = (x+y+z)³ - 3(x+y+z)(xy+yz+zx) + 3xyz\n    86\t\n    87\tAlso: (x-y)²+(y-z)²+(z-x)² = 2(x²+y²+z²) - 2(xy+yz+zx) = 2(e₁² - 2e₂) - 2e₂ = 2(e₁² - 3e₂) = 2(S₁² - 3S₂).\n    88\t\n    89\t### 2.3 Polynomial Functional Equations\n    90\t\n    91\t**Method:** To find all polynomials P satisfying an identity F(P) = 0 or F(P, Q) = 0:\n    92\t1. **Degree bound:** Compare degrees of both sides; the leading terms must match, giving a constraint on deg P.\n    93\t2. **Coefficient matching:** After establishing deg P = d, substitute P(t) = aₐtᵈ + ... and match coefficients.\n    94\t3. **Verification:** Plug the candidate polynomial back into the original identity to confirm.\n    95\t\n    96\t**Degree comparison in asymptotics:** To compare degrees, take a variable to infinity and expand both sides in a power series. The leading terms must agree.\n    97\t\n    98\t**Example:** If the identity equates two expressions, both expanded to order y^{n+1} and y^n, the coefficients of y^{n+1} give a constraint (often automatically satisfied) and the coefficients of y^n give a non-trivial constraint on the degree n.\n    99\t\n   100\t### 2.4 Evaluation Criteria for Polynomial Proofs\n   101\t\n   102\t**Degree bound:** The argument that \"deg P ≤ n\" based on asymptotic expansion must correctly identify the leading terms of both sides. An error in which power of y dominates (e.g., confusing y^n with y^{n+1}) would give the wrong degree constraint.\n   103\t\n   104\t**Even/odd degree:** The claim \"n must be even\" based on cancellation of certain terms: if the coefficient of y^{n+1} on the RHS has a factor ((-1)^n + 1), then this vanishes only when n is odd. The correct conclusion is n must be EVEN (for non-vanishing leading term). An off-by-one error here changes the conclusion.\n   105\t\n   106\t**Coefficient matching:** After establishing the degree, the system of linear equations from coefficient matching must be set up correctly. Common errors: sign errors, wrong expansion of symmetric sum identities, applying Vieta's formulas to the wrong polynomial.\n   107\t\n   108\t---\n   109\t\n   110\t## Part III: Real Analysis and Calculus in Olympiad Proofs\n   111\t\n   112\t### 3.1 Monotonicity via Derivatives\n   113\t\n   114\tA differentiable function f: (a,b) → ℝ is strictly increasing if f'(x) > 0 for all x ∈ (a,b), and strictly decreasing if f'(x) < 0 for all x ∈ (a,b).\n   115\t\n   116\t**Verification requirement:** If a proof asserts f'(x) < 0 to establish monotonicity, it must explicitly compute f'(x) and show it is negative. The assertion \"f'(x) < 0\" is NOT self-evident.\n   117\t\n   118\t**First material issue:** If f'(x) < 0 is claimed but either:\n   119\t(a) f'(x) is not computed, or\n   120\t(b) f'(x) is computed but the inequality f'(x) < 0 does not hold for the relevant x,\n   121\t\n   122\tthen the proof is incorrect at this step.\n   123\t\n   124\t**Common errors with derivatives:**\n   125\t- Differentiating incorrectly (product rule, chain rule errors)\n   126\t- Stating the wrong derivative formula\n   127\t- Claiming the derivative is negative when it could be zero or positive for some values in the domain\n   128\t\n   129\t### 3.2 Compactness and Existence of Minima\n   130\t\n   131\t**Weierstrass extreme value theorem:** A continuous function on a compact (closed and bounded) set in ℝⁿ attains its minimum and maximum.\n   132\t\n   133\t**Non-compact case:** If the domain is not compact (e.g., all of ℝⁿ, or an open set, or unbounded), the function may not attain its minimum. To establish existence of a minimum, one of the following is needed:\n   134\t- Show the domain IS compact\n   135\t- Show the function is coercive (f(x) → ∞ as |x| → ∞), reducing to a compact sublevel set\n   136\t- Direct construction of the minimum\n   137\t\n   138\t**Evaluation criterion for analysis proofs:** If a proof claims \"the minimum is attained\" by a compactness argument, verify:\n   139\t- The domain is indeed compact (closed and bounded), OR\n   140\t- The specific compact set used in the argument is correctly identified and the function's behavior at the boundary/infinity justifies restriction to this compact set\n   141\t\n   142\tIf the domain is not compact and no coercivity argument is given, the existence of the minimum is not established.\n   143\t\n   144\t### 3.3 Continuity and Limit Arguments\n   145\t\n   146\t**Sequential continuity:** f is continuous at a if for every sequence xₙ → a, f(xₙ) → f(a).\n   147\t\n   148\t**Polynomial continuation:** A polynomial identity that holds for all x ≠ c (where c is a single excluded point) also holds at x = c by continuity. More generally, a polynomial identity that holds on a dense set holds everywhere.\n   149\t\n   150\t**Extension by continuity:** If F(x,y) = G(x,y) for all (x,y) avoiding the set {2xy=1} (which is a curve in ℝ²), then by continuity it holds everywhere. This is valid for continuous functions. For polynomials, a stronger argument: if P = Q at infinitely many points, then P ≡ Q as polynomials.\n   151\t\n   152\t---\n   153\t\n   154\t## Part IV: Polynomial Interpolation and Linear Algebra\n   155\t\n   156\t### 4.1 Vandermonde Matrices\n   157\t\n   158\tThe Vandermonde matrix V = (xᵢʲ⁻¹)_{i,j=1,...,n} for distinct points x₁,...,xₙ has determinant Π_{1≤i<j≤n}(xⱼ-xᵢ) ≠ 0. Hence it is invertible.\n   159\t\n   160\t**Consequence:** The system of n equations P(xᵢ) = yᵢ (i=1,...,n) for a polynomial of degree ≤ n-1 has a unique solution given distinct xᵢ.\n   161\t\n   162\t### 4.2 Linear Spaces of Polynomials\n   163\t\n   164\tThe space of polynomials of degree ≤ n over ℝ is an (n+1)-dimensional vector space. Linear constraints (each of the form \"the value at a specific point equals something\") reduce the dimension by 1 per independent constraint.\n   165\t\n   166\t**Evaluation criterion for interpolation proofs:** \n   167\t- A proof that \"the solution space has dimension ≥ 1\" from n constraints in n+1 unknowns is correct (the system is underdetermined).\n   168\t- The claim \"a nonzero polynomial exists of degree AT MOST n satisfying n homogeneous linear conditions\" follows from the dimension count: at most n conditions can reduce (n+1)-dimensional space by at most n, leaving dimension ≥ 1.\n   169\t- The argument \"a solution of degree EXACTLY n exists\" requires showing the solution space is not entirely in the subspace {aₙ = 0}. This needs additional reasoning.\n   170\t\n   171\t### 4.3 Ensuring Exact Degree\n   172\t\n   173\t**Method 1:** If any of the n conditions involves the coefficient aₙ with a nonzero coefficient, then aₙ is not forced to be 0 by the conditions.\n   174\t\n   175\t**Method 2:** If all conditions happen to set xᵢₙ + xⱼₙ = 0 for all pairs, then aₙ = 0 is forced; but this occurs only in special configurations (symmetric about 0 with odd degree).\n   176\t\n   177\t**Evaluation criterion:** The argument \"we can choose a solution with aₙ ≠ 0\" needs to explicitly handle the case where all n conditions have zero coefficient of aₙ (e.g., when all pairs satisfy xᵢₙ + xⱼₙ = 0 for the specific matching chosen). If this case is handled (even briefly), the proof is valid on this point.\n   178\t\n   179\t### 4.4 Matching Construction in Interpolation Problems\n   180\t\n   181\t**Context:** For 2n distinct points x₁,...,x_{2n}, pair them as {i_k, j_k} (k=1,...,n) and require Q(x_{iₖ})+Q(x_{jₖ}) = 0 for each pair.\n   182\t\n   183\t**Homogeneity:** These are n homogeneous linear equations in the n+1 coefficients a₀,...,aₙ. The system always has a nonzero solution (kernel has dimension ≥ 1).\n   184\t\n   185\t**Evaluation criterion:** The pairing ({i_k, j_k}) is a perfect matching on {1,...,2n}. Such a matching exists for any 2n elements (pair them up sequentially or in any bijective way). This is valid — a perfect matching always exists for an even number of elements. An incorrect claim would be that a specific type of matching (e.g., \"adjacent\" pairs) is required; any matching works.\n   186\t\n   187\t---\n   188\t\n   189\t## Part V: Symmetric Sums and Competition Algebra\n   190\t\n   191\t### 5.1 Elementary Symmetric Polynomials\n   192\t\n   193\tFor x, y, z with constraint 2xyz = x+y+z (equivalently 2S₃ = S₁ in terms of elementary symmetric polynomials):\n   194\t- S₁ = x+y+z\n   195\t- S₂ = xy+yz+zx\n   196\t- S₃ = xyz = S₁/2\n   197\t\n   198\tStandard substitutions:\n   199\t- x³+y³+z³ = S₁³-3S₁S₂+3S₃ = S₁³-3S₁S₂+3S₁/2\n   200\t- xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z) for P(t) = at²+bt+c: = a(x³+y³+z³)+b(x²+y²+z²)+c(x+y+z) = a(S₁³-3S₁S₂+3S₁/2)+b(S₁²-2S₂)+cS₁\n   201\t\n   202\t### 5.2 Generating the Degree Bound\n   203\t\n   204\tFor the functional equation P(x)/yz + P(y)/zx + P(z)/xy = P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x):\n   205\t\n   206\tAfter multiplying by xyz = S₃ = S₁/2, the equation becomes:\n   207\t2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) = S₁(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)) ... (*)\n   208\t\n   209\tTo determine deg P, fix x and let y → ∞ with z determined by 2xyz = x+y+z:\n   210\tz = (x+y)/(2xy-1) ≈ 1/(2x) as y → ∞\n   211\t\n   212\tLHS of (*): 2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) ≈ 2yP(y) for large y; if deg P = n, this is ≈ 2aₙy^{n+1}.\n   213\t\n   214\tRHS of (*): S₁ = x+y+z ≈ y; P(x-y) ≈ aₙ(-y)^n = aₙ(-1)^n y^n; P(y-z) ≈ aₙy^n; P(z-x) = O(1).\n   215\tSo P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x) ≈ aₙ((-1)^n+1)y^n.\n   216\tRHS ≈ y · aₙ((-1)^n+1)y^n = aₙ((-1)^n+1)y^{n+1}.\n   217\t\n   218\tMatching y^{n+1} coefficients: 2aₙ = aₙ((-1)^n+1).\n   219\tIf n is odd: (-1)^n = -1, so (-1)^n+1 = 0, giving 2aₙ = 0 → aₙ = 0. Contradiction.\n   220\tIf n is even: (-1)^n = 1, so (-1)^n+1 = 2, giving 2aₙ = 2aₙ. ✓ No constraint.\n   221\t\n   222\tMatching y^n coefficients (with n even, (-1)^n = 1):\n   223\tLHS y^n: 2aₙ₋₁ (from 2yP(y) expanded to next order)\n   224\tRHS y^n: complex expression involving n and x. For the equality to hold for all x, the dependence on x must vanish. This gives n = 2.\n   225\t\n   226\t**Evaluation criterion for degree bound argument:** The key steps are:\n   227\t1. Correctly expand both sides in powers of y\n   228\t2. Correctly identify the leading coefficient of y^{n+1} on both sides\n   229\t3. Determine that n must be even (odd n gives 0 = 2aₙ)\n   230\t4. Expand to next order (y^n) and show n = 2\n   231\t\n   232\tAn error in step 2 or 3 (e.g., claiming n must be odd, or wrong leading coefficient) is a material issue.\n   233\t\n   234\t### 5.3 Completing the Coefficient Matching\n   235\t\n   236\tFor P(t) = at²+bt+c with the constraint 2xyz = x+y+z (so 2S₃ = S₁):\n   237\t\n   238\tLHS: 2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) = 2[a(S₁³-3S₁S₂+3S₁/2)+b(S₁²-2S₂)+cS₁]\n   239\t    = 2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂+3aS₁+2bS₁²-4bS₂+2cS₁\n   240\t\n   241\tRHS: S₁[P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)]\n   242\t   = S₁[a·2(S₁²-3S₂)+b·0+3c]     (using (x-y)²+(y-z)²+(z-x)² = 2(S₁²-3S₂) and linear terms cancel)\n   243\t   = 2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂+3cS₁\n   244\t\n   245\tSetting LHS = RHS:\n   246\t2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂+3aS₁+2bS₁²-4bS₂+2cS₁ = 2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂+3cS₁\n   247\t\n   248\tCancel 2aS₁³-6aS₁S₂:\n   249\t3aS₁+2bS₁²-4bS₂+2cS₁ = 3cS₁\n   250\t\n   251\tSince S₁ and S₂ are \"essentially independent\" (they can vary independently for appropriate x,y,z):\n   252\t- Coefficient of S₁²: 2b = 0 → b = 0\n   253\t- Coefficient of S₂: -4b = 0 ✓ (consistent)\n   254\t- Coefficient of S₁: 3a+2c = 3c → 3a = c → c = 3a\n   255\t\n   256\tHence P(t) = a(t²+3). ✓\n   257\t\n   258\t**Evaluation criterion:** Check each algebraic step:\n   259\t- Is (x-y)²+(y-z)²+(z-x)² = 2(S₁²-3S₂) correct? \n   260\t  LHS = 2(x²+y²+z²)-2(xy+yz+zx) = 2(S₁²-2S₂)-2S₂ = 2S₁²-4S₂-2S₂ = 2S₁²-6S₂. So 2(S₁²-3S₂). ✓\n   261\t- Are the symmetric sum identities applied correctly?\n   262\t\n   263\t---\n   264\t\n   265\t## Part VI: Optimization Theory\n   266\t\n   267\t### 6.1 Existence of Extrema\n   268\t\n   269\t**Necessary condition:** A local extremum of f at x₀ (assuming f differentiable) requires f'(x₀) = 0 or x₀ is a boundary point.\n   270\t\n   271\t**Critical points:** Points where f'(x) = 0 are candidates for extrema. One must still verify it's an actual extremum (not just a stationary point) using the second derivative test or other criteria.\n   272\t\n   273\t**Global vs local:** A local minimum may not be the global minimum. To establish global minimum, either:\n   274\t- Show there's only one critical point and it's a minimum\n   275\t- Compare values at all critical points and boundary points\n   276\t- Use convexity/concavity to ensure uniqueness\n   277\t\n   278\t### 6.2 Convex Optimization\n   279\t\n   280\tA function f is convex if f(λx+(1-λ)y) ≤ λf(x)+(1-λ)f(y) for all x,y in the domain and λ ∈ [0,1]. For differentiable f, convexity is equivalent to f'' ≥ 0 everywhere.\n   281\t\n   282\t**For convex functions:** Any local minimum is a global minimum. If f is strictly convex, the minimum is unique.\n   283\t\n   284\t**Common error in optimization proofs:** Claiming a minimum is achieved without either:\n   285\t(a) Using Weierstrass (requires compact domain)\n   286\t(b) Using coercivity (f → ∞ at infinity)\n   287\t(c) Showing the infimum is attained by direct construction\n   288\t\n   289\tIf neither is provided, existence of the minimum is not established.\n   290\t\n   291\t### 6.3 Lagrange Multipliers\n   292\t\n   293\tFor minimizing f(x) subject to g(x) = c, at a local extremum: ∇f = λ∇g (if ∇g ≠ 0).\n   294\t\n   295\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof using Lagrange multipliers must:\n   296\t- Verify the constraint qualification (∇g ≠ 0 at the critical point)\n   297\t- Find all critical points\n   298\t- Check that the minimum is among the critical points (not on the boundary or at infinity)\n   299\t\n   300\t### 6.4 Skipped Computations in Optimization\n   301\t\n   302\t**Common gap:** An optimization proof sets up the problem (writes down the function to minimize, identifies what the minimum \"should be\") but then skips the actual computation that finds the minimum value. Claims like \"it can be computed that the minimum is...\" without computation are incomplete.\n   303\t\n   304\t**Evaluation criterion:** The computation of the minimum must be explicit. If the minimum is found by AM-GM or Cauchy-Schwarz, the specific application must be shown. If it's found by derivatives, the computation of the critical point must be shown.\n   305\t\n   306\t---\n   307\t\n   308\t## Part VII: Analysis and Compactness\n   309\t\n   310\t### 7.1 Compact Sets in ℝⁿ\n   311\t\n   312\tA subset K ⊆ ℝⁿ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded (Heine-Borel theorem).\n   313\t\n   314\t**Sequences:** Every sequence in a compact set has a convergent subsequence (limit in the same set).\n   315\t\n   316\t**Application:** If the domain of an optimization problem is compact, continuous functions attain their minimum and maximum. This is the key theorem behind existence of optimal solutions.\n   317\t\n   318\t### 7.2 Non-Compact Domains\n   319\t\n   320\t**Half-spaces, hyperplanes, cones:** These are typically closed but not bounded, hence not compact.\n   321\t\n   322\t**Sets defined by infinite constraints:** The intersection of infinitely many closed sets is closed (hence potentially non-compact). The intersection of finitely many closed sets is closed.\n   323\t\n   324\t**Common error:** Claiming a set is compact when it is only closed (but not bounded), or only bounded (but not closed). In ℝⁿ, both conditions are needed.\n   325\t\n   326\t**Specific non-compact example:** For a problem where the variables can take arbitrarily large values subject to given constraints, the feasible region is typically non-compact. The minimum may or may not exist and requires separate analysis.\n   327\t\n   328\t### 7.3 The Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem\n   329\t\n   330\tEvery continuous map from a compact convex set K ⊆ ℝⁿ to itself has a fixed point.\n   331\t\n   332\t**Application in geometry:** For finding specific points (circumcenters, incenters, etc.) as fixed points of maps related to the figure.\n   333\t\n   334\t### 7.4 Evaluation Criteria for Analysis Proofs\n   335\t\n   336\t**Existence of minimum:** Must establish via compactness (domain is compact + Weierstrass) or via direct construction.\n   337\t\n   338\t**Finiteness claims:** \"The infimum is finite\" is usually clear if the problem has any constraint (e.g., a,b,c are bounded below by 0). But attainment of the infimum requires compactness or direct construction.\n   339\t\n   340\t**Limit arguments:** \"As xₙ → x₀, f(xₙ) → f(x₀)\" requires continuity of f. This is automatic for polynomials and rational functions (away from poles), but must be verified for general f.\n   341\t\n   342\t---\n   343\t\n   344\t## Part VIII: Polynomial Interpolation in Functional Settings\n   345\t\n   346\t### 8.1 The Magician Trick Problem Type\n   347\t\n   348\t**Setup:** n points x₁,...,x_{2n} are fixed. A degree-n polynomial P is chosen secretly. The sorted tuple of values (P(x₁),...,P(x_{2n})) (sorted in non-decreasing order) is revealed. Can the polynomial be uniquely recovered?\n   349\t\n   350\t**Answer structure:** If YES, one must show the map P ↦ sorted(P(x₁),...,P(x_{2n})) is injective on degree-n polynomials. If NO, one must exhibit two distinct degree-n polynomials with the same sorted tuple of values.\n   351\t\n   352\t**For NO:** The approach is to find Q ≠ P of degree n with {Q(xᵢ)} = {P(xᵢ)} as multisets (values up to permutation). Taking P = -Q works if Q(xσ(i)) = -Q(xᵢ) for some permutation σ, which is possible if we can find Q with paired values: Q(xᵢ) + Q(xⱼ) = 0 for some perfect matching {i,j}.\n   353\t\n   354\t**Evaluation criterion:** The argument must:\n   355\t1. Construct a valid degree-n polynomial Q with the pairing property (not just degree ≤ n)\n   356\t2. Show Q ≠ 0 (so P = -Q ≠ Q in general)\n   357\t3. Show the multisets {Q(xᵢ)} and {-Q(xᵢ)} = {P(xᵢ)} are equal\n   358\t\n   359\tThe critical step is ensuring deg Q = n exactly (not just ≤ n). This requires showing the degree-n coefficient can be made nonzero, which is the nontrivial part of the argument.\n   360\t\n   361\t### 8.2 Linear Algebra over ℝ\n   362\t\n   363\t**Dimension of kernel:** If A is an m×n matrix with m ≤ n, the kernel of A has dimension ≥ n-m. For m = n, the kernel is trivial iff A is invertible.\n   364\t\n   365\t**Nonzero solutions:** The homogeneous system Ax = 0 (m equations, n unknowns, m < n) always has a nonzero solution.\n   366\t\n   367\t**Subspace inclusion:** The kernel of a linear functional L: V → ℝ (where V is a vector space and L ≠ 0) is a hyperplane (codimension 1 subspace). The kernel of A consists of all vectors orthogonal to the row space of A.\n   368\t\n   369\t**Evaluation criterion:** The claim \"the solution space is not contained in {aₙ = 0}\" must be supported by showing that the n constraints do not all kill the aₙ component. This requires either:\n   370\t- Direct: the column of A corresponding to aₙ is not in the row space of the constraint matrix restricted to other variables\n   371\t- Indirect: at least one constraint has nonzero coefficient for aₙ, AND there's at least one solution with aₙ ≠ 0\n   372\t\n   373\t---\n   374\t\n   375\t## Part IX: Summary of Evaluation Criteria\n   376\t\n   377\t### 9.1 For Inequality Proofs (proof_03 type)\n   378\t\n   379\t1. Is the normalization valid (degrees match, constraints preserved)?\n   380\t2. Is the AM-GM application correct (positive quantities, correct form)?\n   381\t3. Is the algebraic manipulation correct (expanding products, collecting terms)?\n   382\t4. Is the final inequality direction correct?\n   383\t\n   384\t### 9.2 For Monotonicity Proofs (proof_05 type)\n   385\t\n   386\t1. Is f'(x) correctly computed?\n   387\t2. Is the sign of f'(x) correctly determined for the relevant domain?\n   388\t3. If f'(x) < 0 is claimed but actually f'(x) ≥ 0 for some x in the domain, this is the first material issue.\n   389\t\n   390\t### 9.3 For Optimization Proofs (proof_08 type)\n   391\t\n   392\t1. Is existence of the minimum established (compactness or direct construction)?\n   393\t2. Is the critical point computation explicit?\n   394\t3. Is the minimum value correctly computed?\n   395\t4. Are all cases (boundaries, infinity) handled?\n   396\t\n   397\t### 9.4 For Compactness/Analysis Proofs (proof_14 type)\n   398\t\n   399\t1. Is the domain closed and bounded (compact)?\n   400\t2. Is the function continuous?\n   401\t3. Is Weierstrass correctly applied?\n   402\t4. If compactness fails, is an alternative existence argument given?\n   403\t\n   404\t### 9.5 For Polynomial Interpolation Proofs (proof_18 type)\n   405\t\n   406\t1. Is the perfect matching well-defined and explicitly constructed?\n   407\t2. Are the linear constraints correctly formulated?\n   408\t3. Is the dimension count correct (n homogeneous equations in n+1 unknowns)?\n   409\t4. Is the degree-exactly-n argument sound?\n   410\t5. Is the multiset equality correctly verified?\n   411\t\n   412\t### 9.6 For Polynomial Functional Equation Proofs (proof_20 type)\n   413\t\n   414\t1. Is the degree bound correctly derived (matching of leading coefficients)?\n   415\t2. Is the substitution correct (z expressed in terms of x,y)?\n   416\t3. Are the symmetric sum identities applied correctly?\n   417\t4. Is the coefficient matching system correct?\n   418\t5. Is the verification (plugging back) performed?\n   419\t\n   420\t---\n   421\t\n   422\t## Part X: Extended Examples\n   423\t\n   424\t### Example 1: Correct inequality reduction\n   425\t\n   426\t**Claim:** The inequality Σᵢ<ⱼ aᵢaⱼ/(aᵢ+aⱼ) ≤ n/(2s) · Σᵢ<ⱼ aᵢaⱼ reduces to the per-triple inequality aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aᵢ+aⱼ)+aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aᵢ+aₖ)+aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aⱼ+aₖ) ≤ (n-2)/2·(aᵢaⱼ+aᵢaₖ+aⱼaₖ).\n   427\t\n   428\t**Analysis:** This is correct. The double sum Σᵢ<ⱼ Σₖ≠ᵢ,ⱼ aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aᵢ+aⱼ) counts each triple {i,j,k} exactly three times (once for each distinguished pair). The reduction to the per-triple inequality is valid. Then the use of AM-GM to bound each term is:\n   429\t2aᵢaⱼaₖ/(aᵢ+aⱼ) ≤ aₖ(aᵢ+aⱼ)/2 [from xy/(x+y) ≤ (x+y)/4 with z = aₖ]\n   430\t\n   431\tAdding cyclically: ≤ ½(aₖ(aᵢ+aⱼ)+aⱼ(aᵢ+aₖ)+aᵢ(aⱼ+aₖ)) = aᵢaⱼ+aᵢaₖ+aⱼaₖ.\n   432\tDividing by 2: LHS ≤ (aᵢaⱼ+aᵢaₖ+aⱼaₖ)/2.\n   433\t\n   434\tThis is stronger than the ≤ (n-2)/2·(aᵢaⱼ+aᵢaₖ+aⱼaₖ) claim for n ≥ 3. ✓\n   435\t\n   436\t### Example 2: Incorrect derivative claim\n   437\t\n   438\t**Claim:** \"Let f(x) = x ln x - x. Then f'(x) = ln x, and since f'(x) < 0 for x < 1, f is decreasing on (0,1).\"\n   439\t\n   440\t**Analysis:** f'(x) = ln x + x·(1/x) - 1 = ln x + 1 - 1 = ln x. This is CORRECT. And ln x < 0 for 0 < x < 1. So the claim is correct. ✓\n   441\t\n   442\t**Example of incorrect derivative claim:** \"Let g(x) = x/(1+x²). Then g'(x) = 1/(1+x²)², and g is increasing.\" But actually g'(x) = (1+x²-x·2x)/(1+x²)² = (1-x²)/(1+x²)², which is negative for |x| > 1. The claimed formula for g'(x) is wrong, and the monotonicity conclusion is wrong for |x| > 1.\n   443\t\n   444\t### Example 3: Missing compactness in optimization\n   445\t\n   446\t**Claim:** \"The minimum of f(a,b,c) subject to a+b+c = 1, a,b,c > 0 is attained at a = b = c = 1/3.\"\n   447\t\n   448\t**Analysis:** The domain {(a,b,c) : a+b+c=1, a,b,c > 0} is NOT compact (it's open — the corners where some variable = 0 are excluded). However, as any variable approaches 0, f may diverge or approach a boundary value. For this specific claim to be valid, one needs to also check f(a,b,c) → ∞ or ≥ value at (1/3,1/3,1/3) as any variable → 0.\n   449\t\n   450\tIf the proof just claims \"the minimum is at a=b=c=1/3 by symmetry and AM-GM\" without discussing the boundary behavior, it is missing the existence argument.\n   451\t\n   452\t### Example 4: Circular reasoning in set characterization\n   453\t\n   454\t**Claim:** \"Since A_i ∪ B_j ⊆ S_{ij} and |A_i∪B_j| ≤ |S_{ij}| = i+j, the only possibility is S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j.\"\n   455\t\n   456\t**Analysis:** INCORRECT. The fact that A_i∪B_j ⊆ S_{ij} and |A_i∪B_j| ≤ i+j does not imply equality S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j. What's needed is |A_i∪B_j| = i+j, which would then force A_i∪B_j = S_{ij} (as a subset of S_{ij} with the same cardinality). But |A_i∪B_j| = i+j requires A_i∩B_j = ∅. So this argument is circular if it later derives A_i∩B_j = ∅ from S_{ij} = A_i∪B_j. ✗\n   457\t\n   458\t### Example 5: Correct handling of the degree-n condition in interpolation\n   459\t\n   460\t**Claim:** \"The solution space of n homogeneous equations in n+1 unknowns has dimension ≥ 1. To ensure a solution with aₙ ≠ 0 exists: if every solution had aₙ = 0, then the solution space would lie in the hyperplane {aₙ = 0}. But the constraint equations are: for each pair {iₖ,jₖ}: Σₘ aₘ(xᵢₖᵐ + xⱼₖᵐ) = 0. The coefficient of aₙ in the k-th equation is xᵢₖⁿ + xⱼₖⁿ. If all these were 0, then xᵢₖⁿ = -xⱼₖⁿ for all k, requiring xᵢₖ = -xⱼₖ (for n odd) or |xᵢₖ| = |xⱼₖ| (for n even). Since our points are arbitrary, this is generically not the case; and even when it happens for some pair, at least one equation has nonzero coefficient of aₙ, giving a solution with aₙ free. In any specific case, one verifies directly.\"\n   461\t\n   462\t**Analysis:** This argument correctly handles the degree-n condition, noting that the case xᵢₖⁿ+xⱼₖⁿ=0 for all k corresponds to very special configurations, and in general (or by choosing an appropriate matching) at least one equation has nonzero coefficient of aₙ. ✓\n   463\t\n   464\t### Example 6: Symmetric sum identity verification\n   465\t\n   466\t**Claim:** (x-y)²+(y-z)²+(z-x)² = 2(S₁²-3S₂) where S₁ = x+y+z and S₂ = xy+yz+zx.\n   467\t\n   468\t**Verification:** LHS = (x²-2xy+y²)+(y²-2yz+z²)+(z²-2zx+x²)\n   469\t= 2(x²+y²+z²) - 2(xy+yz+zx)\n   470\t= 2(S₁²-2S₂) - 2S₂\n   471\t= 2S₁²-4S₂-2S₂\n   472\t= 2S₁²-6S₂\n   473\t= 2(S₁²-3S₂) ✓\n   474\t\n   475\tThis computation is simple and should not be \"skipped\" in a proof without verification. A proof that states this identity as \"one checks\" is acceptable since the calculation is brief. ✓\n   476\t\n   477\t\n   478\t---\n   479\t\n   480\t## Appendix A: Extended Examples for Algebra and Analysis Proof Evaluation\n   481\t\n   482\t### A.1 Inequality Proofs — 20 Scenarios\n   483\t\n   484\t**Scenario I1 (Correct — AM-GM cascade).** \"sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) <= n/(2s) * sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j.\"\n   485\tProof: Normalize s=1. Then need 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) <= n*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j.\n   486\tRewrite LHS: 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) = 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j*(1-sum_{k!=i,j}a_k)/(a_i+a_j) [using s=1]\n   487\t= 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) + 2*sum_{i<j} sum_{k!=i,j} a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j) [expand: 2*a_i*a_j = 2*a_i*a_j*(a_i+a_j+rest)/(a_i+a_j)]\n   488\tActually: a_i+a_j+sum_{k!=i,j}a_k = s = 1, so a_i*a_j = a_i*a_j*(a_i+a_j)/(a_i+a_j) + ...\n   489\tBetter: 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j) = 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j/1 - 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j*(s-(a_i+a_j))/(a_i+a_j)\n   490\t= 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j - 2*sum_{i<j} sum_{k!=i,j} a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j).\n   491\tRHS n*sum a_i*a_j = 2*sum a_i*a_j + (n-2)*sum a_i*a_j.\n   492\tSo need: 2*sum a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j) <= (n-2)/2 * sum a_i*a_j.\n   493\tThen sum_{i<j} sum_{k!=i,j} = sum_{i<j<k} (sum over 3 pairs) = 3*sum_{i<j<k}.\n   494\tKey inequality (per triple): a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j) + cyclic <= (1/2)*(a_i*a_j+a_i*a_k+a_j*a_k).\n   495\tBy AM-GM: 2*a_i*a_j*a_k/(a_i+a_j) <= a_k*(a_i+a_j)/2. Apply cyclically and add. ✓\n   496\t\n   497\t**Scenario I2 (Correct — normalization valid).** \"Since both sides of the inequality are homogeneous degree 1 in a_1,...,a_n, we may WLOG normalize sum a_i = 1.\"\n   498\tCORRECT if both LHS and RHS are degree 1. LHS = sum a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j): degree 2-1=1. ✓ RHS = n/(2s)*sum a_i*a_j: degree -1+0+2=1. ✓ Normalization is valid. ✓\n   499\t\n   500\t**Scenario I3 (Incorrect — wrong degree).** \"Both sides are degree 2 so normalize a_1+...+a_n=1.\"\n   501\tINCORRECT: As verified above, both sides are degree 1, not 2. A degree-2 homogeneous inequality would normalize differently (e.g., sum a_i^2=1 or max a_i=1). Using sum=1 with degree 1 is correct, but the stated \"degree 2\" is wrong. First material issue: wrong degree claim.\n   502\t\n   503\t**Scenario I4 (Correct — per-triple AM-GM).** \"For any triple (a,b,c): 2abc/(a+b) <= c(a+b)/2.\"\n   504\tProof: From AM-GM: (a+b)^2 >= 4ab, so ab/(a+b) <= (a+b)/4. Multiply by 2c: 2abc/(a+b) <= c(a+b)/2. ✓\n   505\t\n   506\t**Scenario I5 (Correct — cyclic sum).** \"Adding 2abc/(a+b) <= c(a+b)/2 and the two cyclic permutations:\n   507\t2abc/(a+b)+2abc/(a+c)+2abc/(b+c) <= c(a+b)/2 + b(a+c)/2 + a(b+c)/2.\"\n   508\tRHS = (c*a+c*b+b*a+b*c+a*b+a*c)/2 = (2ab+2bc+2ca)/2 = ab+bc+ca.\n   509\tLHS/2 = abc/(a+b)+abc/(a+c)+abc/(b+c) <= (ab+bc+ca)/2. ✓\n   510\t\n   511\t**Scenario I6 (Incorrect — wrong cycle).** \"Cycle (a,b,c) -> (b,c,a) -> (c,a,b) gives same inequality thrice.\"\n   512\tNOT the same inequality: applying to (a,b,c): 2abc/(a+b) term. Applying to (b,c,a): 2bca/(b+c) term. These are DIFFERENT terms. The cyclic sum gives THREE distinct terms, not the same one thrice. Minor error if it leads to correct final sum, major if used as justification for tripling a single term.\n   513\t\n   514\t**Scenario I7 (Correct — degree bound check).** \"For P(t) = a_n*t^n + ..., as y -> infinity with z = (x+y)/(2xy-1) -> 1/(2x):\n   515\tLHS of (*) = 2(x*P(x) + y*P(y) + z*P(z)) ~ 2*y*a_n*y^n = 2*a_n*y^{n+1}.\n   516\tRHS of (*) = (x+y+z)*(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)) ~ y*(a_n*(-y)^n + a_n*y^n + O(1)) = a_n*((-1)^n+1)*y^{n+1}.\"\n   517\tCORRECT computation. Leading terms match when 2a_n = a_n*((-1)^n+1), i.e., 2 = (-1)^n+1. So (-1)^n = 1, n even. ✓\n   518\t\n   519\t**Scenario I8 (Incorrect — wrong parity conclusion).** \"From 2a_n = a_n*((-1)^n+1): if n is odd, (-1)^n=-1, so (-1)^n+1=0, giving 2a_n=0, so a_n=0. Hence n is ODD.\"\n   520\tINCORRECT: n is odd gives a_n=0, contradiction (a_n != 0). So n must be EVEN, not odd. The conclusion \"n is odd\" is backwards from the correct conclusion \"n is even (or a_n=0).\"\n   521\t\n   522\t**Scenario I9 (Correct — coefficient of y^n).** \"After establishing n=2 (from y^{n+1} matching), the coefficient of y^n gives 2*a_{n-1} = a_n*(2-n)*(x+1/(2x)) for all x. Since RHS depends on x but LHS doesn't, the coefficient of x and 1/x must vanish. This forces 2-n=0, giving n=2.\"\n   523\tCORRECT. The constraint 2a_1 = a_2*(2-n)*(x+1/(2x)) for all x != 0 requires a_2*(2-n) = 0. Since a_2 != 0, 2-n = 0, so n=2. ✓\n   524\t\n   525\t**Scenario I10 (Correct — full degree bound argument).** The complete argument:\n   526\t1. P has degree n with leading coefficient a_n != 0.\n   527\t2. Expand both sides of (*) as y -> infinity, z -> 1/(2x).\n   528\t3. Coefficient of y^{n+1}: 2a_n = a_n*((-1)^n+1). This requires (-1)^n = 1, so n even.\n   529\t4. Coefficient of y^n: 2a_{n-1} = a_n*(2-n)*(x+1/(2x)) for all x.\n   530\t5. RHS depends on x unless a_n*(2-n) = 0. Since a_n != 0, 2-n=0, n=2.\n   531\tCORRECT and complete. ✓\n   532\t\n   533\t### A.2 Polynomial Functional Equations — 15 Scenarios\n   534\t\n   535\t**Scenario P1 (Correct — substitution for degree bound).** \"Set y -> infinity, x fixed, z=(x+y)/(2xy-1) -> 1/(2x). Expand both sides of 2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) = S_1*(P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x)).\"\n   536\tCORRECT setup. z -> 1/(2x) as y -> infinity (since z=(x+y)/(2xy-1)=(1/y+1)/(2x-1/y) -> 1/(2x)). ✓\n   537\t\n   538\t**Scenario P2 (Correct — symmetric sum identity).** \"(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2 = 2(x^2+y^2+z^2) - 2(xy+yz+zx) = 2(S_1^2-3S_2).\"\n   539\tExpand: (x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2 = 2x^2+2y^2+2z^2-2xy-2yz-2zx = 2(S_1^2-2S_2)-2S_2 = 2S_1^2-6S_2 = 2(S_1^2-3S_2). ✓\n   540\t\n   541\t**Scenario P3 (Correct — linear term vanishes).** \"(x-y)+(y-z)+(z-x) = 0.\"\n   542\tTrivially: x-y+y-z+z-x = 0. ✓ So the linear terms of P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x) always vanish.\n   543\t\n   544\t**Scenario P4 (Correct — coefficient extraction).** \"Setting P(t)=at^2+bt+c, LHS:\n   545\t2(xP(x)+yP(y)+zP(z)) = 2[a(x^3+y^3+z^3)+b(x^2+y^2+z^2)+c(x+y+z)]\n   546\t= 2a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+3S_3)+2b(S_1^2-2S_2)+2cS_1.\"\n   547\tCORRECT using standard symmetric sum identities. With S_3=S_1/2:\n   548\t= 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3aS_1+2bS_1^2-4bS_2+2cS_1. ✓\n   549\t\n   550\t**Scenario P5 (Correct — RHS computation).** \"RHS = S_1[2a(S_1^2-3S_2)+0+3c] = 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3cS_1.\"\n   551\tSince P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x) = a*2(S_1^2-3S_2)+b*0+3c = 2a(S_1^2-3S_2)+3c.\n   552\tMultiply by S_1: 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3cS_1. ✓\n   553\t\n   554\t**Scenario P6 (Correct — coefficient matching).** \"LHS=RHS:\n   555\t2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3aS_1+2bS_1^2-4bS_2+2cS_1 = 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2+3cS_1.\n   556\tCancel 2aS_1^3-6aS_1S_2:\n   557\t3aS_1+2bS_1^2-4bS_2+2cS_1 = 3cS_1.\n   558\tCoefficient of S_1^2: 2b=0, so b=0.\n   559\tCoefficient of S_2: -4b=0. ✓ (consistent)\n   560\tCoefficient of S_1: 3a+2c=3c, so 3a=c, c=3a.\"\n   561\tCORRECT. ✓\n   562\t\n   563\t**Scenario P7 (Incorrect — wrong identity).** \"x^3+y^3+z^3 = (x+y+z)^3 - 3(x+y+z)(xy+yz+zx).\"\n   564\tINCORRECT: x^3+y^3+z^3 = S_1^3-3S_1S_2+3S_3, not S_1^3-3S_1S_2 (missing 3S_3). First material issue.\n   565\t\n   566\t**Scenario P8 (Correct — verification).** \"P(t)=a(t^2+3): verify the original equation.\n   567\tLHS: P(x)/yz+P(y)/zx+P(z)/xy = a[(x^2+3)/yz+(y^2+3)/zx+(z^2+3)/xy].\n   568\tMultiply by xyz=S_3=S_1/2: a[x(x^2+3)+y(y^2+3)+z(z^2+3)] = a[x^3+y^3+z^3+3(x+y+z)] = a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+3S_1/2+3S_1).\n   569\tRHS: P(x-y)+P(y-z)+P(z-x) = a[(x-y)^2+3+(y-z)^2+3+(z-x)^2+3] = a[2(S_1^2-3S_2)+9].\n   570\tMultiply by xyz=S_1/2: a*S_1/2*[2(S_1^2-3S_2)+9] = a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+9S_1/2).\n   571\tDo these match? LHS gives a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+3S_1/2+3S_1) = a(S_1^3-3S_1S_2+9S_1/2). ✓\"\n   572\t\n   573\t**Scenario P9 (Correct — degree 0 and 1 solutions).** \"P=0 (k=0) is a solution: 0/yz+0/zx+0/xy = 0+0+0. ✓ This corresponds to a=0.\"\n   574\tCORRECT. P=0 is the k=0 case of P(t)=k(t^2+3). ✓\n   575\t\n   576\t### A.3 Optimization and Analysis — 12 Scenarios\n   577\t\n   578\t**Scenario OA1 (Incorrect — missing existence proof).** \"The minimum of f over domain D is attained at the critical point x_0.\"\n   579\tMISSING: Must verify D is compact (Weierstrass) or that f is coercive (f -> infinity as |x| -> infinity in D) to guarantee the minimum is attained.\n   580\t\n   581\t**Scenario OA2 (Correct — compact domain).** \"The domain D = {(a,b,c) : a+b+c=1, a,b,c>=0} is compact (closed and bounded in R^3). By Weierstrass, any continuous f attains its minimum on D.\"\n   582\tCORRECT. D is the simplex, which is compact. ✓\n   583\t\n   584\t**Scenario OA3 (Incorrect — wrong critical point).** \"Setting f'(x)=0 gives x^2=1, so x=1.\"\n   585\tINCORRECT: x^2=1 has two solutions, x=1 and x=-1. Both must be checked to find the minimum. Missing x=-1 is a gap.\n   586\t\n   587\t**Scenario OA4 (Correct — second derivative test).** \"f''(x_0)>0 implies x_0 is a local minimum.\"\n   588\tCORRECT. For twice-differentiable f, f''(x_0)>0 implies x_0 is a strict local minimum. ✓\n   589\t\n   590\t**Scenario OA5 (Incorrect — skipped computation).** \"Critical computations are skipped, w.r.t. deriving the minimum value.\"\n   591\tThis is an example of the first material issue in optimization proofs where critical computations are skipped. The minimum value must be derived explicitly, not just stated. ✓\n   592\t\n   593\t**Scenario OA6 (Correct — coercivity argument).** \"As any variable tends to 0 or infinity with the constraint a+b+c=1, f(a,b,c) tends to +infinity. Therefore the minimum of f is attained in the interior of D.\"\n   594\tCORRECT structure. Must verify the claimed coercivity for the specific f in question.\n   595\t\n   596\t**Scenario OA7 (Correct — compactness argument variant).** \"Since f is continuous and D_R = {x in D : f(x) <= R} is compact for any R, the infimum is attained on D_R, hence globally.\"\n   597\tCORRECT if D_R is indeed compact for some R (compact sublevel sets). This is equivalent to coercivity.\n   598\t\n   599\t**Scenario OA8 (Incorrect — non-compact domain used as compact).** \"The set {(x,y) : x>=0, y>=0, xy=1} is compact.\"\n   600\tINCORRECT: this hyperbola is closed and unbounded, hence not compact. Claiming it's compact is the first material issue.\n   601\t\n   602\t**Scenario OA9 (Correct — finiteness of infimum).** \"Since f(x,y) >= 0 for x,y in D (trivially, as f is a sum of squares), the infimum is >= 0. Since f(0,0)=0, the infimum is 0 and is attained.\"\n   603\tCORRECT. Infimum >= 0 (bounded below) + attained at (0,0) = minimum = 0. ✓\n   604\t\n   605\t**Scenario OA10 (Incorrect — wrong argument regarding minima).** \"The arguments regarding finiteness of minima are incorrect.\" (a common first material issue in analysis proofs involving incorrect compactness reasoning)\n   606\tThis is a description of a first material issue: a proof that claims certain minima are finite using incorrect compactness reasoning would fail here.\n   607\t\n   608\t### A.4 Polynomial Interpolation — 8 Scenarios\n   609\t\n   610\t**Scenario PI1 (Correct — dimension count).** \"n homogeneous equations in n+1 unknowns (a_0,...,a_n) have a nonzero solution by rank-nullity.\"\n   611\tCORRECT: rank of n x (n+1) system is at most n, so null space has dimension >= 1, giving a nonzero solution. ✓\n   612\t\n   613\t**Scenario PI2 (Correct — degree exactly n).** \"To find solution with a_n != 0: if all solutions had a_n=0, the constraint vectors would all be orthogonal to e_{n+1}. This would mean x_{i_k}^n + x_{j_k}^n = 0 for all k, forcing |x_{i_k}| = |x_{j_k}| for n even, or x_{i_k} = -x_{j_k} for n odd. In general position this fails, so a solution with a_n != 0 exists.\"\n   614\tCORRECT in general. ✓\n   615\t\n   616\t**Scenario PI3 (Correct — multiset equality check).** \"With Q(x_{i_k})+Q(x_{j_k})=0: P(x_{i_k}) = -Q(x_{i_k}) = Q(x_{j_k}) and P(x_{j_k}) = -Q(x_{j_k}) = Q(x_{i_k}). So {P(x_i)} = {Q(x_i)} as multisets.\"\n   617\tFor each pair {i_k,j_k}: P takes values -Q(x_{i_k}) and -Q(x_{j_k}) = Q(x_{i_k}) and Q(x_{j_k}) respectively... wait.\n   618\tP(x_{i_k}) = -Q(x_{i_k}) = Q(x_{j_k}) (using Q(x_{i_k})+Q(x_{j_k})=0).\n   619\tP(x_{j_k}) = -Q(x_{j_k}) = Q(x_{i_k}).\n   620\tSo: {P(x_{i_k}), P(x_{j_k})} = {Q(x_{j_k}), Q(x_{i_k})} = {Q(x_{i_k}), Q(x_{j_k})}. ✓\n   621\tSumming over all k: {P(x_i) : i} = {Q(x_i) : i} as multisets. ✓\n   622\t\n   623\t**Scenario PI4 (Correct — perfect matching existence).** \"A perfect matching on 2n points always exists (pair them arbitrarily in n pairs).\"\n   624\tCORRECT. Key properties:\n    52\t- Simple graph: no multi-edges, no self-loops\n    53\t- Complete graph K_n: every pair of vertices connected\n    54\t- Bipartite graph K_{m,n}: vertices split into two groups, edges only between groups\n    55\t- Tree: connected graph with no cycles; has exactly n-1 edges for n vertices\n    56\t\n    57\t**Pigeonhole principle:** If n objects are placed in k bins and n > k, at least one bin has at least ⌈n/k⌉ objects.\n    58\t\n    59\t**Handshaking lemma:** Σ_{v∈V} deg(v) = 2|E|.\n    60\t\n    61\t### 2.2 Matchings and Hall's Theorem\n    62\t\n    63\tA **matching** in a bipartite graph is a set of edges with no shared vertices.\n    64\t\n    65\t**Hall's marriage theorem:** A bipartite graph G = (A∪B, E) has a matching saturating all of A if and only if for every subset S ⊆ A, |N(S)| ≥ |S| (where N(S) is the neighborhood of S in B).\n    66\t\n    67\t**Perfect matching:** Matches every vertex. Key properties:\n    78\t- |B_n| = 2^n\n    79\t- Ranked by cardinality: rank k level has C(n,k) elements\n    80\t- Graded poset with n+1 ranks\n    81\t\n    82\t**Intervals in the Boolean lattice:** For A ⊆ B ⊆ S, the interval [A,B] = {C : A⊆C⊆B} is isomorphic to B_{|B|-|A|} and has 2^{|B|-|A|} elements.\n    83\t\n    84\t### 3.2 Chains and Antichains\n    85\t\n    86\tA **chain** is a totally ordered subset (any two elements comparable). A **antichain** is a set of mutually incomparable elements (no containments).\n    87\t\n    88\t**Dilworth's theorem:** The minimum number of chains needed to cover the poset equals the maximum antichain size.\n    89\t\n    90\t**Sperner's theorem:** The maximum antichain in B_n has size C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) (take all subsets of size ⌊n/2⌋).\n    91\t\n    92\t### 3.3 Multiplicative Functions on the Boolean Lattice\n    93\t\n    94\tA function f: 2^S → ℝ is **multiplicative** over (∪, ∩) if f(T₁)·f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·f(T₁∩T₂) for all T₁,T₂ ⊆ S.\n    95\t\n    96\tThis is a strong structural condition. Not every function satisfying this for \"many pairs\" satisfies it for all pairs.\n    97\t\n    98\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof that f satisfies the multiplicative condition must verify it for ALL pairs (T₁, T₂), not just specific families. The verification \"one checks by routine computation\" is a placeholder that must be backed by an actual argument. If the proof leaves this verification implicit and it is genuinely non-trivial, this constitutes a critical skipped step.\n    99\t\n   100\t**Characterization theorem:** The non-negative functions f: 2^S → ℝ satisfying f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) are exactly those of the form f(T) = 2^{|T∩A|} for some A⊆S (when f(∅)=1), or f(T) = χ_{[U,U∪A']}(T) extended multiplicatively (when f(∅)=0).\n   101\t\n   102\t### 3.4 Möbius Inversion on the Boolean Lattice\n   103\t\n   104\tThe Möbius function for the Boolean lattice B_n is μ(A,B) = (-1)^{|B|-|A|} for A ⊆ B.\n   105\t\n   106\t**Inversion formula:** If g(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} f(U) for all T, then f(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} g(U).\n   107\t\n   108\t**Application to blue-set counting:** If f(T) = #{blue subsets of T}, then the indicator of whether T itself is blue is:\n   109\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} f(U)\n   110\t\n   111\tThis is the Möbius inversion of f (where f(T) = Σ_{U∈B, U⊆T} 1 = Σ_{U⊆T} 1_B(U) is the cumulative count).\n   112\t\n   113\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof using Möbius inversion must correctly state and apply the inversion formula. An error in the formula (wrong signs, wrong indexing) is a material issue. However, the inversion step itself is \"routine\" and may be cited as a known fact without re-proof in a competition context.\n   114\t\n   115\t---\n   116\t\n   117\t## Part IV: Extremal Combinatorics\n   118\t\n   119\t### 4.1 Optimization with Distinct Elements\n   120\t\n   121\t**Basic setup:** Given n distinct positive integers a₁ < a₂ < ... < aₙ, find the minimum value of max(Σ_{i∈I} aᵢ) or other extremal quantities subject to conditions on subset sums.\n   122\t\n   123\t**Key principle:** For k-element subsets, the one with the largest sum consists of the k largest elements {a_{n-k+1}, ..., aₙ}. The one with the smallest sum consists of the k smallest elements {a₁, ..., aₖ}.\n   124\t\n   125\t**Common technique:** Set a_{m} = c (the \"median\" element), then use inequalities:\n   126\t- a_{m-1} ≤ c-1, a_{m-2} ≤ c-2, ..., a_{m-k} ≤ c-k\n   127\t- a_{m+1} ≥ c+1, a_{m+2} ≥ c+2, ..., a_{m+k} ≥ c+k\n   128\t\n   129\tThese give lower and upper bounds on partial sums, which then constrain the possible values of c.\n   130\t\n   131\t### 4.2 Minimality Arguments\n   132\t\n   133\t**Technique:** To show that a minimum value of some parameter is N:\n   134\t1. **Existence:** Construct a configuration achieving the value N\n   135\t2. **Lower bound:** Show no configuration achieves a value less than N\n   136\t\n   137\tFor (1), the construction must be verified to satisfy ALL the problem's conditions. For (2), the argument must work for GENERAL configurations satisfying the problem's conditions, not just special cases.\n   138\t\n   139\t**Evaluation criterion:** A proof that omits the existence direction (just shows the lower bound) proves an upper bound on the minimum, not the minimum itself. A proof that omits the lower bound just gives an example. Both directions are REQUIRED for a complete proof.\n   140\t\n   141\t### 4.3 The Role of Strict vs Non-Strict Inequalities\n   142\t\n   143\tWhen bounding a sum sum_{i=1}^k a_i ≤ kc - k(k+1)/2 (where c is the (k+1)-th element and the elements are distinct integers), the bound comes from:\n   144\ta₁ ≤ c-k, a₂ ≤ c-k+1, ..., aₖ ≤ c-1, so sum ≤ Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ (c-k+i-1) = kc - k(k+1)/2.\n   145\t\n   146\tThis is a UPPER BOUND. The lower bound for a_{k+1},...,a_{2k} uses: a_{k+1+j} ≥ c+j for j=1,...,k.\n   147\t\n   148\t**Evaluation criterion:** Strict vs non-strict inequalities can change the answer by 1. In a minimality problem, if the minimum involves \"≥\" vs \">\" or \"=\" vs \"≤\", check that the proof's inequalities are of the right type.\n   149\t\n   150\t---\n   151\t\n   152\t## Part V: Combinatorial Designs and Constructions\n   153\t\n   154\t### 5.1 Existence Proofs via Explicit Construction\n   155\t\n   156\tWhen a problem asks to show a configuration exists with given properties, the proof must:\n   157\t1. Exhibit an explicit configuration\n   158\t2. Verify EVERY required property for that configuration\n   159\t3. (If asking for minimum) show no smaller/fewer configuration satisfies all properties\n   160\t\n   161\t**Common error:** Exhibiting a configuration and checking only a subset of the required properties, assuming the rest hold.\n   162\t\n   163\t### 5.2 General vs Special Case\n   164\t\n   165\tIf a problem asks to show that for all n (or all k), some property holds, the proof must work for GENERAL n (or k). A proof that only handles specific cases (e.g., n = 1, 2, 3) and extrapolates without justification has a critical gap.\n   166\t\n   167\t**Evaluation criterion:** If the proof shows existence/construction for specific values and claims \"similarly for other values\" or \"by analogous argument,\" check whether the argument is genuinely analogous. If the analogous argument requires non-trivial new ideas, citing it without providing it is a gap.\n   168\t\n   169\t### 5.3 Counting Configurations\n   170\t\n   171\tWhen counting configurations with multiple constraints:\n   172\t\n   173\t**Strategy 1 (Sequential):** Count the number of ways to make each choice in sequence, multiplying at each step (only if choices are independent or conditional counts are computed).\n   174\t\n   175\t**Strategy 2 (Characterize then count):** First show all valid configurations have a specific structural form, then count that form.\n   176\t\n   177\t**Evaluation criterion for Strategy 2:** The \"characterize\" step must be bidirectional:\n   178\t- (⇒) Every valid configuration has the claimed form\n   179\t- (⇐) Every configuration of the claimed form is valid\n   180\t\n   181\tMissing either direction means the count is wrong (either over-counting or under-counting).\n   182\t\n   183\t---\n   184\t\n   185\t## Part VI: Set Systems and Monotone Functions\n   186\t\n   187\t### 6.1 Intersecting Families\n   188\t\n   189\tA family F of sets is **intersecting** if any two members of F have a non-empty intersection. Equivalently, no two members are disjoint.\n   190\t\n   191\t**Key result:** Any intersecting antichain in 2^S has size ≤ C(n-1, ⌊(n-1)/2⌋) (Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem for uniform families).\n   192\t\n   193\tIn the context of proof evaluation, an intersecting family arises naturally from functional conditions like f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) with f(∅) = 0: this forces any two sets in the support of f to intersect.\n   194\t\n   195\t### 6.2 Upward-Closed and Downward-Closed Families\n   196\t\n   197\tA family F is **upward-closed (upset)** if whenever A ∈ F and A ⊆ B ⊆ S, then B ∈ F.\n   198\tA family F is **downward-closed (downset)** if whenever A ∈ F and B ⊆ A, then B ∈ F.\n   199\t\n   200\t**Evaluation criterion:** When a proof concludes that the support of a function is upward-closed from F = {T : T ⊇ U} for some minimal element U, this conclusion requires verifying:\n   201\t- U is indeed in F (f(U) > 0)\n   202\t- U is minimal in F (f(V) = 0 for all proper subsets V ⊊ U)\n   203\t- Any superset of U is in F (f(T) > 0 for all T ⊇ U)\n   204\t\n   205\tThe third point requires explicit verification from the functional condition.\n   206\t\n   207\t### 6.3 Chains in the Boolean Lattice and Order Ideals\n   208\t\n   209\tA **chain** A₀ ⊂ A₁ ⊂ ... ⊂ Aₙ with |Aᵢ| = i is called a **maximal chain** in B_n (since it has length n+1, the maximum possible). The number of maximal chains in B_n is n! (corresponding to the n! orderings of the elements of S).\n   210\t\n   211\t**Application:** When counting pairs of disjoint chains (A₀ ⊂ A₁ ⊂ ... ⊂ Aₙ) and (B₀ ⊂ B₁ ⊂ ... ⊂ Bₙ) with A_n ∩ B_n = ∅ in B_{2n}:\n   212\t1. Choose A_n: C(2n, n) ways (any n-element subset)\n   213\t2. B_n is forced (= complement of A_n since |B_n| = n and A_n ∩ B_n = ∅ and A_n ∪ B_n = {1,...,2n} when n+n = 2n)\n   214\t3. Build the chain inside A_n: n! ways\n   215\t4. Build the chain inside B_n: n! ways\n   216\tTotal: C(2n,n)·n!·n! = (2n)!\n   217\t\n   218\t---\n   219\t\n   220\t## Part VII: Common Proof Structures in Combinatorics Problems\n   221\t\n   222\t### 7.1 Greedy Arguments\n   223\t\n   224\tA greedy algorithm makes locally optimal choices. A greedy proof must:\n   225\t1. Define the greedy choice precisely\n   226\t2. Show the greedy choice doesn't preclude future valid choices (exchange argument or augmenting path argument)\n   227\t3. Show the result of the greedy algorithm has the required properties\n   228\t\n   229\t**Common error:** Assuming greedy is optimal without proving the exchange argument.\n   230\t\n   231\t### 7.2 Induction on Problem Parameters\n   232\t\n   233\t**Base case:** Verify the claim for the smallest valid parameter (n=1, k=0, etc.).\n   234\t\n   235\t**Inductive step:** Assume the claim for all values ≤ n-1, prove for n. The reduction from n to n-1 (or n-k) must be carefully justified.\n   236\t\n   237\t**Evaluation criterion:** If the inductive step says \"apply the induction hypothesis,\" verify that:\n   238\t- The hypothesis applies (the smaller problem satisfies the induction's hypotheses)\n   239\t- The conclusion for the smaller problem correctly implies the conclusion for the larger\n   240\t\n   241\t### 7.3 Extremal Arguments\n   242\t\n   243\t**Setup:** Take an element/configuration with a specific extremal property (minimal, maximal, etc.).\n   244\t\n   245\t**Technique:** Use the extremality to derive structural properties.\n   246\t\n   247\t**Evaluation criterion:** If a proof takes a \"minimal element U in the support of f\" (for example), it must verify that such a minimal element exists (the support is non-empty) and that minimality gives the claimed structure.\n   248\t\n   249\t### 7.4 Bijective Proofs\n   250\t\n   251\tA bijection between two sets proves they have the same cardinality. A bijective proof must:\n   252\t1. Define the map explicitly\n   253\t2. Show it is well-defined (maps valid objects to valid objects)\n   254\t3. Show it is injective (different inputs give different outputs)\n   255\t4. Show it is surjective (every valid output is achieved)\n   256\t\n   257\t**Alternative:** Show the map is a bijection by finding a two-sided inverse.\n   258\t\n   259\t---\n   260\t\n   261\t## Part VIII: Specific Problem Type Guidance\n   262\t\n   263\t### 8.1 Coloring Problems with Multiplicative Condition (proof_13 type)\n   264\t\n   265\t**Problem type:** Color subsets of S blue or red, count colorings where f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)f(T₁∩T₂) for all T₁,T₂ ⊆ S.\n   266\t\n   267\t**Standard case split:** f(∅) = 1 (empty set is blue) vs f(∅) = 0 (empty set is red).\n   268\t\n   269\t**Case 1 (f(∅)=1):**\n   270\t- For i ∉ T: apply functional condition with T₁ = {i}, T₂ = T to get f({i})·f(T) = f(T∪{i})·f(∅) = f(T∪{i})\n   271\t- This gives f(T∪{i}) = λᵢ·f(T) where λᵢ = f({i})\n   272\t- By induction: f(T) = Π_{i∈T} λᵢ = Π_{i∈T} f({i})\n   273\t- Möbius inversion then recovers the blue sets exactly as subsets of A = {i : λᵢ = 2}\n   274\t- Converse: verify that coloring B = P(A) satisfies the multiplicativity for all T₁, T₂\n   275\t\n   276\t**Critical verification in Case 1 (often skipped):** The Möbius inversion step gives the blue set indicator, but one must verify that this formula gives 0 or 1 (not other values), and that the resulting B satisfies the original multiplicativity. This computation is:\n   277\t\n   278\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} f(U) = Σ_{U⊆T} (-1)^{|T|-|U|} · 2^{|U∩A|}\n   279\t\n   280\tLet T∩A = T_A and T\\A = T_B. For U ⊆ T: U = U_A ∪ U_B with U_A ⊆ T_A and U_B ⊆ T_B. Then:\n   281\t\n   282\t1_B(T) = Σ_{U_A⊆T_A, U_B⊆T_B} (-1)^{|T_A|+|T_B|-|U_A|-|U_B|} · 2^{|U_A|}\n   283\t        = [Σ_{U_A⊆T_A} (-1)^{|T_A|-|U_A|} 2^{|U_A|}] · [Σ_{U_B⊆T_B} (-1)^{|T_B|-|U_B|}]\n   284\t\n   285\tThe second factor = Σ_{k=0}^{|T_B|} C(|T_B|,k)(-1)^{|T_B|-k} = (1-1)^{|T_B|} = 0^{|T_B|}.\n   286\t\n   287\tSo 1_B(T) = 0 if |T_B| > 0, i.e., if T ⊄ A.\n   288\tIf T ⊆ A, then T_B = ∅, so 1_B(T) = Σ_{U_A⊆T_A} (-1)^{|T_A|-|U_A|} 2^{|U_A|} = (2-1)^{|T_A|} = 1.\n   289\t\n   290\tSo 1_B(T) = 1 if T ⊆ A and 0 otherwise, i.e., B = P(A). ✓\n   291\t\n   292\t**This computation verifies Case 1.** A proof that only claims \"one checks\" without this computation has a minor omission (the computation is straightforward).\n   293\t\n   294\t**Case 2 (f(∅)=0):** \n   295\t- Functional condition with T₂ disjoint from T₁: f(T₁)f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·f(∅) = 0\n   296\t- So for any T₁, T₂ in the support of f, T₁∩T₂ ≠ ∅ (support is intersecting)\n   297\t- Take minimal element U in support; show f(U) = 1, B∩P(U) = {U}, support = {T : T⊇U}\n   298\t- Reduce to Case 1 on S' = S\\U via g(W) = f(U∪W)\n   299\t- Converse: verify that any interval [U, U∪A'] satisfies multiplicativity for ALL pairs T₁, T₂ ⊆ S\n   300\t\n   301\t**Critical gap in Case 2 converse:** If the proof claims \"one checks that [U, U∪A'] satisfies the condition\" without doing the check, and the check is non-trivial, this is a critical skipped step.\n   302\t\n   303\t**The check:** For B = [U, U∪A'], we have f(T) = g(T\\U)·χ_{T⊇U}(T) where g(W) = 2^{|W∩A'|}. For arbitrary T₁, T₂ ⊆ S:\n   304\t- If T₁ ⊅ U or T₂ ⊅ U: then at least one of f(T₁), f(T₂) equals 0. Also T₁∪T₂ may or may not ⊇ U, and T₁∩T₂ ⊇ U only if both T₁,T₂ ⊇ U (which fails). So at least one of f(T₁∪T₂), f(T₁∩T₂) = 0. The condition 0·f(T₂) = f(T₁∪T₂)·0 becomes 0 = 0 or 0 = 0. ✓\n   305\t- If T₁ ⊇ U and T₂ ⊇ U: then T₁∪T₂ ⊇ U and T₁∩T₂ ⊇ U. Let W₁ = T₁\\U, W₂ = T₂\\U. Then f(Tᵢ) = g(Wᵢ) = 2^{|Wᵢ∩A'|} and similarly. The condition becomes g(W₁)g(W₂) = g(W₁∪W₂)g(W₁∩W₂), i.e., 2^{|W₁∩A'|}·2^{|W₂∩A'|} = 2^{|(W₁∪W₂)∩A'|}·2^{|(W₁∩W₂)∩A'|}. This holds because |W₁∩A'|+|W₂∩A'| = |(W₁∩A')∪(W₂∩A')|+|(W₁∩A')∩(W₂∩A')| = |(W₁∪W₂)∩A'|+|(W₁∩W₂)∩A'| (using |A|+|B| = |A∪B|+|A∩B| for any finite sets). ✓\n   306\t\n   307\tSo the converse IS valid and checkable — but it requires this computation. The proof's \"one checks by routine verification\" is in fact routine (as shown above).
